page.mentor_intro: Gram-negative bloodstream infection is one of the settings where antimicrobial stewardship has most visibly shortened therapy. A decade of non-inferiority trials and meta-analyses now supports 7-day courses for many patients, while multidrug-resistant organisms remain the key evidence gap.

teaching_points.claim: A 2025 systematic review and noninferiority meta-analysis of randomized trials found 7 days of antibiotics noninferior to 14 days for gram-negative bloodstream infection in hospitalized adults.

IDSA's 2025 complicated-UTI guideline suggests 5-7 days of a fluoroquinolone or 7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone when the patient is improving on effective therapy, regardless of associated gram-negative bacteremia.
In Enterobacteriaceae bacteremia, meta-analysis showed no significant difference between short (<=10 days) and longer courses for 30- and 90-day mortality, clinical cure, or relapse.
Short courses are consistently noninferior when the diagnosis is confirmed, the antimicrobial is appropriate, and the patient shows clinical improvement.

For MDR gram-negatives (CRE, difficult-to-treat Pseudomonas, CRAB), IDSA and ESCMID give explicit agent-selection advice but lack detailed duration recommendations; evidence for short courses is limited here.

uncertainties: Optimal duration for carbapenem-resistant organisms and difficult-to-treat Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia.
How source control status should modify the 7-day default.
mcq_angles: Seven versus fourteen days: what the noninferiority meta-analysis supports and its boundaries.
cUTI with gram-negative bacteremia: translating the IDSA 5-7/7-day recommendation to a clinical vignette.
Which patients qualify for short-course therapy (confirmed diagnosis, effective agent, improving).
The MDR-GNB duration evidence gap versus agent-selection guidance.
case_hooks: E. coli bacteremia from pyelonephritis, afebrile and improving on day 3 - stop at day 7?
Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia in a stable patient - how long, and on what evidence?
page.gaps: Pediatric durations, Pseudomonas-specific BSI data, and pathogen-disease combinations beyond Enterobacteriaceae/UTI are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against a full BSI guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: The last decade has transformed treatment of carbapenem-resistant gram-negatives: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-relebactam have moved KPC-producing Enterobacterales from the colistin era into targeted beta-lactam therapy, while KPC variant evolution now threatens the new agents themselves.

teaching_points.claim: Ceftazidime-avibactam is a first-line option for KPC-producing Enterobacterales, with meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-relebactam as alternatives; ceftazidime-avibactam is preferred for OXA-48-like producers.
For KPC strains resistant to ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-relebactam have relative advantages.
Newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations expanded the armamentarium against MDR Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa beyond the polymyxin era.

In-vivo emergence of ceftazidime-avibactam resistance in KPC-E is documented in a systematic review: most cases were Klebsiella pneumoniae ST258 with the D179Y substitution, occurring during treatment of deep-seated infection.
More than 150 blaKPC variants are now reported, most identified in the last three years, and variants restore ceftazidime affinity while weakening avibactam binding - a moving resistance target.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of newer agents when first-line BLBLI therapy fails.
Whether combination therapy (e.g. BLBLI plus aminoglycoside or polymyxin) improves outcomes in high-inoculum infections.
mcq_angles: Agent selection by carbapenemase type: KPC versus OXA-48 versus MBL.
Recognizing and responding to ceftazidime-avibactam resistance emerging on therapy (ST258/D179Y).
Why colistin has been displaced as default therapy for KPC-producing CRE.
The blaKPC variant explosion and what it means for susceptibility reporting.

teaching_points.claim: EULAR's 2022 AAV recommendations were built on a systematic literature review plus expert consensus, incorporating randomized trials published since the 2016 version that change clinical care.
Rituximab is now an established induction option alongside glucocorticoids for ANCA-associated vasculitis, reflected across EULAR, KDIGO and ACR guidance.
Major clinical trials underpinning current ANCA vasculitis treatment have reduced morbidity and improved survival; guideline summaries track these trial milestones.

page.mentor_intro: Graves' hyperthyroidism offers three effective definitive strategies - antithyroid drugs, radioiodine and thyroidectomy - and no modality has proven universally superior. Modern practice starts with antithyroid drugs to restore euthyroidism, then individualises the definitive step around orbitopathy, pregnancy plans and patient preference.

teaching_points.claim: Guideline-based strategy first restores euthyroid status with antithyroid therapy, then selects a definitive modality; no treatment modality has demonstrated superiority, so the choice is shared with the patient.
Radioiodine-131 and thyroidectomy abolish hyperthyroidism but create hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine - a trade of one disease for another rather than a cure.
Radioiodine can aggravate Graves' orbitopathy and requires pre-treatment assessment; pregnancy or pregnancy plans change both treatment choice and monitoring.
A beta-blocker relieves tachycardia, anxiety and tremor while awaiting definitive control.
Long-term antithyroid drug courses are an increasingly used strategy, with contemporary narrative reviews updating their role against radioiodine and surgery.

uncertainties: Which patients achieve durable remission after antithyroid drugs and how to predict relapse.
Optimal role and duration of long-term low-dose antithyroid drug maintenance.

page.mentor_intro: Comparing antithyroid drugs, radioiodine and thyroidectomy for Graves' disease is less about finding a winner than matching trade-offs: remission potential versus definitive control, and the burden of lifelong thyroid hormone replacement after destructive approaches. Guidelines consistently report no modality as universally superior.

teaching_points.claim: Treatment options for Graves' hyperthyroidism have not changed in decades - antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine and thyroidectomy - and reviews of disease burden confirm all three remain the active comparators.
No randomized comparison has established superiority of one modality; guideline strategy therefore emphasises informed, preference-sensitive choice after euthyroidism is restored.
Radioiodine and thyroidectomy reliably abolish hyperthyroidism but commit the patient to lifelong levothyroxine; antithyroid drugs preserve thyroid function but carry relapse risk.
Antithyroid drug treatment duration relates to remission rates, though the meta-analytic evidence to date is in children - extrapolation to adults needs caution.
Long-term antithyroid drug therapy is an increasingly recognised strategy whose updated narrative review maps its place against radioiodine and thyroidectomy.

uncertainties: Adult remission rates by antithyroid drug duration and predictive factors (TRAb, goitre size).
Long-term quality-of-life and cardiovascular outcome differences between modalities.
mcq_angles: A patient-centred modality choice: orbitopathy, pregnancy plans and smoking status as decision modifiers.

page.mentor_intro: Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension is managed by three pathways - endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and prostacyclin analogues - but the defining shift of recent years is treatment strategy: risk-stratified, combination-first, then escalation.

teaching_points.claim: The 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines introduced a refined three-category risk stratification (low, intermediate, high) that guides both initial and subsequent therapy; estimated 1-year mortality exceeds 20% in high-risk patients.

Initial combination therapy for PAH was first proposed for high-risk patients in the 2009 European guidelines, extended to low/intermediate-risk patients by 2015 and later consensus meetings - a concept now central to practice.
Modern progress in PAH therapy comes not from new pathways but from combination strategies across the endothelin, nitric-oxide and prostacyclin pathways plus systematic escalation based on risk.

Upfront dual oral combination therapy with an endothelin receptor antagonist (ERA: ambrisentan or macitentan) and a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (PDE5i: tadalafil or sildenafil) is the standard of care for low- and intermediate-risk PAH (demonstrated in the AMBITION trial), while high-risk patients require immediate triple therapy including parenteral prostacyclin analogs.

uncertainties: Which initial doublet (ERA+PDE5i versus including a prostacyclin pathway agent) best serves intermediate-risk patients.
How to time escalation and when to refer for lung transplantation assessment.

page.mentor_intro: The gut microbiome has moved from speculation to mechanism in GI disease: dysbiosis is now associated with IBS, IBD and colorectal cancer, diet and food additives are established modulators, and prebiotic/probiotic strategies are being refined - though causality and strain specificity remain the frontier.

teaching_points.claim: Dysbiosis - imbalance between beneficial and opportunistic microbiota - is associated with IBS, IBD (ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease) and colorectal cancer.
Dietary fibre from unrefined whole foods benefits gastrointestinal health, with regulatory effects on transit time, stool formation and the gut milieu.
Diets rich in ultra-processed foods are associated with gut disease including IBD, colorectal cancer and IBS; some additives (e.g. certain emulsifiers) directly affect gut health.
Prebiotics and probiotics beneficially modulate the gut microbiome, but formulating specific recommendations for GI conditions remains challenging.
Acute enteric infection is the best-described risk factor for IBS, linking microbiome disturbance to post-infectious functional disease.

page.mentor_intro: Gynaecomastia - benign proliferation of male breast tissue - is common at the physiological extremes of age and, when acquired, a signal to review drugs, hypogonadism and systemic disease. Most adolescent cases need reassurance alone; the clinical task is separating the benign from the pathological.

teaching_points.claim: Gynaecomastia reflects an altered androgen-to-estrogen ratio with contributions from growth hormone, IGF-1, prolactin and aromatase activity.
Common causes are pubertal change, obesity, drugs and hypogonadism; liver and renal disease are among the systemic associations.
Physiological gynaecomastia occurs in almost 25% of cases - newborns, adolescents and older men - and is benign and self-limited.
In adolescents, most cases are idiopathic; if history and examination are reassuring, no further evaluation is required.

page.mentor_intro: Haemodialysis complications cluster around vascular access - the patient's lifeline and its commonest failure point - alongside cardiovascular instability and the broader burden of kidney failure. Access planning is the most evidence-rich and most examinable corner of this topic.

teaching_points.claim: The KDOQI 2019 vascular access update is the comprehensive evidence-based reference for haemodialysis access, replacing the 2006 version.
Arteriovenous access (autogenous fistula or graft) requires an individualised strategy - the 'Patient Life-Plan' - that anticipates future access needs rather than reacting to failure.
KDIGO's 2024 CKD guideline updates the broader evaluation and management frame in which dialysis complications sit.

Intradialytic hypotension (IDH) is the most frequent acute complication of hemodialysis, driven by aggressive ultrafiltration rates exceeding vascular refill capacity; preventative management includes dialysate cooling (35-36°C), avoiding food ingestion during treatment, linear ultrafiltration profiling, and strict dry-weight optimization.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of access creation versus progression to dialysis dependence.
How to reduce the fistula-first default for patients where grafts or catheters serve better.

page.mentor_intro: Haemodynamic monitoring ranges from a simple arterial line to calibrated transpulmonary thermodilution. The common error in training is treating every number as interchangeable: each device answers a different question, carries different assumptions, and fails in predictable ways. This page builds the mental model of what arterial lines, CVP, pulmonary artery catheters, and pulse-contour systems (calibrated PiCCO vs uncalibrated FloTrac) actually measure, and when dynamic tests such as passive leg raising beat static pressure readings.

teaching_points.claim: Arterial catheters remain the gold standard for continuous blood pressure monitoring in the ICU; intermittent non-invasive measurement may not provide enough information to determine the cause of haemodynamic instability or guide intervention.
Pulmonary artery catheter use has declined, but reviews highlight a striking lack of clinician knowledge of PAC-derived measurements; the technique requires considerable skill to interpret correctly.

Pulse-contour devices estimate cardiac output from the arterial pressure waveform; calibrated methods (transpulmonary thermodilution, e.g., PiCCO) and uncalibrated methods (e.g., FloTrac) differ fundamentally in how they maintain accuracy during changing haemodynamics.

Transpulmonary thermodilution provides calibrated cardiac output and volumetric indices, but technical aspects and validity limits must be understood before using derived parameters such as global end-diastolic volume or extravascular lung water in specific clinical settings.

Fluid responsiveness should be predicted with dynamic tests rather than static pressures: passive leg raising-induced changes in cardiac output (and pulse pressure) predict fluid responsiveness with good diagnostic performance in adults.

uncertainties: No retained source demonstrates that any particular monitoring device or strategy improves patient outcomes; device choice remains largely expert-consensus.
How often uncalibrated pulse-contour systems should be recalibrated during rapidly changing haemodynamics is not quantified in the retained abstracts.
mcq_angles: Static CVP vs dynamic passive-leg-raising assessment of fluid responsiveness.

page.mentor_intro: Interpreting a haemoglobin electrophoresis (or HPLC/capillary electrophoresis) report is a pattern-recognition skill that links quantitative haemoglobin fractions to red-cell indices and, ultimately, DNA confirmation. The trainee should learn the two-step discipline: screen with haematological indices plus separation techniques, then confirm variants genetically — never diagnose a carrier from an electrophoresis trace alone.

teaching_points.claim: Detecting and characterising variant haemoglobins and thalassaemias depends on a combination of biophysical, biochemical and genetic assays that provide phenotypic or genotypic evidence of pathology.
Conventional screening combines haematological indices with HPLC or capillary electrophoresis; abnormal screening results in at-risk adults require confirmatory (genetic) testing before counselling.

Different combinations of alpha- and beta-globin gene defects produce distinct disease phenotypes (homozygous beta-thalassaemia, beta-thalassaemia/HbE, Hb Bart's hydrops), so interpretation must integrate Hb fractions such as HbA2 and HbF with red-cell indices.

Elevated HbA2 (>3.5%) on capillary electrophoresis or HPLC confirms the diagnosis of beta-thalassemia trait (differentiating it from iron deficiency anemia), whereas marked elevation of HbF indicates hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) or beta-thalassemia major/intermedia, and HbS migration establishes sickle cell hemoglobinopathies.

uncertainties: How to resolve discordance between capillary electrophoresis and HPLC in individual carriers is not addressed in the retained abstracts.
Cost-effectiveness and choice between screening technologies varies by population prevalence and is not settled in the retained sources.

page.mentor_intro: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a thrombotic microangiopathy defined by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury — but the label covers two very different diseases. Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli HUS in children is largely supportive care; atypical HUS is an uncontrolled-complement disorder whose natural history has been transformed by C5 inhibitors. The first clinical skill is refusing to treat the triad before you know which HUS you are looking at, and excluding TTP.

teaching_points.claim: HUS is characterised by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney failure; most cases are caused by Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli, transmitted through vehicles such as ground beef and unpasteurised milk, and STEC-HUS is the main cause of acute renal failure in children.

The HUS spectrum includes triggers ranging from infection through medication to malignancy and transplantation, all converging on endothelial damage; on that spectrum atypical HUS is the complement-mediated end.

Atypical HUS is a rare thrombotic microangiopathy driven by uncontrolled alternative-complement-pathway activation, with high morbidity and mortality without targeted treatment, so distinguishing it from STEC-HUS and TTP before committing to therapy is critical.
Complement inhibitors such as eculizumab and ravulizumab have transformed the management of atypical HUS, changing both acute outcomes and long-term management of complement-mediated TMA.

uncertainties: Optimal duration and de-escalation of eculizumab/ravulizumab therapy are not defined in the retained abstracts.

page.mentor_intro: HLH is the diagnosis trainees meet too late: a hyperinflammatory storm of cytotoxic T cells, NK cells and macrophages that mimics sepsis, flare and liver failure all at once. Recognition rests on a constellation — fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, coagulopathy, very high ferritin — plus a determined search for the trigger. Management has two parallel tracks: control the immune activation and treat whatever provoked it.

teaching_points.claim: HLH is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome associated with multiple-organ dysfunction; fever, cytopenias, coagulopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are hallmark findings, and early recognition is critical.
The disease is driven by uncontrolled activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes, natural killer cells and macrophages, producing hypercytokinemia and immune-mediated injury of multiple organ systems.

Primary (genetic) HLH predominates in children, whereas secondary (acquired) HLH — frequently triggered by infection — dominates in adults; management recommendations for adults emphasise trigger-directed treatment alongside immunosuppression.
Untreated HLH carries high mortality, and a multidisciplinary approach is needed for diagnosis and management.

page.mentor_intro: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked factor VIII and IX deficiencies whose modern story is a treatment revolution — from on-demand replacement to regular prophylaxis, extended half-life products, the bispecific antibody emicizumab, and now gene therapy. The trainee should anchor on three things: severity is defined by factor activity, joints are the organ that suffers, and the ageing haemophilia population now faces the same comorbidity trade-offs as everyone else.

teaching_points.claim: Haemophilia A and B are congenital X-linked bleeding disorders caused by deficiency of factor VIII and factor IX respectively; severe deficiency, defined as less than 1% of normal factor activity, is associated with spontaneous bleeding within the first years of life.

Recurrent joint bleeding (haemarthrosis) is the most frequent clinical manifestation of severe haemophilia, and unless appropriately managed — including subclinical bleeds — it progresses to haemophilic arthropathy.
The World Federation of Hemophilia 3rd-edition guidelines are the global reference standard for the management of haemophilia.

Emicizumab, a bispecific antibody recognising FIX(a)/FX that mimics FVIIIa cofactor activity, transformed prophylaxis through subcutaneous administration and a long half-life, in patients with or without FVIII inhibitors.
Effective treatment has increased life expectancy, creating a middle-aged and elderly population with haemophilia whose management is complicated by the opposing risks of comorbidities and bleeding.

uncertainties: Long-term durability and eligibility criteria for gene therapy are still evolving and are not settled in the retained sources.
Sequencing of non-factor therapies (emicizumab, siRNA agents) relative to extended half-life factor concentrates is not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: For a patient with severe haemophilia A, prophylaxis is the default philosophy: keep trough factor levels high enough that joints never bleed. The modern question is no longer whether to give prophylaxis, but which agent — intravenous extended-half-life factor VIII, or subcutaneous emicizumab that works even when an inhibitor has destroyed the patient's factor VIII. This page contrasts those options and the evidence comparing them.

teaching_points.claim: Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody recognising FIX(a)/FX that mimics FVIIIa cofactor activity; its long half-life and subcutaneous injectability dramatically improved haemophilia A treatment regardless of FVIII inhibitor status.

Emicizumab was developed in response to the unmet needs of adherence to prophylaxis and the lack of effective long-term prophylaxis, especially in patients with inhibitors; it is the first non-factor medicine for subcutaneous administration in severe and moderate haemophilia A with or without inhibitors.

In the phase 3 XTEND-1 trial, efanesoctocog alfa prophylaxis provided superior bleed protection compared with pre-trial FVIII prophylaxis in patients with severe haemophilia A, and an indirect comparison addressed its efficacy relative to emicizumab in patients without inhibitors.
Regular FVIII replacement prophylaxis remains the gold standard for moderate-to-severe haemophilia A, with extended half-life products reducing infusion burden compared with conventional treatment.

For decades the only way to prevent bleeding was factor infusion; without it, patients face debilitating joint damage from recurrent haemarthroses and life-threatening bleeds including intracranial haemorrhage — the rationale for effective prophylaxis in both inhibitor and non-inhibitor patients.

uncertainties: Management of breakthrough bleeds in patients on emicizumab, including bypassing-agent choice and dosing, is not covered in the retained abstracts.
Indirect-comparison limitations between efanesoctocog alfa and emicizumab mean head-to-head evidence is still lacking.

page.mentor_intro: Haemorrhagic stroke — intracerebral haemorrhage above all — carries the worst early prognosis of any stroke type, and the pace of the first hours decides the outcome. Trainees should hold three facts firmly: it is the minority of strokes but a disproportionate share of stroke deaths; untreated hypertension is its engine worldwide; and management is a race against haematoma expansion rather than a hunt for reperfusion.

teaching_points.claim: Hemorrhagic stroke comprises about 20% of all strokes, with intracerebral haemorrhage the most common type; its frequency is increased where hypertension is untreated, and it carries a disproportionately high risk of early mortality and long-term disability.
Stroke is the second leading cause of death and a major cause of disability worldwide; although ischaemic stroke is more frequent, haemorrhagic stroke is responsible for more deaths.
Intracerebral haemorrhage is a devastating form of stroke with high morbidity and mortality, and its incidence has increased worldwide over the past 40 years.
Contemporary ICH care addresses the cause, mechanisms of injury, and current treatment strategies, including the need to limit ongoing injury after the initial bleed.

Treatment is site-specific — surgery first for the oral cavity, organ-preservation chemoradiation for larynx/hypopharynx, and now perioperative immunotherapy trials rewriting the resectable-disease playbook.

teaching_points.claim: Most head and neck cancers arise from the mucosal epithelium of the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx (HNSCC); oral cavity and laryngeal cancers are generally associated with tobacco and alcohol, whereas pharyngeal cancers are increasingly linked to HPV.
Head and neck cancer is the seventh most common cancer worldwide, with approximately 71,110 individuals diagnosed in the US in 2024.
Established risk factors include tobacco exposure and alcohol dependence, with oncogenic-virus infection increasingly associated with cancers of the pharyngeal subsites.

For oral cavity cancer, the standard of care is primary surgical resection with or without postoperative adjuvant therapy, and despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, survival outcomes remain suboptimal.
Positive randomised trials of perioperative immune-checkpoint inhibition (KEYNOTE-689 and NIVOPOSTOP) may redefine current and future treatment paradigms for resectable, locally advanced HNSCC.

uncertainties: De-escalation strategies for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (reduced radiation or chemotherapy intensity) are not resolved in the retained abstracts.

page.mentor_intro: S. aureus is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infection — central-line bloodstream infections, surgical site infections, and more — and nasal carriage is the reservoir most interventions target. Decolonization (topical antiseptics, intranasal antibiotic regimens, and targeted screening) sits alongside contact precautions and bundles as the core preventive toolkit. The trainee should understand who to screen, what regimens exist, and where the evidence is strongest — cardiac and orthopaedic surgery — versus where it is weaker.

teaching_points.claim: S. aureus is a common skin commensal and a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections including central-line-associated bloodstream infection and surgical site infection, which makes decolonization a central prevention strategy.
Nasal colonization with MRSA is the key target for eradication interventions, and multiple interventions targeting the nasal microbiome have been developed for this purpose.

Healthcare-adapted MRSA spread globally over 50 years, and community strains capable of infecting healthy individuals have since emerged; control requires strategies for both healthcare- and community-associated spread.
S. aureus is the most common microbial cause of surgical site infections, and screening with decolonization before surgery is used to reduce SSI risk, particularly in high-risk procedures.
Staphylococcal screening and suppression is an interventional strategy aimed at reduction of surgical site infections; its effectiveness depends on the screening strategy and agent used.

uncertainties: Optimal decolonization regimen, duration, and the role of systemic versus topical agents are not settled in the retained abstracts.
How decolonization interacts with antimicrobial stewardship and resistance selection is not quantified in the retained sources.

page.mentor_intro: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome — dyspnoea or exertional limitation from impaired ventricular filling or ejection — that now divides by ejection fraction, because therapy that transforms HFrEF does little or nothing for HFpEF beyond SGLT2 inhibitors. Anchor on the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline as the framework, then learn the phenotype split (roughly half of all HF is preserved EF) and the four pillars of HFrEF disease-modifying therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline replaces both the 2013 ACCF/AHA guideline and the 2017 focused update, and is the current American framework for heart failure management.
The 2023 ESC focused update introduced key new recommendations led by SGLT2 inhibitors across the ejection-fraction spectrum, reflecting major recent progress in HF management.

Worldwide HF burden has grown to an estimated 23 million people, with approximately half of cases being HFrEF; HF is a clinical syndrome of dyspnoea or exertional limitation from impaired ventricular filling or ejection.
HFpEF represents at least half of all heart failure cases, and its recognition is rising with population ageing and comorbidity burden such as obesity and diabetes.
HF prevalence is increasing because of population ageing and improved survival after acute cardiovascular events, despite effective therapies — making long-term management a growing clinical load.

page.mentor_intro: Three trials reset HFrEF practice. PARADIGM-HF showed sacubitril/valsartan beat enalapril; DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced showed SGLT2 inhibitors cut cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation in patients with and without diabetes. Together they form the spine of modern guideline-directed therapy — and this page reads them as a set, including the sobering finding that real-world patients often fail the trials' eligibility criteria.

teaching_points.claim: Landmark trials established new treatments for HFrEF: sacubitril/valsartan was superior to enalapril in PARADIGM-HF, and SGLT2 inhibitors were added to the therapeutic armamentarium.

A network meta-analysis compared the treatment arms of sacubitril/valsartan, vericiguat and the SGLT2 inhibitors dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, each proven effective in phase 3 HFrEF trials, allowing relative efficacy to be estimated across drugs.

When eligibility criteria from DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced and PARADIGM-HF are applied to real outpatient populations with chronic heart failure, a substantial proportion of routine patients fall outside trial inclusion criteria — a key caveat when extrapolating trial effect sizes to clinic practice.

Cross-trial aggregate-data analyses estimate the expected combined benefit of comprehensive (quintuple) disease-modifying pharmacological treatment in HFrEF, suggesting effects accumulate when therapies are combined.

uncertainties: Cross-trial and network meta-analyses carry indirect-comparison limitations; true head-to-head outcome data between individual agents are lacking.
How trial-ineligible patients (eGFR limits, blood-pressure floors, recent hospitalisation) respond to the same drugs is less certain.

page.mentor_intro: For years HFpEF had no therapy that moved outcomes — every trial failed until SGLT2 inhibitors. EMPEROR-Preserved showed empagliflozin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation in HFpEF, driven by fewer worsening-HF events, positioning SGLT2 inhibitors as the new standard of care in this phenotype. Understand both the result and its texture: the benefit is real, but it is hospitalisation-driven rather than a clear mortality signal.

teaching_points.claim: In EMPEROR-Preserved, empagliflozin reduced the risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure in HFpEF (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69-0.90, P<.001), an effect driven by a reduction in worsening HF events; SGLT2 inhibitors are therefore likely to become the new standard of care in HFpEF.
The 2023 ESC focused update introduced SGLT2 inhibitors as a key new recommendation across the heart-failure spectrum, reflecting the drug class's progress from diabetes trials into HFpEF management.

HFpEF prevalence is increasing across all populations with high rates of hospitalization and mortality (up to 80% and 50% respectively within 5 years in the cited review), and comorbidity-driven systemic inflammation underlies its pathophysiology.

SGLT2 inhibitors protect the heart and kidneys of patients with or without type 2 diabetes and with preserved or reduced kidney function, through both glucose-dependent and glucose-independent mechanisms.

page.mentor_intro: HFrEF is the phenotype where drugs reliably save lives. Network meta-analyses of the contemporary trials converge on the same message: the combination of beta-blocker, ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor is the most effective pharmacological strategy for reducing mortality. The clinical gap is implementation — most eligible patients never reach target doses of all four classes. Learn the evidence hierarchy, then learn how to actually get the drugs in.

A 2022 network meta-analysis estimated and compared aggregate treatment benefits of pharmacological therapy combinations in HFrEF, because the effects of contemporary therapy combinations were not well characterised.

The 2025 updated network meta-analysis found that a combination of beta-blockers, ARNi, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors was the most effective pharmacological approach for reducing all-cause mortality.
HFrEF makes up approximately half of the worldwide heart-failure burden (an estimated 23 million people), and presents as dyspnoea or exertional limitation from impaired ventricular ejection.

SGLT2 inhibitors have been studied across the cardiometabolic spectrum (heart failure, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, post-myocardial infarction), with heart-failure outcome benefits that extend beyond any single disease context.

page.mentor_intro: Heart-failure admissions often follow days of silently rising filling pressures that clinic visits miss. Remote haemodynamic monitoring — led by the pulmonary-artery pressure sensor (CardioMEMS) — aims to catch that rise and act on it before the patient decompensates. The evidence landscape is mixed, however: devices are approved and clinically available, but questions about which patients benefit and how programmes should be implemented remain live.

teaching_points.claim: Wireless haemodynamic monitoring in heart failure allows volume assessment without physical examination, and data from these devices are used to assist patient management and avoid heart-failure hospitalisations.
Interest in remote haemodynamic monitoring is driven by persistently high HF mortality despite treatment advances, and by the rising global prevalence of HF and its burden on hospital resources.

Traditional management based on intermittent clinic visits and subjective symptom reporting often fails to detect early decompensation, motivating a monitoring landscape that includes both implantable and non-implantable technologies.

page.mentor_intro: Remote HF monitoring has three lanes: blood biomarkers (BNP/NT-proBNP), device-based sensors already present in many patients (pacemakers and defibrillators that track impedance and other trends), and structured telemonitoring. Each lane detects different signals at different time horizons, and each has distinct failure modes — biomarkers fluctuate with renal function, device algorithms alarm imperfectly, and telemonitoring trials have been mixed. The skill is matching the lane to the patient.

teaching_points.claim: B-type natriuretic peptide, recognised since 1988 as a powerful cardiovascular biomarker, is central to heart-failure monitoring, with ongoing effort devoted to precise assay and biosensor-based measurement.

Cardiac implantable electronic devices include remote monitoring tools intended to predict worsening heart failure and avert hospitalisations, but device measurements such as intrathoracic impedance face practical and interpretive challenges.

HF symptoms reflect elevated ventricular filling pressures, and tests that characterise diastolic function help identify the pressure elevation that precedes decompensation — informing how often and how to test.

Digital biomarkers derived from digital health technologies enable quantifiable, near-continuous, real-world capture of pathophysiological signals, and their role in cardiovascular medicine is formalised in an ESC Working Group scientific statement.

page.mentor_intro: SGLT2 inhibitors are the defining heart-failure drug story of this decade: a diabetes drug class that turned out to reduce cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation in HFrEF patients with and without diabetes, then extended benefit into HFpEF. The trainee should know the trial spine (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced), the meta-analytic consensus, the nuance that in-hospital initiation data are suggestive rather than definitive, and how diabetes status modifies — mostly by not modifying — the effect.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis of EMPEROR-Reduced and DAPA-HF showed that SGLT2 inhibition (empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure in HFrEF patients.

In the DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 trial, in-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or worsening HF through 2 months in hospitalised HF patients; however, the totality of randomised trial data suggests in-hospital SGLT2i initiation may reduce early cardiovascular death or worsening HF and all-cause mortality.
The 2023 ESC focused update made SGLT2 inhibitors a headline recommendation in HF management, reflecting trial results that now span the ejection-fraction spectrum.

SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists entered cardiology from glucose-lowering therapy, with cardiovascular outcome trial evidence establishing protection beyond glycaemic control — including in heart failure.

Collaborative meta-analysis of large placebo-controlled trials confirmed that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce adverse kidney and cardiovascular outcomes across patients with heart failure, chronic kidney disease, or type 2 diabetes with high atherosclerotic risk, informing how diabetes status modulates benefit.

uncertainties: The signal for benefit of starting SGLT2 inhibitors during an acute HF admission is suggestive from pooled data but not proven by the individual DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 trial.
Optimal duration and whether effects persist through advanced CKD (stage 4) are incompletely defined in the retained sources.

page.mentor_intro: HFrEF is where modern cardiology most clearly saves lives with drugs. page.mentor_intro: HIT is the thrombocytopenia that bleeds in name only — it is, paradoxically, a profoundly prothrombotic drug reaction. Antibodies against PF4/heparin complexes activate platelets through Fc receptors, and the downstream events (arterial and venous thrombosis, limb loss, death) are driven by continued heparin exposure. The reflexes to build: suspect it on timing and thrombosis pattern, score it pre-test, stop all heparin immediately, and anticoagulate with a non-heparin agent even before confirmatory testing returns.

teaching_points.claim: HIT is an immune reaction to heparin associated with thrombocytopenia, thrombotic risk and high morbidity and mortality; given how commonly heparin is used and how often hospitalized patients are thrombocytopenic, a practical diagnostic and management framework is essential.

HIT is caused by antibodies to complexes of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin; pathogenic PF4/heparin antibodies bind and activate cellular Fc-gamma-RIIA on platelets and monocytes, propagating a prothrombotic state.
Autoimmune HIT is a severe subtype with atypical clinical features caused by highly pathological IgG antibodies that activate platelets even in the absence of heparin.

Thrombocytopenia and heparin exposure are both common in critically ill patients, yet immune HIT rarely accounts for thrombocytopenia in this population — pre-test probability assessment is what separates the few true cases from the many false alarms.

uncertainties: Optimal management of autoimmune HIT, including the role of intravenous immunoglobulin and longer anticoagulation, is not settled in the retained abstracts.

page.mentor_intro: After a first episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy, most patients will recur without prevention, and each recurrence worsens prognosis and quality of life. Secondary prevention rests on two drugs with complementary jobs: lactulose, the non-absorbable disaccharide that traps ammonium in the colon, and rifaximin, the poorly absorbed antibiotic added when episodes break through — now supported by meta-analysis as prevention in its own right. Every recurrence should also trigger a search for the precipitant, because most are iatrogenic or gastrointestinal.

teaching_points.claim: Rifaximin is recommended for the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, and a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis assessed its safety and efficacy for preventing HE in patients with cirrhosis.
Evidence for long-term (>=6 months) pharmacological management of HE with lactulose and/or rifaximin has been consolidated in a dedicated review, addressing effectiveness and safety/tolerability.

Hepatic encephalopathy is a major neuropsychiatric complication of cirrhosis ranging from mild confusion to coma, and it is an important cause of recurrent admissions — framing the prevention priority.
Ammonia is a major neurotoxin implicated in the pathogenesis, progression and severity of HE, with contributions from multiple organs; therapies target ammonia production and handling.

Overt HE is a generally reversible but prognostically serious complication of cirrhosis, associated with poor hospitalisation- and mortality-related outcomes, which makes improving clinical outcomes through pharmacologic treatment a priority.

uncertainties: Whether rifaximin monotherapy prevents first episodes (primary prevention) as effectively as it prevents recurrence is not established in the retained abstracts.
The comparative effectiveness of lactulose alone versus lactulose plus rifaximin for secondary prevention needs individual-patient interpretation of trial data.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatitis C went from a chronic, often silent killer to a curable infection in under a decade: pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral combinations (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) deliver sustained virological response — SVR12, the practical definition of cure — in the overwhelming majority of patients, regardless of genotype. An estimated 71.1 million individuals are chronically infected with HCV worldwide (about 1% of the population), with transmission most commonly associated with blood exposure — the population screening must reach.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatitis D is the defective satellite virus that only exists alongside hepatitis B — it needs HBsAg to enter and propagate — and it converts a manageable HBV infection into the most severe form of human viral hepatitis. The clinical fork is coinfection (HDV and HBV acquired together, often transient) versus superinfection (HDV landing on established chronic HBV, which usually becomes chronic and aggressive). Treatment was peginterferon for three decades with minority response rates; bulevirtide, the first-in-class entry inhibitor, has finally given the field an approved targeted drug.

teaching_points.claim: Chronic hepatitis D results from infection with HBV and HDV, and is the most severe form of human viral hepatitis; current treatment options consist of interferon alfa, effective only in a minority of patients.

Chronic hepatitis D results from infection with both HBV and HDV together, and it is the most severe form of human viral hepatitis — which is why HDV screening matters in every patient with chronic HBV.

Pegylated interferon-alpha treatment of chronic HDV gives variable and often poor responses; bulevirtide was recently approved with promising results, and meta-analysis now compares regimens comparatively.

Bulevirtide, a first-in-class entry inhibitor, is the first drug formally approved for chronic hepatitis delta, whereas pegylated interferon has been used off-label since the 1990s; current evidence compares bulevirtide monotherapy with combination treatment.
Blocking cell entry is a suitable therapeutic approach, and bulevirtide works by inhibiting the bile-acid transporter NTCP that HDV uses for hepatocyte entry.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of bulevirtide therapy and durability of response after stopping are not settled in the retained sources.
Whether combination bulevirtide plus peginterferon outperforms either alone needs head-to-head confirmation beyond current evidence.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the dominant primary liver cancer (about 90% of cases) and the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, rising on the back of cirrhosis, HBV/HCV and metabolic liver disease. Management is stage-dependent — resection, ablation, transplant for early disease; locoregional therapy for intermediate; systemic immunotherapy-based regimens for advanced — so the first clinical skill is correct staging, and the second is surveillance discipline in cirrhotic patients, because early HCC is the HCC that gets cured.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors have emerged as the primary treatment for advanced HCC and shown promise in the neoadjuvant setting, while liver transplantation remains the preferred treatment for patients within criteria with unresectable early disease.
Focal liver lesions are an increasingly common incidental finding on abdominal imaging, and structured evaluation distinguishes HCC from benign lesions without biopsy in many cases.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is the dyspnoea of cirrhosis that gets missed: intrapulmonary vascular dilatation and shunting produce impaired gas exchange and arterial hypoxaemia in a patient with liver disease or portal hypertension. The diagnostic triad is liver disease, intrapulmonary vasodilatation and hypoxaemia; contrast echocardiography demonstrates the shunt. It worsens prognosis, it matters enormously at transplant assessment, and apart from liver transplantation there is no definitive therapy — though oxygen and careful candidate selection are the practical tools.

teaching_points.claim: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a pulmonary vascular complication of liver disease, characterised by intrapulmonary vascular dilatations and shunts resulting in impaired gas exchange, and it adversely affects prognosis.
HPS occurs in patients with chronic liver disease and/or portal hypertension, and intrapulmonary vascular dilatation may induce severe hypoxaemia through microvascular dilation and shunting.
HPS should be considered for any dyspnoea in cirrhotic patients; it is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

In liver transplant candidates, HPS must be distinguished from portopulmonary hypertension (elevated pulmonary pressures and vascular remodelling), because the two have opposite implications for transplant eligibility.
The diagnostic triad of hepatopulmonary syndrome is liver disease, pulmonary vascular dilatations and arterial hypoxaemia, and it is usually associated with cirrhosis of any origin.

uncertainties: No effective medical therapy exists; the role of experimental agents and the thresholds for transplant priority (MELD exception) are not detailed in the retained abstracts.
Optimal contrast-echo protocol and shunt quantification for diagnosis are not standardised in the retained sources.

page.mentor_intro: The hepatorenal syndrome is the kidney failure of advanced cirrhosis that is functional, not structural: splanchnic vasodilatation and a hyperdynamic circulation leave the kidneys maximally vasoconstricted, and creatinine rises without primary renal disease. page.mentor_intro: HRS is the kidney failure that cirrhosis causes by haemodynamics alone: splanchnic arterial vasodilatation progresses until effective arterial volume and central blood volume fall, vasoconstrictor systems activate to their limit, and extreme renal vasoconstriction drops the GFR. Modern terminology splits it into HRS-AKI and HRS-CKD; HRS-AKI accounts for roughly one in five AKI presentations in cirrhosis; and because there is no gold standard test, diagnosis remains one of exclusion — which is where most management errors begin.

teaching_points.claim: HRS is a form of kidney dysfunction characteristically occurring in cirrhosis, with marked impairment of kidney function in response to circulatory and haemodynamic alterations of advanced liver disease.

Patients with cirrhosis are prone to AKI, which carries markedly increased in-hospital morbidity and mortality and risk of progression to CKD; the ADQI/ICA consensus addresses AKI management in this population.
Terminology has changed: acute HRS is now referred to as AKI-HRS and chronic HRS as chronic kidney disease-CKD-HRS, aligning HRS with the universal AKI framework.
HRS is a primarily functional form of AKI that develops in decompensated cirrhosis; the pathophysiologic cascade begins with pooling of blood in the splanchnic system.

HRS-AKI occurs in the setting of advanced chronic liver disease, portal hypertension and ascites, and is found in about 20% of patients presenting to hospital with AKI — though it may coexist with other kidney injuries.

HRS-1 is a severe form of AKI in advanced cirrhosis and ascites whose pathogenesis is rooted in marked maladaptive renal vasoconstriction, and the lack of a gold-standard test makes diagnosis and treatment selection challenging.

uncertainties: HRS-AKI can coexist with other kidney injuries (sepsis-associated, ischemic, drug-induced), complicating both diagnosis and trial interpretation.
Whether novel biomarkers will supplant creatinine-based criteria in cirrhosis is unresolved.

Management then moves quickly: albumin volume expansion to test responsiveness, vasoconstrictor therapy to reverse the renal vasoconstriction, evaluation for liver transplantation, and renal replacement therapy when vasoconstrictors fail or are contraindicated.

page.mentor_intro: Terlipressin is the vasoconstrictor that made HRS treatable: a V1-receptor agonist that constricts the splanchnic bed, restoring effective arterial volume and relieving renal vasoconstriction when combined with albumin. Long the international standard of care, it was only recently approved for HRS-AKI in the United States — and its evidence base is now mature enough that meta-analyses of randomised trials define both its efficacy and its safety boundaries, including ischaemic adverse events that demand careful patient selection.

teaching_points.claim: The definition and diagnostic criteria of HRS-AKI have undergone recent changes, and terlipressin has recently been approved as pharmacotherapy for HRS-AKI in the United States.
Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials confirms terlipressin (with albumin) as an effective treatment for HRS, consolidating the evidence base for its use.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis re-assessed terlipressin versus placebo or noradrenaline for HRS, examining both efficacy and safety in light of HRS's poor prognosis and unmet therapeutic need.
Terlipressin is the most widely used treatment for HRS, though therapy effects were historically inconsistent, prompting repeated meta-analytic assessment of its safety and efficacy.

uncertainties: Ischaemic adverse events (cardiac, intestinal, digital) temper terlipressin use in patients with vascular disease or shock; the risk-benefit threshold is not crisply defined in the retained abstracts.
Whether noradrenaline is truly non-inferior to terlipressin — particularly in ICU settings — remains an active comparison.

page.mentor_intro: Vasoconstrictor therapy is the pharmacological reversal of HRS pathophysiology: constrict the over-dilated splanchnic circulation, restore effective arterial volume, and let the kidneys reopen. The available classes — terlipressin, noradrenaline, and the oral midodrine-octreotide combination — differ in potency, evidence depth, setting (ward vs ICU) and availability. Meta-analyses support vasoactive drugs as a class for HRS-1, with terlipressin the most studied, and choice driven by haemodynamic monitoring capacity and contraindications.

teaching_points.claim: HRS, the extreme manifestation of renal impairment in cirrhosis, features reduced renal blood flow and GFR, and its management centres on vasoconstrictor therapy combined with albumin.

HRS is characterised by increased splanchnic blood flow, a hyperdynamic state, decreased central volume, activation of vasoconstrictor systems and extreme kidney vasoconstriction — the rationale for pharmacological splanchnic vasoconstriction.

Systematic review with meta-analysis supports vasoactive drugs for HRS type 1 — a functional, rapidly progressive but potentially reversible AKI characterised by intense renal arterial vasoconstriction and very poor prognosis.
Different pharmacological therapies for HRS have variable efficacy, and meta-analytic comparison of drug classes informs the choice among available vasoconstrictor regimens.

uncertainties: Whether oral combinations (midodrine-octreotide) match parenteral agents in efficacy remains uncertain.
Response predictors (baseline creatinine, bilirubin, arterial pressure) that should guide agent selection are not quantified in the retained abstracts.

page.mentor_intro: HER2-positive breast cancer used to be the aggressive subtype; adjuvant trastuzumab turned it into one of the more curable ones. About 15-20% of breast cancers overexpress HER2, and adding trastuzumab to chemotherapy produced one of the largest survival benefits ever recorded in adjuvant oncology. The modern craft is duration and escalation: one year of trastuzumab as the default, neoadjuvant therapy when downsizing matters, and escalation to dual HER2 blockade or T-DM1 for residual disease after neoadjuvant treatment.

page.mentor_intro: Antibody-drug conjugates have reset the ceiling for HER2-positive breast cancer. Trastuzumab deruxtecan — a HER2 antibody carrying a topoisomerase-I payload with a high drug-to-antibody ratio — succeeded where earlier ADCs stalled and now defines later-line, and increasingly earlier, treatment of advanced disease. Managing ADCs well means mastering their distinctive toxicities (notably interstitial lung disease) and understanding how they fit into the wider HER2 landscape of monoclonal antibodies, tyrosine-kinase inhibitors and dual blockade.

teaching_points.claim: Trastuzumab deruxtecan is an antibody-drug conjugate consisting of a humanised anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody linked to a topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload (DXd), with a high drug-to-antibody ratio.

Single-arm meta-analysis of T-DXd in HER2-expressing solid tumours confirms its efficacy and safety profile across tumour types.

HER2-positive breast cancer carries five-year survival around 30% at the advanced stage, and anti-HER2 treatment development — now including ADCs — has produced a paradigm shift in management and outcomes.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of ADCs versus TKIs and dual blockade, and re-challenge strategies after progression, are not settled.

page.mentor_intro: A handful of polyposis syndromes explain a small but preventable fraction of colorectal cancer, and they reward precise recognition: FAP and its attenuated form, MUTYH-associated polyposis, the hamartomatous syndromes (juvenile polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers), and the Lynch syndromes nearby. page.mentor_intro: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in northern European populations and one of the most satisfying to treat: the biochemical signature is elevated transferrin saturation, the gene is usually HFE C282Y, and venesection removes the excess iron before it destroys organs. The tragedy is underdiagnosis — arthropathy, diabetes, cirrhosis and cardiomyopathy are preventable when phlebotomy starts early, which is why unexplained fatigue with abnormal iron studies should always prompt the ferritin-and-transferrin-saturation pair.

teaching_points.claim: Haemochromatosis is characterised by elevated transferrin saturation and progressive iron loading that mainly affects the liver; early diagnosis and treatment by phlebotomy can prevent cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, arthropathy and other complications.

Hereditary haemochromatosis is one of the most common genetic disorders among persons of northern European descent, with recent advances in diagnosis, management and molecular diagnostic testing reflected in the ACG guideline.
Haemochromatosis is overdiagnosed in patients without true iron overload and underdiagnosed in many patients; early diagnosis by genetic testing and therapy are emphasised.
Most patients remain asymptomatic, but others develop advanced organ damage — arthropathy, diabetes — that reduces quality of life and survival, defining the treatment urgency.

Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder that disrupts iron homeostasis, causing systemic iron overload, and is the most common inherited disorder among people of northern European ancestry.

uncertainties: Penetrance of HFE C282Y homozygosity is incomplete — many carriers never develop iron overload, complicating screening policy.
The role of hepcidin-pathway agents for patients unable to tolerate phlebotomy is investigational.

page.mentor_intro: Roughly a third of phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry an identifiable germline mutation, and the genotype now organises everything: VHL, NF1, RET, and the SDHx genes each carry distinct tumour spectra, malignancy risk and surveillance rhythms. teaching_points.claim: Pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas have a distinctive molecular landscape allowing assignment to clusters by genetic alteration; around 30-35% of Caucasian patients harbour germline mutations, underpinning personalised management.

Phaeochromocytomas are rare adrenal-medulla tumours that may be sporadic or part of a hereditary syndrome, and a considerable number carry germline or somatic mutations inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a complex autosomal-dominant disorder caused by germline NF1 tumour-suppressor mutations, with characteristic pigmentary features and a well-recognised phaeochromocytoma association.

Plasma or fractionated urine metanephrines are the biochemical test of choice for diagnosis, and the preoperative approach to phaeochromocytoma centres on alpha-blockade before any surgical manipulation.

page.mentor_intro: Hereditary spherocytosis and elliptocytosis are disorders of the red-cell skeleton: defects in spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 or protein 4.2 weaken the membrane, splenic conditioning does the rest, and the result is a chronic haemolysis that announces itself through jaundice, gallstones and a positive family history. Hereditary erythrocyte membrane disorders are caused by mutations in genes encoding transmembrane or cytoskeletal proteins, with decreased cell deformability and shortened erythrocyte survival as the main consequences.
Structural understanding of inherited red-cell membrane disorders explains altered cell function, reduced red-cell survival and the resulting haemolytic anaemia.

page.mentor_intro: Herpes simplex encephalitis is the neurological emergency where the treatment decision precedes the diagnosis: acyclovir must start on suspicion, because delay measurably worsens outcome and no surrogate marker can safely exclude HSE early. HSV-1 is the commonest sporadic encephalitis in adults, PCR of CSF is the diagnostic mainstay, and the modern complication to recognise is autoimmune encephalitis that can follow the infection — so deterioration after apparently successful treatment is not necessarily failure.

teaching_points.claim: Advances in antiviral medications and supportive treatments have equipped physicians to combat the most severe manifestations of HSV disease; prompt recognition and treatment of HSV-1 encephalitis are essential.

Encephalitis is most commonly caused by viral infection, especially HSV type 1, although autoimmune causes such as NMDA-receptor-antibody encephalitis are increasingly recognised — a differential that shapes empirical therapy.
Herpes simplex encephalitis has been successfully treated with acyclovir, though it remains a cause of significant morbidity even with treatment.

Immediate empirical intravenous aciclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours, adjusted for renal function) must be administered without delay upon clinical suspicion of herpes simplex encephalitis; treatment is continued for 14 to 21 days with CSF HSV-PCR re-testing at the conclusion of therapy to confirm viral clearance prior to cessation.

uncertainties: Optimal acyclovir duration and whether oral follow-on therapy adds benefit are not resolved in the retained abstracts.

page.mentor_intro: A hiatal hernia is the stomach's migration through the diaphragmatic hiatus — the sliding type I being by far the commonest and mostly an incidental partner of reflux, while the para-oesophageal types (II-IV) carry mechanical complications like volvulus, obstruction and bleeding. Most need no treatment; the ones that do are either reflux-dominant (managed as GERD, with the ASGE guideline framing diagnosis and therapy) or mechanical (where surgical repair becomes the conversation).

teaching_points.claim: Esophageal hiatal hernia involves abnormal entry of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity and is classified by the relationship of the oesophagogastric junction to the diaphragm; the sliding type I is the most frequent category.
GERD pathogenesis is complex, involving reflux exposure, epithelial resistance and visceral sensitivity, and hiatal hernia is a key anatomical amplifier of reflux.
The ASGE 2025 guideline provides an evidence-based approach to diagnosing and managing GERD — the framework within which reflux symptoms attributed to hiatal hernia are managed.

Symptomatic sliding (Type I) hiatal hernias are primarily managed medically with proton pump inhibitors, lifestyle modifications, and weight reduction, whereas paraesophageal (Types II-IV) hernias carrying risks of gastric volvulus, strangulation, or bleeding require elective laparoscopic repair with crural closure and fundoplication in suitable surgical candidates.

uncertainties: Which sliding hiatal hernias benefit from surgical fundoplication beyond reflux control is individualised and debated.
Surveillance intervals for para-oesophageal hernias managed non-operatively are not standardised in the retained sources.

HS is a chronic, debilitating inflammatory disease derived from the pilosebaceous unit affecting approximately 1% of the general population, with nodules, abscesses and tunnels as clinical hallmarks.
HS is a complex immune-mediated disorder initially presenting as folliculitis that can progress to advanced lesions such as fistulas requiring extensive surgical intervention.

page.mentor_intro: High-altitude pulmonary edema is the deadliest of the acute altitude illnesses and the one most often missed early, because its first symptoms — exertional dyspnoea, cough, reduced exercise tolerance — look like simple fatigue at altitude. It is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema driven by hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, arriving one to five days after ascent, and it is preventable with graded ascent and treatable with descent and oxygen. Every physician advising travellers, trekkers, or workers deploying to altitude should know its time course, its susceptibility patterns, and the absolute priority of not waiting for it to 'settle'.

teaching_points.claim: Three forms of acute altitude illness — acute mountain sickness, high-altitude cerebral oedema and high-altitude pulmonary oedema — can each arise 1–5 days after ascent to altitudes of 2500 m or higher.
HAPE is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema resulting from excessive hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, rather than left-heart failure.

The prevalence of acute altitude illness varies with acclimatisation status, rate of ascent and individual susceptibility; chronic mountain sickness affects permanent high-altitude resident populations.
Clinical frameworks exist for counselling and evaluating patients before travel to altitude and for the prevention and treatment of the main forms of acute altitude illness.

uncertainties: Pharmacological prophylaxis choices (nifedipine, PDE5 inhibitors, acetazolamide) for HAPE-susceptible individuals are not fully standardised.
The relative roles of descent, portable hyperbaric chambers and in-situ oxygen in moderate HAPE are guided mainly by observational experience.
mcq_angles: Time window (1–5 days) and altitude threshold (≥2500 m) for acute altitude illness.
Pathophysiology: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction producing non-cardiogenic oedema.

Prevention strategies: graded ascent, acclimatisation days, avoiding rapid gain in sleeping altitude.

page.mentor_intro: Choosing between high-flow nasal oxygen, CPAP and bilevel NIV in acute hypoxaemic failure is now one of the most consequential triage decisions in the ICU, because the wrong choice does not merely fail — it delays intubation past the point where it helps. The first official clinical practice guideline on non-invasive respiratory support has been published specifically because modality selection was so variable. Knowing what each device does physiologically, when each is indicated, and how to recognise failure early is core competency for any physician managing acute respiratory failure.

teaching_points.claim: Non-invasive respiratory support strategies — HFNC, NIV and CPAP — may prevent intubation and improve outcomes in acute hypoxaemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure, but uncertainty about optimal patient and modality selection led to the first official clinical practice guideline.

High-flow nasal therapy provides low-level positive airway pressure, anatomical dead-space washout, good tolerance, and can be used during breaks from CPAP or BiPAP; CPAP and BiPAP deliver distinct physiological effects and require interface- and settings-specific expertise.

Extubation failure — reintubation within 2–7 days of planned extubation — is associated with prolonged ventilation, increased ventilator-associated pneumonia, longer ICU and hospital stays, and increased mortality.
High-quality evidence guiding HFNC discontinuation is lacking; weaning of flow, FiO2, or both is largely left to clinician discretion, and failure to de-escalate has measurable consequences.

uncertainties: Which hypoxaemic patients benefit from NIV versus HFNC first-line, and how to identify those in whom NIV merely delays intubation, remain contested.
Optimal HFNC weaning and liberation protocols (what to reduce first, how fast) are not evidence-defined.
mcq_angles: Physiological comparison: HFNC (dead-space washout, low PEEP) versus CPAP/BiPAP.
Post-extubation failure definition (reintubation within 2–7 days) and its consequences.
Guideline-based modality selection for hypoxaemic versus hypercapnic failure.
Recognising NIRS failure and indications to escalate to intubation.

page.mentor_intro: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen has moved from novelty to first-line therapy in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure within a decade, because it does several things simple oxygen cannot: it washes out anatomical dead space, generates a small positive-pressure effect, delivers a constant FiO2, and is comfortable enough that patients actually keep it on. The European Respiratory Society guideline formalises where the evidence supports it, the Cochrane review and meta-analysis quantify the benefit versus conventional oxygen, and understanding the device physiology is what lets you use it intelligently rather than reflexively.

teaching_points.claim: The ERS clinical practice guideline provides GRADE-based recommendations for HFNC alongside other non-invasive forms of respiratory support in adults with acute respiratory failure.

HFNC uses an air/oxygen blender, active humidifier and heated single tube to deliver flows up to 60 L/min, with physiological advantages including reduced anatomical dead space, a PEEP effect, constant FiO2 and good humidification.
A Cochrane systematic review evaluates HFNC versus standard oxygen therapy or non-invasive ventilation for adults with, or at risk of, acute respiratory failure in the ICU.
Meta-analysis of randomised trials compares HFNC with conventional oxygen therapy specifically in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, pooling safety and efficacy outcomes.

Optimal flow and FiO2 titration, and objective thresholds for escalation, are not standardised across studies.

page.mentor_intro: A hip fracture is never just an orthopaedic problem — it is a whole-patient event that lands on an older adult with multiple comorbidities, and the quality of the medical care around the operation determines a large share of the outcome. The internist's role spans preoperative risk assessment and risk reduction, timing of surgery, fluid optimisation, anaesthesia-mode selection and secondary-fracture prevention. The evidence for each component is thinner than patients assume, which makes disciplined perioperative optimisation, not any single technique, the real intervention.

teaching_points.claim: Hip fracture is a frequent cause of hospitalisation in the elderly with significant morbidity and mortality, and the internist/hospitalist plays a critical role across preoperative risk assessment, risk reduction, and timing of surgery.

An organised, systematic, coordinated multidisciplinary approach to perioperative management of geriatric surgical patients reduces complications, improves outcomes and lowers cost, and includes work-up and treatment of osteoporosis and fragility fractures.

In proximal femoral fracture, the role of advanced methods of perioperative fluid optimisation (invasive haemodynamic monitoring, protocolised strategies) in reducing risk remains unclear, per a Cochrane review.
Evidence comparing modes of anaesthesia for hip fracture surgery has been limited by heterogeneity in how perioperative outcomes are reported and defined.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of surgery (early versus delayed for medical optimisation) and which preoperative corrections change outcomes.

page.mentor_intro: Starting antiretroviral therapy is no longer a decision about whether but about with what and how fast. Contemporary guidelines recommend rapid initiation for everyone diagnosed, and the modern first-line landscape is dominated by integrase-inhibitor single-tablet regimens — above all bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide — chosen for efficacy, high resistance barrier, safety and simplicity. Regimen selection for a treatment-naive adult now turns on comorbidity fit, drug interactions, and how quickly the patient can start, with two-drug simplification reserved for specific maintenance situations.

teaching_points.claim: The 2024 IAS-USA panel updated consensus recommendations for HIV treatment and prevention from 249 relevant citations identified from literature searches.

A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis compares safety outcomes of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide with other ART regimens in treatment-naive people with HIV-1, addressing a key driver of regimen selection.

Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide is a once-daily single-tablet regimen whose phase 3 trials showed noninferiority to dolutegravir-based therapy; bictegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor with a high genetic barrier to resistance.

Strong evidence supports selected two-drug regimens as a strategy to address long-term toxicity, cost and convenience concerns of lifelong therapy, though not all two-drug combinations are equivalent.

uncertainties: Long-term metabolic effects of integrase inhibitors, including weight gain, are still being characterised.
Eligibility boundaries and durability of two-drug maintenance regimens versus standard three-drug therapy are not fully settled.

page.mentor_intro: Rheumatic complaints in a person with HIV sit at a genuinely three-way diagnostic fork: they may be direct viral or immune-dysregulation effects, musculoskeletal opportunistic infection, or immune reconstitution after starting ART. The spectrum runs from trivial self-limiting arthralgia through seronegative spondyloarthropathy and HIV-associated arthritis to vasculitis and myopathy. ART transformed the whole picture — prevalence patterns shifted and immune-mediated disease re-emerged with immune restoration — so the era in which a patient was treated matters as much as the joint that hurts.

teaching_points.claim: Rheumatic manifestations of HIV encompass arthralgia, HIV-associated arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, inflammatory myopathies, vasculitides and opportunistic musculoskeletal infections, arising from direct viral effects, immune dysregulation, opportunistic infection or ART-induced complications.
With highly active antiretroviral therapy and restored immunity, multiple immune-mediated rheumatic diseases have resurfaced in the HIV population.

Described articular syndromes include HIV-associated arthropathy, seronegative spondyloarthropathies (reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, undifferentiated SpA), rheumatoid arthritis and painful articular syndrome.

Combination ART has normalised life expectancy for adherent patients, so HIV management must now also address long-term complications of HIV and its treatment, including the evolving spectrum of rheumatic syndromes.

uncertainties: Safety and timing of immunosuppression and biologics in patients with untreated or uncontrolled HIV are not well defined.

page.mentor_intro: The question 'when should this patient start ART?' has a definitive answer now: immediately, regardless of CD4 count. The trials behind treat-all showed clinical and transmission benefits that ended the CD4-threshold era, and implementation studies such as Eswatini's MaxART trial proved a treat-all strategy is deliverable in real health systems. CD4 counts have not disappeared — they still stratify opportunistic-infection risk and flag advanced disease — but they no longer gate therapy. What remains is execution: same-day starts, linkage to care, and durable suppression, with roughly half of people with HIV worldwide still not on suppressive ART.

teaching_points.claim: Starting ART early, followed by continuous lifetime treatment, most effectively achieves durable virologic suppression and immune restoration, improving clinical outcomes and preventing sexual transmission.
Following randomised trials showing clinical and public-health benefits of immediate initiation, the CD4 count's role has shifted away from deciding when to start ART.

The MaxART Early Access to ART for All trial in Eswatini demonstrated that a Treat-All strategy can be implemented within a government-managed public health system to advance the UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets.

page.mentor_intro: Opportunistic infections are the price HIV extracts for untreated immunosuppression, and most of that price is avoidable: every major OI is tied to a CD4 threshold that should trigger either prophylaxis or heightened surveillance. Pneumocystis pneumonia remains the canonical example — CD4 below 200 cells/mm3 demands co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and the same drug treats established disease — while toxoplasmosis, MAC and CMV retinitis each occupy their own strata deeper in the CD4 nadir. With effective ART, the modern skill is not just starting prophylaxis but knowing when stopping is safe.

teaching_points.claim: In HIV-positive patients the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is strongly correlated with decreased CD4 cell count, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole chemoprophylaxis is highly effective.
Evidence supports discontinuing primary and secondary PJP prophylaxis once CD4 counts have recovered on ART, per a systematic review of discontinuation studies.

TMP-SMX is the first-line agent for treating PJP; dihydropteroate synthase mutations raise potential sulfamide resistance, and PJP still occurs with late presentation or virologic/immunologic failure despite cART.
EACS guideline version 13.0 (2025) was comprehensively revised and reorganised into HIV management/prevention and comorbidity parts, covering first-line regimens and related-infection management.
Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis reduces morbidity and mortality in people with HIV; systematic-review evidence informs WHO guidance on initiation, discontinuation and dose.

uncertainties: Exact CD4 thresholds and required duration of CD4 recovery differ between guidelines for stopping primary versus secondary PJP prophylaxis.
The clinical impact of TMP-SMX resistance mutations on treatment outcomes is incompletely defined.
mcq_angles: PJP prophylaxis threshold (CD4 <200 cells/mm3) and first-line agent (TMP-SMX).
When prophylaxis can be safely discontinued after ART-mediated CD4 recovery.
Adjunctive corticosteroids in moderate-to-severe PJP (guideline-based).
CD4-stratified OI risk: toxoplasmosis and MAC territory (<100) versus CMV retinitis (<50), per EACS.

A patient with PJP and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air is admitted; outline treatment and the indication for adjunctive steroids.
