page.mentor_intro: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is the most powerful prevention tool HIV medicine has ever had, and its failure so far is one of uptake, not efficacy: a daily tenofovir/emtricitabine pill (or two-monthly long-acting cabotegravir, which outperformed the oral standard in a landmark trial) reduces acquisition dramatically in randomised evidence, yet fewer than a fifth of those who could benefit in the US use it. The 2025 Canadian guideline update formalises indications and regimens, and dedicated guidance now addresses populations whose data lagged — notably transgender and nonbinary people, for whom hormone interactions and representation in trials remain live concerns.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 Canadian guideline updates clinical indications and drug regimens for both PrEP and PEP, drawing on systematic reviews and community-based organisation input.
PrEP effectiveness is well demonstrated in cisgender populations, while empirical data specific to transgender and nonbinary persons remain limited, warranting dedicated clinical guidance.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials confirms the clinical effectiveness and safety of oral tenofovir-containing PrEP against HIV acquisition.
Long-acting cabotegravir dosed every 8 weeks has low adherence demands and demonstrated efficacy versus oral TDF/FTC for PrEP; it is the only long-acting agent FDA-approved for HIV PrEP.
A single daily TDF/emtricitabine pill prevents HIV transmission, yet is used by fewer than 20% of people who could benefit in the United States.

uncertainties: Barriers to PrEP uptake and how best to implement long-acting injectable PrEP at scale are unresolved.
Renal and bone monitoring frequency, and drug interactions with gender-affirming hormones, need individualised application.
mcq_angles: PrEP regimen options: daily oral TDF/FTC, long-acting cabotegravir, and their comparative evidence.
Eligibility assessment and key populations, including transgender and nonbinary patients.
Trial evidence for cabotegravir versus oral PrEP.
Monitoring on PrEP: HIV testing, renal function, STI screening.
case_hooks: An MSM patient requests PrEP; choose a regimen and outline baseline assessment and follow-up monitoring.
A patient struggling with daily oral adherence asks about alternatives; discuss long-acting cabotegravir and its initiation schedule.
page.gaps: On-demand (2-1-1) dosing, STI screening intervals, renal monitoring protocols and pregnancy-related guidance are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the full Canadian 2025 guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: PrEP's problem is no longer whether it works but whether people can get it, stay on it, and be supported through the cycles of starting, stopping and restarting that real life imposes. Implementation science now dominates the literature: systematic reviews of best practices, global syntheses of provider barriers, and frameworks describing how programs must move from development and diffusion to genuine integration. Two populations remain systematically under-served — gay and bisexual men facing access disparities, and pregnant and postpartum women, for whom prevention is also child health.

PrEP implementation has moved through waves of development (2012–2015) and diffusion (2016–2018); reducing persistent disparities in access requires a next wave focused on integration of services.
Pregnancy is a critical window to elicit HIV vulnerability, offer testing, and provide PrEP for the pregnancy, postpartum period and future conception planning.

page.mentor_intro: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate with emtricitabine is the drug pair on which oral PrEP was built, and its clinical profile is unusually favourable: trial-level efficacy of 74–92% among participants with detectable drug levels, a safety record gathered across large prevention trials, and adverse events that are real but mostly manageable — nausea at initiation, small declines in renal function, and bone-density effects that matter mainly in younger patients. Knowing this safety architecture is what lets clinicians prescribe confidently and monitor selectively rather than reflexively.

teaching_points.claim: Prophylactic TDF-based regimens reduce the risk of HIV infection by 74 to 92% among participants with detectable drug levels, and available evidence supports PrEP efficacy when combined with other preventive methods.
Safety concerns are a recognised challenge in PrEP implementation, and dedicated reviews discuss the adverse-event profile and its management.
Adverse events observed in clinical trials of TDF/FTC for PrEP are documented in a dedicated drug-safety evaluation, informing monitoring practice.

Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) or tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (TAF/FTC) provides >99% protection against sexual HIV acquisition when taken with high adherence; pre-initiation testing mandates confirmed negative 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody testing, hepatitis B screening, and baseline eGFR assessment with quarterly follow-up.

uncertainties: Long-term (beyond trial follow-up) renal and bone effects of TDF-based PrEP in younger populations need ongoing surveillance.
How to individualise monitoring frequency for patients with borderline renal function is practice-dependent.
mcq_angles: Efficacy magnitude of TDF/FTC PrEP and the central role of adherence (detectable drug levels).
Adverse-effect profile: GI intolerance, renal tubular effects, bone density.

page.mentor_intro: The prognosis question in HIV has flipped completely: it is no longer 'how long' but 'how close to normal'. With modern ART, published life-expectancy estimates for people with HIV on treatment approach those of the general population, though a gap persists that depends on when treatment starts, baseline CD4, and health system context. The residual burden has also shifted — from AIDS-defining illness to non-AIDS comorbidity — which is why markers such as the CD4/CD8 ratio are being studied to flag patients whose immune dysfunction persists despite viral suppression. Late diagnosis remains the single most powerful determinant of a worse prognosis even after ART begins.

teaching_points.claim: A systematic review of published estimates finds life expectancy of HIV-positive adults on ART increasingly approaches that of the general population, though gaps remain by timing of initiation and setting.
Individuals first diagnosed with advanced HIV have higher mortality than those diagnosed earlier, even after starting ART, making early diagnosis the key prognostic lever.
The CD4/CD8 ratio and CD8+ T-cell count are being evaluated as prognostic markers for non-AIDS mortality in treated people living with HIV, beyond what CD4 count alone explains.

uncertainties: How much of the residual life-expectancy gap is attributable to persistent immune activation versus lifestyle and traditional risk factors.
Whether CD4/CD8-ratio-guided interventions actually improve non-AIDS outcomes is unproven.
mcq_angles: Life expectancy of treated HIV versus the general population, and what modifies the gap.
Advanced HIV at diagnosis as a prognostic determinant despite ART.
Non-AIDS mortality and emerging markers (CD4/CD8 ratio, CD8 count).
Prognosis counselling: what to tell a newly diagnosed patient.
case_hooks: A newly diagnosed 30-year-old asks 'will I live a normal life?'; construct an evidence-based answer.
Two patients start ART — one with CD4 600, one with CD4 40; compare expected trajectories and what changes counselling.
page.gaps: Quantitative life-expectancy figures by region and subgroup, and smoking/ lifestyle adjustment data, are not extractable from the retained abstracts; verify against the full systematic review before approval.

page.mentor_intro: HIV testing technology has quietly revolutionised the epidemic's control: the evolution from antibody-only assays through fourth-generation antigen/antibody tests to nucleic-acid detection has compressed the window period dramatically, and each advance matters most in acute infection, when viral load and transmissibility peak. Universal screening is now recommended for all adolescents and adults at least once, with repeat testing for those at risk — yet testing is also where the cascade leaks, since a reactive test that is not confirmed and linked achieves nothing.

teaching_points.claim: The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends universal HIV screening at least once for adolescents and adults aged 15 to 65, with additional screening for higher-risk patients, reflecting recent changes in testing technology.
Appropriate screening is the cornerstone of HIV-related care, with several recent changes in testing technology and screening recommendations.

The earliest months of HIV infection carry high viral loads and elevated transmissibility; narrowing the window between acquisition and a reactive test, followed by rapid ART linkage, is the key transmission-prevention opportunity.

uncertainties: Optimal screening intervals for higher-risk groups beyond 'at least annual' vary by guideline.
Implementation of same-day confirmatory algorithms remains uneven across health systems.

page.mentor_intro: Hodgkin lymphoma is the model of a curable malignancy: a disease whose modern combination chemotherapy and risk-stratified radiotherapy transformed survival from months to the great majority of patients cured. It divides into classical Hodgkin lymphoma — with its nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-depleted and lymphocyte-rich subtypes — and nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease, which behaves differently enough to manage as a related but distinct entity. Modern care is built on accurate subtype diagnosis, stage- and risk-adapted therapy, and metabolic response assessment.

teaching_points.claim: Hodgkin lymphoma comprises two distinct entities — classical HL and nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL — with classical subtypes including nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte depletion and lymphocyte-rich.

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma has an incidence of approximately 85,000 patients globally per year with a predilection for adolescents and young adults aged 15–39, and outcomes have improved dramatically since the introduction of combination chemotherapy.
Contemporary management rests on diagnosis, risk-stratification and stage-adapted therapy, updated in the 2025 review of the field.

uncertainties: How to minimise late toxicity (cardiac, second malignancy) while preserving cure rates in young, cured populations.
Optimal management of nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL, which diverges from classical HL pathways, is less standardised.

page.mentor_intro: More than 80% of advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma is now cured, so the frontline question has become how to escalate for those at highest risk of relapse without over-treating everyone else. Brentuximab vedotin — an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate — entered first-line therapy for advanced disease on the strength of the ECHELON-1-era evidence, trading modest toxicity for relapse reduction. Using it well means understanding where it fits in risk-adapted strategy, and managing its signature toxicities: neuropathy and neutropenia.

teaching_points.claim: More than 80% of patients with advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma are cured with contemporary approaches; the challenge is escalating therapy for high-risk patients while de-escalating safely for lower-risk patients.

Treatment intensity adaptation to early metabolic response assessed by PET/CT has been a cornerstone of risk stratification in advanced-stage HL, and monoclonal antibodies are being incorporated into first-line classical HL treatment.
Brentuximab vedotin is effective and well tolerated in classical Hodgkin lymphoma and was initially FDA-approved after failure of autologous transplant or at least two prior chemotherapy lines.

Neutropenia, including febrile neutropenia, is a significant frontline toxicity of advanced HL therapy, with risk differing across regimens and patient characteristics, and guideline-based management principles apply.

uncertainties: Whether PET-adapted de-escalation can spare toxicity without sacrificing cure is being refined trial by trial.
Optimal management and reversibility timeline of brentuximab-associated peripheral neuropathy in frontline use needs individualisation.

page.mentor_intro: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is the commonest breast cancer biology and the one in which the gap between early and advanced disease is most stark: adjuvant endocrine therapy converts early disease into high cure rates, yet advanced HR+ disease, though indolent, remains incurable and lethal. Modern management layers CDK4/6 inhibition onto endocrine backbone in the advanced setting, hunts resistance mechanisms — above all ESR1 mutations from aromatase-inhibitor pressure — and is now deploying PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibitors for tumours carrying those aberrations. Sequencing these tools intelligently is the core clinical skill.

teaching_points.claim: Breast cancer is highly heterogeneous, and treatment strategies vary by molecular features including hormone receptor and HER2 status.

Adjuvant endocrine therapy has improved outcomes in early-stage HR-positive disease, with choice of agent driven by menopausal state, patient preference and side effects, and molecular profiling enabling tailoring.
Dysregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway is increasingly recognised as a key driver in HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer, and inhibitors of this pathway are an established therapeutic class.
ESR1 mutations are a common mechanism of acquired resistance to aromatase-inhibitor estrogen deprivation in metastatic HR-positive disease and are an emerging biomarker guiding therapy selection.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing after CDK4/6 inhibitor progression (PI3K/AKT/mTOR agents, SERDs, ADCs) is evolving rapidly.
Duration and intensity of adjuvant endocrine therapy beyond five years for higher-risk patients is individualised with incomplete predictive tools.
mcq_angles: Endocrine agent selection by menopausal status (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, ovarian suppression).
CDK4/6 inhibitor role on the endocrine backbone in advanced disease.

page.mentor_intro: Hormone therapy for cardiovascular prevention is one of medicine's most instructive reversals. page.mentor_intro: When hospital pneumonia involves multidrug-resistant organisms, empiric therapy becomes a race between the antibiogram and the bedside: delay in appropriate therapy costs lives, but indiscriminate broad-spectrum use breeds the next resistance cycle. The modern armoury has expanded beyond carbapenems — new beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, cefiderocol, and sulbactam-durlobactam — while AmpC-producing Enterobacterales force tricky choices between third-generation cephalosporins, piperacillin-tazobactam and carbapenems. Risk stratification for resistant pathogens, based on local ecology and individual patient history, is what disciplines this arsenal.

page.mentor_intro: The first hour of septic shock is where mortality is decided, and its logic is simple even when the execution is not: recognise early, act simultaneously rather than sequentially, and re-measure. Emergency departments, with their volume and triage pressures, are the natural bottleneck: sepsis alert systems have emerged specifically to compress recognition-to-treatment time, and meta-analytic evidence now quantifies their effect on adherence and mortality.

page.mentor_intro: Septic and cardiogenic shock can look identical at the bedside — cold, hypotensive, obtunded — and treating the wrong one is actively harmful: fluids that rescue sepsis drown a failing ventricle, while inotropes started for cardiogenic shock can worsen septic vasoplegia. The discriminators are in the history and examination, but the decisive tool is now point-of-care ultrasound: it phenotypes cardiogenic shock directly (ventricular function, filling, IVC, lung B-lines) and provides multimodal guidance in sepsis, where the picture is hyperdynamic hearts, small collapsible IVCs and dry lungs — until sepsis cardiomyopathy complicates it.

teaching_points.claim: Cardiogenic shock is characterised by significant morbidity and mortality despite improving diagnosis and treatment; early recognition and accurate haemodynamic phenotyping by point-of-care ultrasound are crucial to improving prognosis.

Point-of-care ultrasound is a cost-effective, safe bedside modality that has emerged as an excellent multimodal tool for early diagnosis and management of sepsis and septic shock in the emergency department.

Hemodynamically, septic shock is characteristically hyperdynamic with warm extremities, low systemic vascular resistance, and normal-to-elevated cardiac output, whereas cardiogenic shock features cold extremities, high systemic vascular resistance, elevated filling pressures, and depressed cardiac index.

Bedside echocardiography immediately differentiates etiologies by revealing hyperkinetic left ventricular contraction and collapsed inferior vena cava in hypovolemic/distributive septic shock versus severely depressed ejection fraction, elevated E/e', and plethoric IVC in cardiogenic shock.

uncertainties: Mixed or septic cardiomyopathy phenotypes defy binary classification and need serial reassessment rather than a single label.
How far POCUS-derived haemodynamics should drive vasopressor and fluid decisions beyond clinical gestalt is still being defined.

page.mentor_intro: HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma is one of the fastest-rising cancers in high-income countries — and paradoxically one of the most curable, with a prognosis good enough that the 8th edition AJCC/UICC staging system now stages HPV-positive OPSCC separately from its HPV-negative counterpart. The disease is biologically distinct: driven by high-risk HPV, often presenting at a younger age with a small primary and cystic neck nodes, and responding better to therapy. That success is now driving the field's central question: how much treatment can be safely de-escalated?

teaching_points.claim: HPV-positive OPSCC has one of the most rapidly increasing incidences of any cancer in high-income countries, and the 8th edition UICC/AJCC staging separates it from HPV-negative disease to account for its improved prognosis.

HPV-positive OPSCC is driven primarily by HPV-16 oncoproteins E6 and E7, which degrade p53 and inactivate retinoblastoma (Rb) protein respectively, producing surrogate p16 overexpression on immunohistochemistry.

uncertainties: De-escalation trials (reduced radiation, chemotherapy sparing in favourable subgroups) are refining but not yet rewriting standard therapy.
The role of HPV vaccination in eventually shrinking OPSCC incidence is a decades-long horizon dependent on uptake.

page.mentor_intro: The FUTURE programme trials were the proof that changed cervical cancer from a screening-managed disease to a preventable one: prophylactic HPV vaccination against HPV16/18 — the types causing roughly 70% of cervical cancers — showed near-complete protection against vaccine-type precancer in per-protocol analyses of young women. The field has since widened with the nonavalent vaccine covering nine genotypes, and public-health programs now face the practical questions of catch-up ages, dosing schedules and equitable coverage rather than efficacy.

teaching_points.claim: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types is causally linked to cervical precancer and cancer; HPV16 and HPV18 cause approximately 70% of cervical cancers worldwide, and prophylactic vaccines protect against cervical precancer in randomised evidence synthesised by meta-analysis.

Routine vaccination at ages 9-12 prior to sexual debut and HPV exposure maximizes population herd immunity and long-term reduction in invasive cervical carcinoma.

page.mentor_intro: Helicobacter pylori remains the dominant infectious cause of gastritis, peptic ulcer, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma — and paradoxically, it has become harder to treat. Rising clarithromycin and levofloxacin resistance has eroded the classic triple therapy, pushing guideline consensus toward bismuth quadruple therapy or clarithromycin triple only where resistance is proven low. The modern approach is test-and-treat for appropriate patients, always with local resistance data and confirmation of eradication after therapy.

teaching_points.claim: H. pylori eradication has become increasingly challenging worldwide due to rising antimicrobial resistance, particularly to clarithromycin and levofloxacin, making bismuth quadruple therapy the preferred first-line regimen in high-resistance regions.

The Toronto Consensus and Maastricht VI guidelines recommend 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline) or non-bismuth concomitant quadruple therapy where bismuth is unavailable.

Confirmation of eradication with a validated urea breath test, monoclonal stool antigen test, or endoscopy-based biopsy must be performed at least 4 weeks after antibiotic completion and at least 2 weeks after stopping PPIs to avoid false-negative results.

uncertainties: Optimal first-line regimens vary by region with clarithromycin resistance thresholds; no single regimen fits all settings.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatorenal syndrome is the extreme manifestation of kidney dysfunction in cirrhosis — renal hypoperfusion driven by splanchnic vasodilation and effective arterial underfilling, not by intrinsic renal disease. Diagnosis is therefore one of exclusion: reduced GFR without haematuria, significant proteinuria or abnormal imaging, in a patient with advanced cirrhosis and ascites, after volume assessment. Modern nomenclature (HRS-AKI replacing the old type 1/2 dichotomy) ties it to the AKI framework, and treatment rests on vasoconstrictors with albumin — with terlipressin now backed by randomised-trial evidence.

teaching_points.claim: HRS is diagnosed when kidney function is reduced without evidence of intrinsic kidney disease such as haematuria, proteinuria or abnormal kidney imaging; it reflects reduced renal blood flow and GFR as the extreme of circulatory dysfunction in cirrhosis.
HRS characteristically occurs in advanced cirrhosis, driven by circulatory and haemodynamic alterations aggravated by systemic inflammation and bacterial translocation.
An ADQI/International Club of Ascites consensus addresses AKI in cirrhosis, a complication markedly increasing in-hospital morbidity and mortality, with HRS a specific phenotype.

Cirrhosis progresses through compensated, decompensated and further-decompensated stages with median survival of more than 15 years, 2 years and 9 months respectively, with worsening portal hypertension and vasodilatory dysfunction driving complications such as HRS.

uncertainties: Diagnostic cut-offs (creatinine thresholds in sarcopenic cirrhotics) are imperfect, and biomarkers distinguishing HRS from ATN remain investigational.
Optimal vasoconstrictor selection (terlipressin versus noradrenaline) and albumin dosing schedules vary by setting.

page.mentor_intro: Huntington disease has no disease-modifying therapy, so chorea management sits at the centre of what clinicians can actually offer. Chorea — random, jerk-like movements migrating between body parts — is the most common motor manifestation, interfering with daily activities, injuring patients and eroding quality of life. The therapeutic mainstay is VMAT2 inhibition: tetrabenazine's legacy is real efficacy weighed against depression and parkinsonism, while deutetrabenazine's deuterium substitution confers a longer half-life, less-frequent dosing and an improved tolerability profile — the reason it became the modern default.

teaching_points.claim: Chorea is defined as jerk-like movements moving randomly between body parts, caused by various disorders; current symptomatic therapy is quite effective, though few aetiology-targeted therapies exist.

Deutetrabenazine is FDA-approved for chorea in Huntington's disease; deuterium substitution gives a longer half-life allowing less-frequent daily dosing, and as a reversible VMAT2 inhibitor it depletes monoamines.

In Huntington's disease, an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment, chorea is the most common motor manifestation and may interfere with daily activities, reduce quality of life and cause injury.

First-line pharmacotherapy for debilitating chorea in Huntington disease includes vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) inhibitors (deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine, valbenazine) due to lower risks of tardive dyskinesia compared to typical antipsychotics; patients must be systematically screened and monitored for medication-induced depression and suicidality.

uncertainties: Whether suppressing chorea with VMAT2 inhibitors alters long-term functional outcomes beyond symptom relief is unknown.
Treatment of the non-choreic motor and neuropsychiatric burden (bradykinesia, depression, suicidality) needs separate, individualised strategies.

page.mentor_intro: The hybrid closed loop system is the closest thing to an artificial pancreas that mainstream care currently has: a continuous glucose sensor feeding an algorithm that adjusts pump-delivered insulin in real time, with the user still announcing meals. Building on pump and CGM technology that already improves HbA1c, time-in-range and hypoglycaemia burden, closed loops reduce the daily cognitive load of type 1 diabetes. The field has now matured enough for network meta-analysis to compare competing systems head-to-head, which is exactly the evidence clinicians need when choosing between them.

teaching_points.claim: Diabetes technologies represent a paradigm shift in type 1 diabetes care: pumps and continuous glucose monitors improve HbA1c, enhance time in range, limit severe hypoglycaemia and reduce diabetes distress, and the artificial pancreas extends this trajectory.
A network meta-analysis of randomised trials compares the efficacy and safety of different hybrid closed loop systems, including the Minimed 670G class, across children, adolescents and adults.

page.mentor_intro: Hydroxychloroquine is the closest thing SLE has to a foundation drug: almost universally recommended for its immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects, with benefits that extend beyond symptom control. Its liability is dose-limiting retinal toxicity — potentially irreversible, which makes early detection the whole game, and screening rather than blanket avoidance the accepted strategy. Balancing therapeutic levels against ocular safety, and layering cardiac monitoring for the QT-prolongation concern, is the core prescribing skill.

teaching_points.claim: Hydroxychloroquine has gained prominence in SLE treatment through a multifaceted mechanism of action as a lipophilic, lysosomotropic agent that accumulates in lysosomes and alkalinises them.
HCQ is a cornerstone of SLE therapy, but long-term exposure can cause potentially irreversible retinopathy in which early detection is critical.
To minimize lifetime risk of irreversible bull's-eye retinopathy, daily hydroxychloroquine dosing should not exceed 5.0 mg/kg actual body weight per day (AAO guidelines).

Annual retinal screening with spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and automated visual fields (10-2, or 24-2 in Asian patients) is recommended after 5 years of therapy, or earlier in high-risk patients.

uncertainties: Individual susceptibility to retinopathy varies unpredictably, so screening intervals and dose ceilings remain population-level rather than personalised.
Cardiac toxicity (QT prolongation, cardiomyopathy) monitoring practice is less standardised than retinal screening.

page.mentor_intro: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening is one of the few areas where ophthalmology has produced precise, iterative, dose-anchored guidance — and then revised it as prevalence data changed. The Marmor-led AAO recommendations established the framework: toxicity is parafoveal in most patients, risk rises steeply with dose and duration, and OCT is the screening tool of choice. The 2025 revision updates that framework for current knowledge, while rheumatology-facing reviews translate the same evidence into prescribing behaviour: keep doses at or below the accepted ceiling, and screen on schedule rather than stopping a drug that most patients need.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 AAO revision updates the hydroxychloroquine screening recommendations originally published a decade earlier, reflecting new knowledge about toxicity patterns.

The 2016 revision updated recommendations in light of new information about toxicity prevalence, risk factors, fundus distribution and screening-tool effectiveness, with the locus of damage parafoveal in most patients.
Research advances in HCQ retinopathy have direct implications for rheumatology care, where HCQ remains almost universally recommended in SLE and the toxicity is the major dose-limiting concern.

According to the revised American Academy of Ophthalmology (Marmor) guidelines, the maximum recommended daily dose of hydroxychloroquine is <=5.0 mg/kg actual body weight; annual retinal screening with spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and automated visual fields (10-2, or 24-2 in Asian patients) should begin within 5 years of therapy initiation, or earlier in high-risk patients.

uncertainties: The retina typically remains clinically normal for many years, with unpredictable individual susceptibility defining residual risk.
Optimal screening intervals for very low-risk patients versus high-risk (renal impairment, tamoxifen) subgroups continue to be individualised.

page.mentor_intro: Hypercalcaemia is common — roughly 1% of the population — and its severity grading drives everything: mild hypercalcaemia is usually asymptomatic or vaguely constitutional, while severe hypercalcaemia is a medical emergency of dehydration, confusion, shortened QT and crisis-level calcium. The two questions that organise every case are 'how high' and 'why': primary hyperparathyroidism dominates the outpatient mild-to-moderate end of the spectrum, malignancy dominates the severe end, and the PTH level separates them in a single test.

teaching_points.claim: Primary hyperparathyroidism, the most common cause of hypercalcemia, is most often identified in postmenopausal women, with clinical presentation evolving over 40 years into distinct phenotypes.
Hypercalcemia affects approximately 1% of the worldwide population; mild hypercalcemia (total calcium <12 mg/dL) is usually asymptomatic but may cause fatigue and constipation in about 20%.
Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for over 90% of all hypercalcemia cases; elevated or inappropriately normal intact PTH confirms parathyroid-dependent hypercalcemia.

Initial emergency stabilization of symptomatic or severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL [>3.5 mmol/L]) mandates vigorous isotonic saline hydration (200-300 mL/h) followed by intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) or calcitonin.

uncertainties: Whether asymptomatic mild hypercalcaemia from PHPT always warrants parathyroidectomy is individualised by guidelines.
The calcium-adjustment formulas and ionised-calcium thresholds in hypoalbuminaemia vary in reliability.

page.mentor_intro: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is the commonest metabolic complication of cancer and the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in hospitalised patients, affecting over a quarter of patients with cancer across its phenotypes — humoral (PTHrP-driven), osteolytic, and the rarer calcitriol-secreting and ectopic-PTH forms. Its epidemiology is shifting: incidence may be declining as cancer therapy improves, and mortality from HCM has fallen markedly with effective chemotherapy. Acute management remains hydration plus an antiresorptive — bisphosphonate or denosumab — with treatment of the underlying malignancy as the definitive lever.

teaching_points.claim: An Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline addresses treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy in adults; HCM is the most common metabolic complication of malignancy, with incidence possibly declining due to potent chemotherapeutic agents.
HCM affects over a quarter of patients being treated for cancer, with humoral, osteolytic, ectopic-hyperparathyroidism and vitamin-D-secreting lymphoma mechanisms.
Cancer-related hypercalcemia occurs in about 20–30% of patients with advanced cancer and is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalised patients.

For severe hypercalcemia of malignancy refractory to intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid 4 mg), the fully human monoclonal anti-RANKL antibody denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously) effectively normalizes serum calcium, particularly in renal impairment where bisphosphonates are contraindicated.

uncertainties: Choosing between bisphosphonates and denosumab — including cost, renal function constraints and hypocalcaemia risk — is individualised.
How emerging cancer therapies are reshaping HCM incidence and prognosis is an evolving picture.
mcq_angles: HCM phenotypes and their mechanisms (PTHrP versus osteolysis versus calcitriol).
Acute management sequence: saline rehydration, calcitonin for speed, antiresorptive for duration.
Denosumab versus bisphosphonate selection logic.
HCM as a poor-prognosis marker and the case for treating the malignancy.
case_hooks: A patient with metastatic breast cancer has calcium 3.4 mmol/L; sequence acute therapy and decide between bisphosphonate and denosumab.
A newly diagnosed myeloma patient presents with back pain and hypercalcaemia; connect the mechanism (osteolysis) to management.

Hypercalcemia of Malignancy: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications of Concurrently Elevated PTHrP and Calcitriol.

page.mentor_intro: The physiology of malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia explains its treatment: humoral hypercalcaemia mediated by PTHrP drives most cases, with osteolytic metastatic disease and calcitriol-secreting lymphomas completing the picture — and mixed PTHrP-plus-calcitriol elevations, once thought rare, are increasingly recognised across solid and haematological malignancies. Every therapy maps onto that physiology: aggressive saline rehydration restores the depleted extracellular volume, calcitonin lowers calcium within hours, and bisphosphonates or denosumab shut down the osteoclast-driven resorption that sustains it.

teaching_points.claim: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia — the most common cause of hypercalcemia in the emergency department — arises from direct bone resorption by metastases, vitamin D-secreting malignancies, and increased PTH or PTHrP levels.

Concurrent elevations in PTHrP and calcitriol, initially considered rare and solid-tumour-associated, are increasingly detected in hypercalcemic patients across solid and hematologic malignancies, with diagnostic and therapeutic implications.

PTH-related protein (PTHrP) secretion accounts for ~80% of hypercalcemia of malignancy (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy), characteristically producing high serum calcium with suppressed intact PTH and normal/low 1,25-(OH)2D.

Intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over 15 min) or denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) achieve sustained calcium normalization in >85% of malignancy cases, with denosumab preferred in renal impairment.

uncertainties: The diagnostic work-up of mixed-mechanism HCM is being re-evaluated as concurrent PTHrP/calcitriol elevations are recognised more often.
Whether earlier denosumab use in renal impairment changes outcomes versus cautious bisphosphonate use is practice-dependent.
mcq_angles: PTHrP physiology: why PTH is suppressed and why osteoclast activation is indirect.
Treatment timeline: saline (hours), calcitonin (days), bisphosphonate/denosumab (days to weeks).
Denosumab advantages in renal impairment and hypocalcaemia risk.
Recognising calcitriol-mediated HCM in lymphoma.
case_hooks: A hypercalcemic patient with lung cancer has suppressed PTH and elevated PTHrP; explain the mechanism and choose definitive therapy.
A lymphoma patient's hypercalcaemia persists after bisphosphonate; consider the calcitriol mechanism.

page.mentor_intro: Hypercapnic respiratory failure — ventilatory failure producing a rising PaCO2, usually on a background of COPD, obesity or neuromuscular disease — is the one form of acute respiratory failure where non-invasive ventilation is not just an option but the standard of care that changed outcomes. The ERS/ATS guideline anchors NIV application across acute respiratory failure aetiologies, while the COPD-exacerbation literature supplies the clinical context: exacerbations drive disease progression, wellbeing and mortality, and correcting the hypercapnia early is what breaks the downward spiral.

teaching_points.claim: The ERS/ATS guideline provides recommendations for clinical application of noninvasive ventilation across aetiologies of acute respiratory failure, based on current literature.

COPD exacerbations — acute deterioration in respiratory symptoms — fundamentally impact disease progression, comorbidities, wellbeing and mortality, and carry the largest share of COPD's socioeconomic burden.
Arterial blood gas criteria identifying acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure include PaCO2 > 45 mmHg with uncompensated acidemia (pH < 7.35).
Controlled oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 88-92% prevents worsening hypercapnia secondary to loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction (V/Q mismatch) and the Haldane effect.

uncertainties: NIV in hypercapnic failure from non-COPD causes (obesity-hypoventilation, neuromuscular) is extrapolated from thinner evidence.
The role of high-flow nasal oxygen as an alternative or bridge in milder hypercapnia is still being defined.

When NIV fails: intubation criteria and ceilings of care.

page.mentor_intro: In acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from a COPD exacerbation, NIV with bilevel support is the intervention with the strongest evidence in the whole of acute respiratory medicine — the Cochrane lineage showing it reduces acidosis, respiratory rate, intubation and mortality. But 'start NIV' is only half the competence: knowing the criteria that predict success, recognising failure early, and understanding where the newer evidence places high-flow nasal therapy relative to bilevel support is what separates protocol following from skilled management.

teaching_points.claim: NIV with bilevel positive airway pressure is commonly used and evidence-supported for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to COPD exacerbation, as evaluated in a systematic review.
A network meta-analysis compares non-invasive respiratory support modalities for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, with treatment failure, all-cause mortality and intubation as outcomes.

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BIPAP) is the first-line therapy for COPD exacerbations with persistent respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25-7.35, PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) despite optimal medical therapy, reducing intubation rates by >60%.

Immediate indications for invasive mechanical ventilation over NIV include severe encephalopathy, hemodynamic instability, uncontrolled vomiting, high aspiration risk, or failure of pH to improve after 1-2 hours of NIV.

uncertainties: Patient-selection boundaries for NIV versus early intubation (severe acidosis, altered consciousness, comorbidity burden) remain judgement-heavy.
Where high-flow nasal therapy sits for milder hypercapnia or as NIV-tolerance rescue is being defined by comparative trials.
mcq_angles: NIV success predictors: pH threshold, conscious level, cooperation.
Failure criteria: worsening acidosis despite NIV, exhaustion, hypoxia.
Cochrane-evidenced benefits: mortality and intubation reduction.
Modality comparison from the network meta-analysis.

page.mentor_intro: Hyperemesis gravidarum is the severe end of the nausea-and-vomiting-of-pregnancy spectrum and the leading cause of hospitalisation in early pregnancy, affecting roughly 0.3–3% of pregnancies and carrying real maternal morbidity. Most NVP peaks between 7 and 12 weeks and resolves by week 20, which frames both the natural history and the safety calculus of treatment. Management is stepwise — dietary and ginger first, then antiemetics, with ondansetron's reassuring data quieting much of the first-trimester anxiety — and escalates to rehydration, thiamine and occasionally steroids for refractory disease.

teaching_points.claim: Hyperemesis gravidarum, affecting approximately 0.3–3% of pregnancies, is the leading cause of hospitalisation during early pregnancy and is associated with substantial maternal morbidity.
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy affects about 75% of women, begins early in the first trimester, peaks between 7 and 12 weeks, and abates by week 20 in over 90%.
ACOG Practice Bulletin 153 provides evidence-based management guidance for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, recognising its impact on quality of life, healthcare costs and work absence.
Ginger supplementation has been evaluated in a systematic review for alleviating hyperemesis gravidarum, reflecting demand for alternatives to prescription medication.

page.mentor_intro: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is where a blood count becomes a multi-organ emergency: abnormal eosinophil accumulation independent of secondary causes, with highly variable manifestations driven by which organs the cells infiltrate — heart, lung, gut, skin, nervous system. The field's modern backbone is classification: separating reactive (secondary) from clonal (primary, e.g. FIP1L1-PDGFRA) disease, because targeted therapy — imatinib for the tyrosine-kinase-driven form — transformed one subtype from chronic illness to molecularly-curable disease. Hypereosinophilia above 1.5 × 10⁹/L with end-organ damage defines the syndrome, and corticosteroids remain the rapid organ-protection bridge.

teaching_points.claim: The eosinophilias span non-hematologic (secondary/reactive) and hematologic (primary/clonal) disorders with potential end-organ damage; hypereosinophilia is generally defined as a peripheral blood eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 10⁹/L.
Hypereosinophilic syndrome comprises disorders of abnormal eosinophil accumulation in blood or peripheral tissues independent of known secondary causes, with highly variable clinical manifestations.
Refined international diagnostic criteria and classification separate eosinophilia from hypereosinophilic syndrome, with organ damage often prompting the HES diagnosis.

Diagnostic evaluation of hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) requires demonstrating persistent absolute eosinophilia >=1.5 x 10^9/L with eosinophil-mediated end-organ damage (cardiac fibrosis, thromboembolism, neuropathy); screening for the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene via RT-PCR or FISH is mandatory, as positive cases achieve rapid, complete hematologic remission with low-dose imatinib.

uncertainties: Organ-damage prediction from eosinophil counts alone is poor, so surveillance intensity is empirical.
Sequencing of steroids, imatinib and emerging targeted agents in non-clonal HES is individualised.
mcq_angles: Definition thresholds and the reactive versus clonal classification.
End-organ patterns: Loeffler endocarditis, neuropathy, dermatologic and GI involvement.
FIP1L1-PDGFRA and the imatinib-responsive subtype.
Steroids as acute organ-protection therapy.

page.mentor_intro: Hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state is the hyperglycaemic emergency of older, type 2, often previously-undiagnosed diabetic patients — profound hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolarity with enough residual insulin to suppress ketogenesis, so no significant acidosis. It carries higher mortality than DKA, driven by the age and comorbidity of its victims, and its treatment is a discipline of slow rehydration and careful osmolality decline: fluids first, insulin lower-dose, and obsessive attention to sodium correction as glucose falls.

teaching_points.claim: DKA and HHS are the most serious hyperglycemic emergencies; HHS occurs more in adult and elderly type 2 diabetes patients, with overlapping clinical features.
DKA and HHS are life-threatening complications increasing mortality and morbidity, and reaching uniform consensus on diagnostic criteria and treatment remains a challenge.
DKA and HHS are characterised by insulinopaenia and severe hyperglycaemia, requiring prompt recognition, diagnosis and treatment.

uncertainties: Diagnostic boundaries between HHS, HHS-DKA overlap and severe hyperglycaemia are variably defined across guidelines.
Optimal rehydration tonicity, osmolality decline targets and anticoagulation in HHS remain practice-dependent.

page.mentor_intro: Hyperkalaemia is the electrolyte emergency everyone meets first and understands last: common, frequently iatrogenic, and dangerous because of malignant arrhythmia. Its management has three tiers with different speeds and purposes — membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium, intracellular shift with insulin-dextrose and beta-agonists, and actual potassium removal with dialysis or binders — and the art lies in knowing which tier the patient needs and how long each buys. Controversies persist, not least around the older exchange resins and the role of the newer binders.

teaching_points.claim: Hyperkalaemia is a common, potentially life-threatening electrolyte abnormality because of its association with malignant cardiac arrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest, encountered across acute and chronic care and disproportionately affecting patients with kidney disease, heart failure and diabetes.
Classic hyperkalemia treatments and their controversies are evaluated in a dedicated review, including new medications for management.

Severe hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes: peaked T waves, widened QRS, PR prolongation) requires immediate membrane stabilization with intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) within 1-3 minutes.

Intracellular potassium shift therapies (regular insulin 10 units IV with 25-50g dextrose, and inhaled nebulized albuterol) act within 15-30 minutes, temporizing while elimination via loop diuretics, potassium binders (patiromer, SZC), or hemodialysis is arranged.

uncertainties: Treatment thresholds for mild asymptomatic hyperkalaemia, especially with ECG ambiguity, vary across guidelines.
The clinical value of newer potassium binders in chronic management versus acute settings is still being defined.
mcq_angles: ECG progression: peaked T waves, PR prolongation, sine wave.
Three-tier management and the speed of each intervention.
Common precipitants: CKD, RAAS inhibitors, potassium-sparing drugs, tissue breakdown.
Pseudohyperkalaemia and confirmatory testing.

page.mentor_intro: Emergency hyperkalaemia treatment is a study in timelines: calcium works in minutes, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium over an hour or two, and dialysis or binders are the only true removal. The KDIGO conference summary anchors the modern ED approach, including the pivotal insight that ECG changes are neither perfectly sensitive nor specific — which pushes treatment decisions toward the clinical picture and potassium trend rather than a single number. In cardiology patients the stakes are doubled: RAAS inhibitors and MRA therapy that prolong life also cause the hyperkalaemia, creating a treat-the-number versus protect-the-therapy dilemma.

teaching_points.claim: A KDIGO consensus conference summarises acute hyperkalemia in the emergency department, noting predisposing conditions (kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes, tissue trauma) and medications including RAAS inhibitors.
Treatment options have evolved only modestly since the cation-exchange-resin era, while newer agents have entered the landscape, as reviewed in a 'something old, something new' framework.
Hyperkalaemia is one of the most common electrolyte disorders in cardiovascular patients; in population cohorts up to four in ten developed hyperkalaemia, in addition to drug-related risks.

uncertainties: Whether ECG-guided treatment thresholds improve outcomes over potassium-guided thresholds is not established.
Balancing life-prolonging RAAS-inhibitor therapy against recurrent hyperkalaemia needs individualised protocols.

page.mentor_intro: No universally accepted consensus exists on hyperkalaemia management — thresholds, monitoring cadence and escalation vary across guidelines — which makes the underlying physiology the only reliable guide. Diagnosis starts with confirming the potassium is real (pseudohyperkalaemia is common), then grading severity and ECG changes. The newest chapter in management is pharmacological removal: the expert-panel literature on patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate reframes chronic hyperkalaemia as a manageable condition rather than an automatic reason to stop RAAS-inhibitor therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Despite various guidelines, no universally accepted consensus exists on hyperkalemia monitoring and management, with variation in potassium thresholds and management approaches.
A multidisciplinary expert panel addresses the role of new potassium binders in hyperkalemia management, a condition frequent in CKD, heart failure, diabetes, hypertension and RAAS-inhibitor use.
Timely recognition and appropriate treatment of acute hyperkalaemia are critical to prevent arrhythmias and death, per an evidence-based emergency-care review.

Emergency management of severe or ECG-manifest hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, widened QRS) requires immediate intravenous calcium gluconate or calcium chloride for cardiac membrane stabilization, followed by intracellular shifting agents (IV insulin with dextrose, inhaled salbutamol), and definitive potassium removal via loop diuretics, gastrointestinal cation exchangers (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), or emergency hemodialysis.

uncertainties: Whether chronic binder therapy to enable RAAS inhibitors improves hard cardiovascular outcomes is not yet proven.
Guideline heterogeneity in thresholds reflects absent trial-level evidence for specific cut-offs.

page.mentor_intro: Hypermobility spectrum disorders and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome occupy the space between asymptomatic joint laxity and connective-tissue disease, and they are diagnosed late because they demand heightened clinical suspicion rather than a single test. The Beighton score quantifies laxity, but the clinical burden is systemic: gastrointestinal dysmotility and disorders of gut-brain interaction, autonomic dysfunction including POTS, chronic pain and fatigue. Modern guidance recognises this multi-system reality, with AGA guidance addressing the GI-autonomic overlap that drives much of the quality-of-life impact.

page.mentor_intro: Hypernatraemia is a disorder of water balance, not sodium excess: total-body water deficit relative to sodium, generated either because intake failed (impaired thirst, no access, intubation) or because renal or extrarenal losses outpaced it. That framing makes the diagnostic approach logical — assess volume status, then urine osmolality and sodium — and the treatment dangerous if rushed: chronic hypernatraemia must be corrected slowly to avoid cerebral oedema, while acute-onset hypernatraemia can be corrected faster. Most cases signal an underlying access or consciousness problem and carry real mortality when mismanaged.

teaching_points.claim: Hypernatremia is a disorder of the homeostatic balance of body water and sodium content, and that imbalance is the basis of the diagnostic approach.
In chronic dysnatremias a slow correction rate (<10 mmol/L/24 h) is indicated to avoid neurological complications, whereas acute dysnatremias (<48 h onset) may justify more rapid correction.

Water deficit should be calculated ([Target Na - Current Na] / Current Na * Total Body Water) and replaced predominantly with free water (oral/enteral water or IV 5% dextrose) while matching ongoing urinary and insensible losses.
In chronic hypernatremia (>48 hours), the correction rate must not exceed 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent fatal cerebral edema resulting from intracellular idiogenic osmolyte swelling.

uncertainties: The safe correction ceiling in individual patients, especially with coexisting hyponatraemia risk factors, is approximated rather than precise.
Whether desmopressin adjuncts to prevent overcorrection improve outcomes is not established.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic algorithm: volume status, urine osmolality, urine sodium.
Central versus nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and the desmopressin test.

page.mentor_intro: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is what happens when an immune response to an inhaled antigen becomes an interstitial lung disease: complex, heterogeneous, and organised in modern guidelines around fibrotic and non-fibrotic phenotypes, which differ in course, management and prognosis. The antigen is often domestic or occupational — bird exposures, moulds, farming dusts — and the occupational-ILD literature reminds us the true burden is underestimated through under-recognition. Diagnosis is a convergence of exposure history, imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage and sometimes biopsy, and treatment begins with antigen removal.

teaching_points.claim: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a complex, heterogeneous interstitial lung disease occurring when susceptible individuals develop exaggerated immune responses to inhaled antigens; guidelines organise evaluation around fibrotic and non-fibrotic phenotypes.
Millions of workers are exposed to substances causing occupational interstitial lung diseases, with the burden likely underestimated through under-recognition and under-reporting.

High-resolution chest CT typically shows centrilobular ground-glass nodules, mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expiratory imaging (headcheese sign/three-density pattern), and upper-to-mid lung zone distribution.
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) characteristically demonstrates marked lymphocytosis (>20-30%, often >50%) with a decreased CD4/CD8 ratio, distinguishing HP from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

uncertainties: Antigen identification fails in a substantial minority despite detailed exposure assessment.
Immunosuppression benefit in fibrotic HP versus non-fibrotic HP differs and is less evidence-based than in other ILDs.

page.mentor_intro: The single most effective treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis is not a drug — it is removing the antigen, and it works best in the non-fibrotic phenotype before irreversible remodelling sets in. But removal only works if you find the antigen, which is why the updated clinical definition and diagnostic recommendations from the international collaboration matter so much in practice: they sharpen exposure elicitation and phenotype assignment. Where fibrosis has established, the conversation shifts to immunosuppression, antifibrotic-adjacent strategies and transplant assessment.

teaching_points.claim: An international collaboration has updated the clinical definition and diagnostic recommendations for hypersensitivity pneumonitis, focusing on fibrotic and non-fibrotic phenotypes, and their transfer to clinical practice is shaping management and prognosis.

HP ranges from acute manifestations to progressive fibrosis and is classified as nonfibrotic or fibrotic based on imaging and histopathological features, with pathophysiology driven by inhaled environmental antigens.

Strict environmental antigen avoidance (e.g. removing avian pets, remediating indoor mould, avoiding contaminated humidifiers) is the single most critical intervention capable of halting disease progression and avoiding lung fibrosis.

Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily tapered over months) improve symptoms and lung mechanics in inflammatory/non-fibrotic HP, whereas fibrotic HP requires consideration of antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) and lung transplant evaluation.

uncertainties: How aggressively to immunosuppress fibrotic HP, and whether antifibrotic therapy has a role, remains incompletely evidence-based.
The prognosis impact of strict antigen avoidance versus partial reduction is not quantified.
mcq_angles: Antigen avoidance as first-line therapy, and what to do when no antigen is found.
Fibrotic versus non-fibrotic prognostic divergence.
Updated international diagnostic criteria and their phenotype focus.
Escalation pathway: steroids, steroid-sparing agents, antifibrotics, transplant.

page.mentor_intro: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is not one disease but a family of them, and the antigen defines the member: bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung, hot-tub lung and the summer-type HP of humid climates each carry their own exposure pattern, clinical phenotype and prognosis. Systematic curation of reported HP-associated exposures — long missing — now underpins confident antigen identification, which remains the single most valuable diagnostic and therapeutic act in the disease, because removal of the right exposure is the only intervention that changes the natural history.

teaching_points.claim: A scoping review systematically identified reported exposures associated with HP and their clinical phenotypes, addressing the absence of curated exposure lists to inform diagnosis.

Major occupational and domestic triggers include avian antigens (pigeon, parakeet, and goose-feather bedding causing bird fancier's lung) and thermophilic actinomycetes (Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula in moldy hay causing farmer's lung).

Industrial exposure variants include isocyanate-induced HP in spray painters, metalworking fluid HP ('machine operator's lung'), and cheese washer's lung (Penicillium roqueforti), highlighting the necessity of detailed occupational histories.

Prognosis strongly correlates with specific causative antigens and host clearance: avian antigen exposure and occult domestic exposures carry higher risks of progression to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis than episodic farming antigens.

uncertainties: Many HP patients have no identifiable antigen despite systematic exposure assessment, limiting phenotype-based prognosis.
The strength of association between specific antigens and fibrotic versus non-fibrotic courses is incompletely quantified.
mcq_angles: Classic antigen-disease pairings: birds, moulds, farming dusts, hot-tub aerosols.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertension management is the highest-yield intervention in cardiovascular medicine, and it is a moving target: the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline now retires and replaces the 2017 framework, resetting definitions, targets and treatment pathways. The through-line of modern guidance is earlier action — diagnosing with proper technique and out-of-office confirmation, starting pharmacotherapy promptly at threshold, and using combination therapy upfront for most patients — while an evidence-based update tracks the trials that shaped each change since 2017.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline for the prevention, detection, evaluation and management of high blood pressure in adults retires and replaces the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline.
Important findings bearing on hypertension prevention, detection and management have accumulated since the 2017 guideline, summarised and contextualised in an evidence-based update.

First-line antihypertensive classes with proven cardiovascular morbidity and mortality reductions encompass thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide), ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

Initial dual-combination therapy using two complementary first-line agents of different classes is recommended for patients with Stage 2 hypertension (BP >= 140/90 mmHg) or BP >20/10 mmHg over target.

uncertainties: Out-of-office confirmation logistics and white-coat versus masked hypertension management remain incompletely implemented.
How the 2025 revisions change real-world control rates versus the 2017 framework is an open implementation question.

page.mentor_intro: Blood-pressure targets are where guidelines genuinely diverge — and understanding why is more useful than memorising numbers. The American tradition targets ≤130/80 for most adults on intensive-control evidence; European guidance historically tolerated higher targets for achieved-benefit simplicity; and pragmatic primary-care frameworks like Hypertension Canada's exist because control rates regress when guidance is not implementable. An in-depth review of the 2021-era guidelines maps the concordant core (treat early, combine agents, measure properly) against the discordant edges (targets, initial combinations).

teaching_points.claim: The Hypertension Canada guideline provides pragmatic primary-care-focused recommendations to improve adult hypertension management, addressing regressing treatment and control rates.

Multiple evidence-based national and international hypertension guidelines published within four years show mostly concordant recommendations with some discordant opinions, mapped in an in-depth review.
Major international guidelines converge on recommending a target systolic blood pressure <130 mmHg and diastolic <80 mmHg for most adults with confirmed hypertension and elevated cardiovascular risk.

Out-of-office blood pressure confirmation using automated office blood pressure (AOBP), ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), or home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) is mandatory to rule out white-coat and masked hypertension.

uncertainties: Whether the intensive <130/80 target generalises to all subgroups outside trial populations is debated.
How to operationalise individualised targets in routine practice is unresolved across guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: How low to drive blood pressure is hypertension's defining controversy. Intensive control — the ≤130/80 philosophy — has trial evidence for cardiovascular protection, but its net clinical benefit varies by target and patient characteristics, and benefit-harm trade-off analyses now quantify what guidelines assert. The counterpoint literature reminds us the optimal target remains undefined, that more intense therapy carries hypotension, renal and electrolyte costs, and that 'lower is better' is a population claim that needs individual calibration at the bedside.

teaching_points.claim: Although intensive blood pressure control is recommended by major guidelines, its overall benefit-harm balance remains uncertain; net clinical benefit varies by blood pressure target and patient characteristics.

The optimal target blood pressure is undefined and controversial; recent American guidelines recommend ≤130/80 mm Hg for essentially all adults, while more intense versus standard therapy trade-offs continue to be debated.

Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering (target <120 mmHg vs <140 mmHg) significantly reduces major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in high-risk non-diabetic adults (SPRINT trial).

Intensive therapy requires close surveillance for predictable adverse effects, including asymptomatic serum creatinine rise, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia).

uncertainties: The harms threshold — at what achieved BP hypotension-related events offset cardiovascular gains — differs by frailty and age.
Real-world adherence to intensive targets is substantially worse than trial conditions, diluting population benefit.
mcq_angles: SPRINT-style intensive-control evidence and its generalisability.

page.mentor_intro: Treating hypertension in the very elderly is where the evidence-based and the humane can collide. Systolic hypertension dominates as arteries stiffen, and trial data support treatment well into the ninth decade — but frailty, orthostasis, polypharmacy and limited life expectancy all argue for targets individualised beyond the population guideline. The Cochrage update on higher targets found the major trials aimed at modest systolic goals and demonstrated cardiovascular benefit, while frailty-focused guidance stresses standing pressures, deprescribing review and shared decision-making over rigid numbers.

teaching_points.claim: Arterial hypertension prevalence rises with age, mainly systolic hypertension from arterial stiffening, and chronic elevation remains a major cardiovascular risk factor in older populations.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia — are among the leading causes of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide, complicating a substantial share of pregnancies. page.mentor_intro: Pre-eclampsia is a life-threatening, uniquely human disease of pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality — with consequences that outlast delivery, since survivors carry increased lifetime risks of stroke, cardiovascular disease and diabetes. The modern paradigm has shifted upstream: first-trimester combined screening (maternal factors, blood pressure, uterine-artery Doppler, biomarkers) to identify high-risk women, and low-dose aspirin started by 16 weeks to prevent early-onset disease, the subtype with the worst outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: Pre-eclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality; survivors have reduced life expectancy with increased risks of stroke, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

Early-onset pre-eclampsia requiring preterm delivery carries higher complication risks, and low-dose aspirin initiated before 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia in high-risk women identified by first-trimester screening.
Hypertensive disorders complicate approximately 16% of pregnancies in the United States, and low-dose aspirin initiation by 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia in high-risk women.

Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed by new-onset hypertension (>=140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks of gestation accompanied by proteinuria (>=300 mg/24h or protein:creatinine ratio >=30 mg/mmol) or maternal organ dysfunction; definitive management is planned delivery, with intravenous magnesium sulfate indicated for eclampsia prophylaxis and oral labetalol, nifedipine, or hydralazine for severe hypertension.

uncertainties: Which screening algorithm performs best in different populations is still being optimised.
Post-partum cardiovascular risk-reduction strategies for pre-eclampsia survivors are not yet formalised.

page.mentor_intro: A hypertensive emergency is not a number — it is acute blood-pressure rise with new or worsening end-organ damage, and everything follows from identifying the damaged organ: encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary oedema, or acute kidney injury. Management is deliberately heterogeneous and agent-matched: labetalol, nicardipine, esmolol, glyceryl trinitrate and sodium nitroprusside each fit specific organ scenarios, and the goal is controlled, partial reduction — typically around 20–25% in the first hours — because normalising pressure too fast steals cerebral and coronary perfusion. Malignant hypertension, defined by retinal haemorrhages or exudates with acute renal deterioration, is the phenotype that most often reaches the ICU.

teaching_points.claim: A hypertensive crisis is a sudden, significant BP rise to 180/120 mmHg or higher and is a medical emergency capable of causing heart attack, stroke and other life-threatening problems; management strategies are evaluated in a systematic review.

Patients with hypertensive emergencies, malignant hypertension and acute severe hypertension are managed heterogeneously; initiating therapy and setting acute BP goals requires scenario-specific considerations, per the British and Irish Hypertension Society.
Malignant hypertension is defined by bilateral retinal haemorrhages or exudates, with or without papilloedema, plus acute heart failure and acute deterioration in renal function.

Hypertensive emergency requires acute severe blood pressure elevation (>180/120 mmHg) with evidence of impending or progressive acute target organ damage; parenteral titratable antihypertensives (labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, sodium nitroprusside) are indicated to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 20-25% over the first hour (except in aortic dissection where systolic BP <120 mmHg within 20 minutes is targeted).

uncertainties: The ideal first-line IV agent by clinical scenario remains partly institution- and resource-dependent.
Precise BP-reduction targets in each end-organ emergency vary across position documents.
mcq_angles: Emergency versus urgency distinction and the end-organ survey.
Agent selection by scenario (aortic dissection, eclampsia, pulmonary oedema).
The controlled-partial-reduction principle and its physiology.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — nephroangiosclerosis — is the kidney disease that accompanies chronic essential hypertension, known for over a century and still diagnosed more by clinical context than by biopsy, which is reserved for doubtful or atypical cases. The clinical picture is one of slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with subnephrotic proteinuria in a patient with long-standing, often poorly controlled hypertension. The modern nuance is that the causal arrow is not always simple: some 'hypertensive' nephrosclerosis may reflect primary renal microvascular disease driving the hypertension rather than vice versa, particularly in certain ancestries.

teaching_points.claim: Nephroangiosclerosis — kidney disease accompanying chronic essential hypertension — has been recognised for over a century; definitive diagnosis is by renal biopsy, reserved for doubtful or atypical cases.

Pathologically, chronic arteriolosclerosis is characterized by medial hypertrophy, intimal hyalinosis of afferent arterioles, and downstream ischemic glomerulosclerosis, leading to progressive non-proteinuric or subnephrotic renal decline.

High-risk APOL1 genetic variants (G1 and G2 alleles) strongly predispose individuals of African ancestry to accelerated hypertensive nephrosclerosis and aggressive progression toward end-stage renal disease.

Blood pressure control targeting <130/80 mmHg using RAAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors or ARBs) combined with lifestyle sodium restriction (<2 g/day) represents the cornerstone of secondary renal protection.

uncertainties: The bidirectionality question — whether renal microvascular disease precedes hypertension in some patients — is unresolved.
Whether aggressive BP control halts established nephrosclerosis beyond general CKD benefit is inferred rather than proven.

page.mentor_intro: Hyperthyroidism is common — roughly 0.2–1.4% of people worldwide — and its management rewards precise diagnosis because the aetiology dictates the treatment. Overt disease is biochemically defined by suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and/or T3; beyond that, the thyrotoxicosis work-up separates true hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodular goitre — hormone overproduction) from thyroiditis (hormone leak), using TRAb, uptake scanning and clinical signs such as orbitopathy. Each pathway has distinct therapy: antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, surgery, or simply time and beta-blockade.

teaching_points.claim: Overt hyperthyroidism — suppressed TSH with high T3 and/or free T4 — affects approximately 0.2% to 1.4% of people worldwide; subclinical disease is defined by low TSH with normal hormone levels.

page.mentor_intro: Separating Graves' disease from toxic nodular goitre is the pivotal fork in thyrotoxicosis management, and the ATA guideline supplies the algorithm. Both share suppressed TSH and elevated hormones; they diverge on TRAb — positive in Graves', negative in nodular disease — and on the radionuclide uptake scan, which shows diffuse uptake in Graves' versus patchy or focal uptake in toxic nodular goitre. The distinction is not academic: Graves' warrants consideration of antithyroid drugs as first-line with thionamide complications in view, while toxic nodular goitre virtually never remits on drugs and heads toward radioiodine or surgery.

teaching_points.claim: The ATA guideline describes evidence-based diagnosis and management of hyperthyroidism and other causes of thyrotoxicosis, where appropriate treatment requires accurate diagnosis and is influenced by comorbidity and patient preference.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TRAb / TSI) demonstrate >97-99% sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing Graves' disease, distinguishing it from toxic nodular goitre and destructive thyroiditis without radioiodine uptake scans.

Toxic multinodular goitre and solitary toxic adenoma are caused by activating TSH-receptor somatic mutations; unlike Graves' disease, they never remit spontaneously and require definitive therapy (radioactive iodine or surgical resection).

First-line antithyroid drug therapy for Graves' disease is methimazole (MMI), except during the first trimester of pregnancy or in thyroid storm where propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred due to MMI-associated embryopathy.

uncertainties: TRAb-negative thyrotoxicosis sometimes needs imaging to resolve the aetiology, and uptake scans are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Whether Graves' first-line should be thionamides or radioiodine varies by guideline, geography and patient factors.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertriglyceridaemia is a two-front problem: very high levels drive acute pancreatitis — the traditional emergency — while moderate elevations contribute to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease through triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, a causal role now supported by multiple lines of evidence. Management starts with the threshold logic: pancreatitis risk rises steeply above roughly 10 mmol/L, demanding immediate triglyceride lowering with fibrates and strict dietary fat restriction. The cardiovascular front is where the field is moving fastest, with emerging agents targeting triglyceride-rich lipoproteins addressing the unmet need left by fibrates and omega-3s.

teaching_points.claim: Hypertriglyceridemia is associated with increased risk of acute pancreatitis and has more recently been linked to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
HTG arises from defects in triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism, with increased morbidity and mortality from pancreatitis and ASCVD; traditional therapies include fibrates and omega-3 agents.
Multiple lines of evidence support a causal role of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of novel targeted therapies.

Severe hypertriglyceridemia (fasting triglycerides >10 mmol/L or >885 mg/dL) confers an acute risk of acute pancreatitis; initial emergency therapy focuses on strict dietary fat restriction (<10-15% of calories), alcohol abstinence, insulin infusion if hyperglycemic, and rapid initiation of fibrates (fenofibrate) or high-dose prescription omega-3 fatty acids (icosapent ethyl).

uncertainties: Whether triglyceride-lowering beyond LDL reduction improves cardiovascular outcomes awaits outcomes-trial confirmation for the newest agents.
The precise pancreatitis-risk threshold varies across studies and guideline statements.

page.mentor_intro: Mavacamten opened a new era in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by targeting the disease mechanism itself: a selective, reversible cardiac myosin inhibitor that reduces excessive actin-myosin cross-bridging, easing hypercontractility, improving compliance and — critically — reducing the left-ventricular outflow-tract gradient that defines obstructive disease. For patients whose symptoms persisted despite beta-blockers and disopyramide, the myosin-inhibitor class converts 'optimise and accept' into a pharmacological option with measurable gradient and symptom endpoints, at the price of needing careful echo-supervised titration for systolic dysfunction.

teaching_points.claim: Mavacamten, the first selective reversible cardiac myosin inhibitor, reduces excessive actin-myosin cross-bridging, decreasing myocardial hypercontractility in obstructive HCM.
Obstructive HCM results from asymmetric septal hypertrophy obstructing left-ventricular outflow and is linked to sarcomeric-protein gene mutations.
HCM involves abnormal left-ventricular hypertrophy without common causes; the most common form involves the basal septum and can obstruct the LV outflow tract, causing exertional symptoms.

uncertainties: Long-term outcomes — whether myosin inhibitors alter mortality or just symptoms and gradients — are not yet established.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has transformed from a feared diagnosis of sudden death into a contemporary, highly treatable condition, and the 2024 AHA/ACC guideline consolidates that shift. Two skills organise care: relieving obstruction — pharmacologically with beta-blockers, disopyramide and now mavacamten, or procedurally with septal myectomy or alcohol ablation — and stratifying sudden-cardiac-death risk to decide who needs an ICD. Personalised pathways along these axes now alter the natural history of a disease that remains the commonest inherited cardiomyopathy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2024 AHA/ACC and partner-society guideline provides comprehensive recommendations for HCM management.

HCM is a relatively common, globally distributed, often inherited primary cardiac disease that has become a contemporary highly treatable condition, with options that alter natural history along personalised pathways.

HCM is a common yet under-recognised genetic structural heart condition characterised by left-ventricular hypertrophy, presenting as obstructive disease with elevated LVOT gradients or non-obstructive disease.

In symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LVOT gradient >=50 mmHg), first-line medical therapy begins with non-vasodilating beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten provides significant reductions in LVOT obstruction and NYHA class improvement, reserving surgical septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for refractory cases.
