page.mentor_intro: Hyperuricaemia is the biochemical substrate of gout — monosodium urate crystals form when urate exceeds its solubility threshold — and gout is the commonest inflammatory arthritis worldwide, affecting 41 million adults and still rising. Management remains stubbornly suboptimal: renal and gut urate excretion sit centrally in regulation, which is why urate-lowering therapy targets excretion pathways, and why diet — while contributory — is rarely sufficient alone. The modern frame is multifactorial: genetic predisposition, environmental stimuli and gut dysbiosis all feed a disease that is curable with properly titrated urate-lowering therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis driven by the precipitation of monosodium urate crystals in articular and periarticular tissues when serum urate levels exceed physiological solubility (~6.8 mg/dL or 400 umol/L).

Gout affects over 41 million adults globally; genetic variation in renal (URAT1, GLUT9) and intestinal (ABCG2) urate transporters accounts for the majority of hyperuricemia, with dietary purines, alcohol, and metabolic syndrome acting as secondary modulators.

The American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol first-line) for patients with frequent flares (>=2/year), tophi, or radiographic damage, titrating treat-to-target to maintain serum urate <6.0 mg/dL (<360 umol/L).

Anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis (colchicine 0.5-0.6 mg daily or low-dose NSAID) is mandatory during the first 3-6 months of urate-lowering initiation, and HLA-B*5801 screening is indicated in high-risk ethnic groups before allopurinol exposure.

uncertainties: The treat-to-target serum-urate threshold and how aggressively to push in tophaceous disease varies by guideline.
When asymptomatic hyperuricaemia itself warrants treatment is unresolved.

page.mentor_intro: Hypocalcaemia ranges from an asymptomatic biochemical finding to tetany, seizures and laryngospasm, and its urgency tracks both the level and the speed of fall — chronic hypocalcaemia is tolerated at concentrations that would be dangerous if acute. The diagnostic frame mirrors the PTH axis: hypocalcaemia with low or inappropriately normal PTH points to parathyroid failure (surgical hypoparathyroidism is the commonest cause after thyroid surgery), while high PTH indicates secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency or chronic kidney disease. Acute symptomatic disease is a calcium-and-magnesium emergency.

teaching_points.claim: Normal serum calcium is 8–10 mg/dL, and abnormal levels should be confirmed with albumin-adjusted or ionized calcium before acting.
Hypoparathyroidism is the most common complication of bilateral thyroid operations, and strategies for minimising and preventing it are defined by an ATA Surgical Affairs Committee statement.

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, perioral paresthesias, Chvostek/Trousseau signs, or QTc prolongation) requires immediate IV calcium gluconate (1-2 g in 50 mL D5W over 10-20 min) under continuous cardiac monitoring.

Concurrent hypomagnesemia must be checked and aggressively repleted; low magnesium induces end-organ PTH resistance and impairs PTH secretion, rendering hypocalcemia refractory to calcium supplementation alone.

page.mentor_intro: Hypoglycaemia is the limiting toxicity of insulin and sulfonylurea therapy: common, frightening, and associated with distress, medication nonadherence and cardiovascular events. The classification matters — level 1 (alert), level 2 (clinically significant, <3.0 mmol/L), level 3 (severe, requiring assistance) — because treatment thresholds and documentation obligations differ. The cruellest complication is hypoglycaemia unawareness: repeated episodes blunt the autonomic warning system, so neuroglycopenia arrives without warning, a problem addressed by hypoglycaemia avoidance and structured education.

teaching_points.claim: Hypoglycemia unawareness describes diminished autonomic and neuroglycopenic warning symptoms, carrying major clinical implications for people with diabetes and others.

An Endocrine Society guideline addresses management of people with diabetes at high risk of hypoglycaemia on insulin and sulfonylureas, where hypoglycaemia drives distress, nonadherence and morbidity.
Hypoglycaemia complicates management of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and remains a barrier to optimal glycaemic control despite newer technologies.

Clinically significant hypoglycemia (Level 2: <3.0 mmol/L or <54 mg/dL; Level 3: severe cognitive impairment requiring third-party assistance) necessitates rapid treatment with 15-20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate or parenteral glucagon; in patients with hypoglycemia unawareness, relaxed glycemic targets and continuous glucose monitoring with predictive low-glucose alerts restore autonomic warning symptoms.

uncertainties: Whether CGM-driven alert systems eliminate severe hypoglycaemia in all risk groups is still being tested.
The best protocol for restoring hypoglycaemia awareness (strict avoidance versus technology) is individualised.

page.mentor_intro: The hypogranular (microgranular) variant of acute promyelocytic leukaemia is the morphology trap of haematopathology: blasts so fine-grained that the diagnostic granules are invisible on light microscopy, sometimes masquerading as monocytic leukaemias — yet carrying the same t(15;17) PML::RARA rearrangement, the same life-threatening coagulopathy, and the same curative ATRA-arsenic pathway. Worse, a minority have cryptic or variant rearrangements invisible to standard cytogenetics and even FISH, where RT-PCR and optical genome mapping rescue the diagnosis. Missing it delays ATRA, and every hour of delay costs lives.

teaching_points.claim: APL is a distinct AML subtype with a unique morphological appearance, associated coagulopathy and canonical balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17.
APL management evolved with ATRA plus anthracycline chemotherapy providing cure rates exceeding 80%, and modern regimens continue to refine this combination.

APL is characterised by abnormal promyelocytes and t(15;17) PML::RARA, but rare patients have cryptic or variant rearrangements where RT-PCR and optical genome mapping secure the diagnosis; ATRA/arsenic is largely curative provided the diagnosis is made.

Hypogranular (microgranular) variant acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) frequently presents with bilobed or folded monocytoid nuclei mimicking acute monocytic leukemia, often accompanied by severe coagulopathy and prominent leukocytosis; rapid confirmation via PML-RARA RT-PCR or FISH is mandatory, with immediate initiation of ATRA and arsenic trioxide (ATO) upon morphological suspicion.

page.mentor_intro: Hypokalaemia is a potassium- and magnesium-dependent problem with a blood-pressure and acid-base fingerprint: the combination of hypokalaemia with hypertension points to mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism, Cushing's, licorice), while hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis and normotension suggests renal losses from diuretics, vomiting or the inherited tubulopathies — Gitelman syndrome being the classic hypokalaemic-metabolic-alkalosis-with-hypomagnesaemia diagnosis. Iatrogenic causes matter too: beta-lactam antibiotics are an under-recognised cause of potentially serious hypokalaemia. ECG effects — U waves, flattened T waves, arrhythmia — and rhabdomyolysis mark severity.

teaching_points.claim: Beta-lactam antibiotic-associated hypokalemia is a potentially life-threatening electrolyte disorder reviewed in a dedicated narrative review.
Gitelman syndrome is a rare salt-losing tubulopathy characterised by hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria, caused by inactivating SLC12A3 mutations.

Serum potassium < 3.0 mmol/L or ECG abnormalities (flattened T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves, ventricular arrhythmias) necessitates prompt intravenous potassium chloride infusion (10-20 mmol/h with cardiac monitoring).

Refractory hypokalemia is commonly driven by coexisting hypomagnesemia; intracellular magnesium depletion impairs Na+/K+-ATPase and disinhibits ROMK potassium channels, causing persistent renal potassium wasting.

uncertainties: Potassium-replacement route and speed thresholds, especially with ECG changes, vary by protocol.
Optimal magnesium co-repletion targets and chronic tubulopathy management are individualised.
mcq_angles: Blood-pressure and acid-base-based differential of hypokalaemia.
ECG changes and arrhythmia risk thresholds.
Renal-versus-GI losses: urinary potassium and chloride.

page.mentor_intro: Hyponatraemia is the commonest electrolyte disorder — around 5% of adults and 35% of hospitalised patients — and even mild cases carry falls, cognitive impairment and mortality signal. The diagnostic spine is volume assessment and urine osmolality, separating hypotonic from non-hypotonic causes, then narrowing within the hypotonic group by urine sodium: SIAD dominates the euvolaemic category through non-osmotic AVP release, while diuretics and hypovolaemia lead the low-urine-sodium group. The treatment paradox frames everything: too slow risks osmotic demyelination from chronic hyponatraemia, too fast risks cerebral oedema in acute hyponatraemia — and severe symptomatic disease earns hypertonic saline under close monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: Hyponatremia is the most common electrolyte disorder, affecting approximately 5% of adults and 35% of hospitalised patients; it is defined by serum sodium below 135 mEq/L and most commonly results from water retention, with even mild cases carrying risk.
SIAD is the most frequent cause of hypotonic hyponatraemia, mediated by non-osmotic arginine-vasopressin release, and affects more than 15% of hospitalised patients overall.
Emergency-department hyponatraemia presents with unspecific symptoms including recent falls, weakness and vertigo, with common causes including diuretics.

uncertainties: Vaptan use outside ICU settings and fluid-restriction-versus-salt-plus-loop strategies in SIAD vary by guideline.

page.mentor_intro: The correction-rate question in hyponatraemia is medicine at its most precarious: correct too fast and you risk osmotic demyelination syndrome; correct too slowly and observational data now suggest mortality rises. Guidelines recommend limiting the first-24-hour correction increment to prevent ODS, and meta-analytic evidence quantifies the ODS risk associated with overly rapid correction. The practical skill is monitoring: checking sodium frequently enough to detect an over-correction while it is still reversible, with re-lowering strategies ready — because the correction limit is a ceiling, not a target.

teaching_points.claim: Guidelines recommend limiting correction of severe hyponatraemia in the first 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome, yet recent evidence suggests slower correction rates are associated with increased mortality.
A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association between overly rapid sodium correction and osmotic demyelination syndrome in hospitalised adults.

In chronic hyponatremia (>48h), the maximum recommended correction rate is 8 mmol/L in any 24-hour period (and 4-6 mmol/L/24h in high-risk patients with cirrhosis, advanced malnutrition, or alcoholism) to avoid osmotic demyelination.

Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma, brainstem herniation) requires immediate administration of 3% hypertonic saline (100-150 mL bolus over 10-20 min, repeatable up to 3 times) to rapidly raise serum sodium by 4-6 mmol/L.

uncertainties: The exact mortality-optimal correction band sits within a contested zone between ODS risk at the top and under-correction harm at the bottom.
Whether desmopressin-based re-lowering protocols improve outcomes is supported by physiology more than trials.

page.mentor_intro: Hypoparathyroidism is defined by hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and inadequate PTH — usually acquired surgically after thyroid or parathyroid operations, but with an important medical differential (autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, activating calcium-sensor mutations). Management has historically meant calcium plus active vitamin D in large doses, trading hypercalciuria and renal-stone risk against symptom control. The post-2022 era adds PTH-replacement therapy — the first hormone-replacement approach that mimics physiology — alongside updated guidance on causes, complications and chronic management.

teaching_points.claim: Hypoparathyroidism is characterised by hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and inadequate PTH levels or function; the most common nonsurgical causes are reviewed, with autoimmune disease prominent.
Since the 2022 Second International Workshop summary statement, updates are available in the causes, complications and treatment of adult chronic hypoparathyroidism.

Standard maintenance medical therapy combines oral elemental calcium (1-2 g daily) with active vitamin D metabolites (calcitriol 0.25-1.0 ug daily), targeting low-normal serum calcium to prevent hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.

Recombinant human PTH (e.g. rhPTH[1-84] or palopegteriparatide) is indicated for patients with refractory disease experiencing recurrent tetany, severe quality of life impairment, or progressive hypercalciuric renal calcifications despite active vitamin D.

uncertainties: Which chronic patients qualify for PTH replacement versus conventional therapy is being refined.
Long-term renal and neuropsychological outcomes of conventional large-dose therapy remain concerns.

page.mentor_intro: Hypophosphataemia becomes a bone disease when FGF23 drives it. FGF23 — the phosphate-wasting hormone acting with Klotho — suppresses tubular phosphate reabsorption and blunts vitamin D activation; when PHEX mutations let it run unchecked, the result is X-linked hypophosphataemia: the commonest inherited phosphate-wasting disorder, with rickets, lower-limb deformity, dental defects and disproportionate short stature in children and persistent complications in adults. Burosumab, the anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody, converted XLH from a high-burden phosphate-and-burider regimen into targeted therapy aimed at the mechanism itself.

teaching_points.claim: X-linked hypophosphataemia is the most common cause of inherited phosphate wasting, causing rickets, lower-limb deformities, pain, poor dental mineralisation and disproportionate short stature in children.
FGF23, with its co-receptor Klotho, regulates phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D hydroxylation in the renal proximal tubules; the most common FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemia is XLH.
XLH is caused by pathogenic PHEX variants with X-linked dominant inheritance, producing metabolic bone disease through dysregulated FGF23.

X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) and tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) are driven by pathological fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23) excess, causing renal phosphate wasting and impaired 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis; the fully human monoclonal anti-FGF-23 antibody burosumab restores phosphate homeostasis, enhances bone healing, and superiorly improves linear growth and physical function compared to conventional oral phosphate/calcitriol therapy.

uncertainties: Long-term adult XLH management and burosumab continuation criteria are still being defined.
FGF23 measurement standardisation limits its use as a routine diagnostic marker.

page.mentor_intro: Hypopituitarism — deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones, sometimes with posterior involvement — is dangerous less for what it lacks than for what clinicians forget to replace: cortisol deficiency from ACTH loss is the key driver of its excess mortality. Causes span pituitary neuroendocrine tumours, hypothalamic lesions, surgery, radiotherapy and trauma. Management is axis-by-axis and hierarchy-aware: cortisol first, thyroid second (never thyroxine before steroids), then sex steroids, growth hormone where indicated, and desmopressin for posterior deficiency. The insulin tolerance test remains the gold-standard dynamic test of the HPA axis when secondary adrenal insufficiency needs confirmation.

teaching_points.claim: Hypopituitarism is deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones and is associated with excess mortality, cortisol deficiency from ACTH loss being a key risk factor.
Updated reviews cover the aetiologies of hypopituitarism — including pituitary neuroendocrine tumours, hypothalamic lesions and genetic mutations — and current diagnostic and management approaches.

Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone 15-20 mg daily in divided doses) MUST be initiated prior to or concurrently with levothyroxine replacement to prevent precipitating a fatal acute adrenal crisis.

Secondary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed via the insulin tolerance test (gold standard) or short cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test; secondary hypothyroidism is characterized by low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4.

uncertainties: The insulin tolerance test's role is narrowing as safer stimulation tests gain ground, but equivalence in all scenarios is debated.
Growth-hormone replacement in older adults and after cancer remains individualised.

page.mentor_intro: Hypothyroidism is among the commonest endocrine disorders — prevalence 0.3–12% worldwide depending on iodine intake, commoner in women and older adults — and it touches nearly every organ system, from fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance to bradycardia, heart failure and, rarely, myxoedema coma. Most cases are primary (Hashimoto's), diagnosed by elevated TSH with low free T4, and treatment is levothyroxine replacement titrated to TSH. The clinical craft lies in the edges: subclinical disease, pregnancy targets, drug interactions and the patient who feels unwell despite normal numbers.

teaching_points.claim: Hypothyroidism is a common condition worldwide affecting almost all body systems, with presentations ranging from asymptomatic to, rarely, life-threatening.
Prevalence ranges from 0.3% to 12% worldwide depending on iodine intake, is more common in women and older adults, and untreated disease can cause heart failure and myxoedema.

Levothyroxine monotherapy (starting dose 1.6 ug/kg ideal body weight daily in young healthy adults, or 25-50 ug daily in elderly or patients with coronary disease) is the undisputed first-line treatment of choice.

Monitoring requires serum TSH re-evaluation 6-8 weeks after initiation or dosage adjustments; levothyroxine must be taken on an empty stomach with plain water at least 30-60 minutes before breakfast to ensure reliable absorption.

page.mentor_intro: Subclinical hypothyroidism — elevated TSH with normal free T4 — affects up to 10% of adults, is usually autoimmune in origin, and is where guideline divergence is widest: treat the young and symptomatic, watch the old and asymptomatic, and agonise over everyone in between. TSH targets on levothyroxine similarly depend on age and context, and older-adult dosing starts low and titrates slowly to avoid atrial fibrillation and fractures. The evidence tension is real: mild biochemical abnormality versus modest symptom burden, with cardiovascular-risk signals that have not resolved the treatment question.

teaching_points.claim: Subclinical hypothyroidism — elevated TSH with normal free T4 — affects up to 10% of the adult population and is most often caused by autoimmune thyroiditis.

Subclinical hypothyroidism, defined as TSH above the reference range (generally 4.5 mIU/L or higher) with normal free T4, is frequently found in older individuals, and international guidelines differ on management.

Subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal free T4) warrants levothyroxine therapy when TSH is >=10 mIU/L, in patients aged <65-70 years with symptoms/goitre/positive TPO antibodies, or in women planning pregnancy.

In elderly patients (>70-80 years) with mild subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH < 10 mIU/L), randomized trials (e.g. TRUST trial) demonstrate no benefit from levothyroxine on cognitive function or cardiovascular outcomes, favoring watchful waiting.

The TSH threshold for treating older adults is a genuine guideline discordance zone.

page.mentor_intro: Central hypoventilation from CNS depressants is an epidemic-shaped emergency: opioids suppress the respiratory drive at the brainstem, producing a characteristic slow, shallow breathing pattern that progresses to hypoxia-mediated injury. Overdose management centres on airway support and naloxone reversal — titrated to restore ventilation, not full alertness — while a growing literature examines non-opioid respiratory stimulants as adjuncts. In the perioperative and chronic-pain settings the same physiology operates more insidiously, compounded by obesity hypoventilation and benzodiazepine co-exposure, making screening and monitoring the real prevention.

teaching_points.claim: Opioid overdose occurs when CNS and respiratory drive are suppressed through opioid-receptor action, and acute management strategies in emergency and critical care are updated in a dedicated review.
Opioid-related adverse effects include respiratory depression, and countering opioid-induced respiratory depression with non-opioid respiratory stimulants is an active research area.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is underdiagnosed and carries significant perioperative risk through heightened sensitivity to CNS depressants, warranting screening and adapted management.

Acute central hypoventilation induced by opioids, benzodiazepines, or other central nervous system depressants causes hypercapnic respiratory failure, respiratory acidosis, and lethargy; immediate management prioritizes airway protection and bag-valve-mask ventilation, followed by titrated intravenous naloxone (for opioids) or flumazenil (cautiously in selected isolated benzodiazepine overdoses, avoiding precipitating withdrawal seizures in chronic users).

uncertainties: Routine naloxone co-prescribing impact and the optimal monitoring technology for ward-based opioid use remain debated.
Respiratory-stimulant adjuncts are investigational rather than standard care.

page.mentor_intro: The single most important fact about IBD in pregnancy is that active disease harms the pregnancy far more than the medications do: quiescent disease at conception predicts a smooth course, while active flares drive preterm birth, low birth weight and pregnancy loss. The therapeutic implication runs against maternal instinct but with the evidence: continue 5-ASA, thiopurines and biologics through conception and pregnancy, adjust anti-TNF scheduling around the third trimester, and avoid methotrexate entirely. Preconception disease control is the intervention that changes outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease are chronic heterogeneous inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract; BSG consensus guidelines provide adult management frameworks relevant to pregnancy planning and care.

Maintaining remission prior to conception and throughout gestation is paramount; active maternal bowel inflammation confers a substantially greater risk of miscarriage, preterm delivery, and low birth weight than guideline maintenance medications.

Biologic therapies (anti-TNF agents: infliximab, adalimumab; vedolizumab; ustekinumab) are generally safe throughout pregnancy, with active transplacental transfer occurring predominantly in the third trimester via fetal Fc receptors.

Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy and conception (teratogenic embryopathy); tofacitinib should be avoided, whereas thiopurines (azathioprine) and 5-ASAs (except those with dibutyl phthalate coating) are safe to continue.

uncertainties: Optimal anti-TNF drug-level monitoring and third-trimester dosing schedules vary by agent and guideline.
Small-molecule (JAK/S1P) safety data in pregnancy remain limited.

page.mentor_intro: An ICD that keeps firing at the end of life can turn a peaceful death into a sequence of painful shocks — and deactivating it is legally and ethically permissible, amounting to withdrawal of treatment rather than euthanasia, since the device merely prevents arrhythmia death and does nothing else for the patient. The failure is conversational: patients, families and professionals all report discomfort initiating the discussion, so deactivation conversations happen late or never. Guidance from the Resuscitation Council and cardiovascular societies frames advance-care planning that names the device explicitly, while attitude research maps exactly where the reluctance sits.

teaching_points.claim: UK resuscitation, cardiovascular and palliative-care councils jointly recognise the importance of clear, consistent guidance on cardiovascular implanted electronic devices towards the end of life and around death.

ICDs prevent sudden cardiac death but, if not deactivated in the terminal phase, may deliver shocks that pose problems during dying; attitudes of patients, relatives and professionals toward deactivation are surveyed.

Proactive discussions regarding shock deactivation should occur early upon transition to palliative care or development of terminal illness to prevent traumatic, painful, and distressing shocks during the dying process.

ICD shock deactivation does not affect bradycardia pacing functions; patient or surrogate refusal of shock therapy is ethically and legally equivalent to refusing other life-sustaining medical interventions.

uncertainties: Whether routine advance device planning at implantation changes end-of-life outcomes is not established.
Decision-making capacity and surrogate-consent pathways for deactivation vary by jurisdiction.

page.mentor_intro: Secondary-prevention ICDs are the most firmly indicated devices in electrophysiology: survivors of ventricular fibrillation or haemodynamically unstable sustained ventricular tachycardia not due to a reversible cause receive them on the strength of the landmark MADIT-lineage trials showing sudden-death reduction. Modern practice adds two refinements: programming that avoids unnecessary shocks (detection intervals and discriminators matter as much as the indication), and the expanding subcutaneous-ICD option that eliminates transvenous lead complications — with a trade-off in pacing capability that defines who qualifies for which system.

teaching_points.claim: Implantable devices are indicated in primary and secondary prevention of life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias; early studies including the landmark MADIT trials established ICD benefit.
ICDs reduce sudden cardiac death in primary and secondary prevention; transvenous implantation carries lead-related complications that the subcutaneous approach avoids, with selection trade-offs.

Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are indicated for secondary prevention in survivors of cardiac arrest due to VF or hemodynamically unstable sustained VT in the absence of a completely reversible acute cause (AVID, CASH, and CIDS trials).

Contemporary programming strategies (high-rate cutoffs >200 bpm and delayed detection intervals >60 seconds) substantially reduce inappropriate and unnecessary shocks and improve survival without increasing syncope.

uncertainties: Optimal programming parameters (detection zones, SVT discriminators) continue to be refined against shock rates.
Which secondary-prevention patients are better served by subcutaneous versus transvenous systems is individualised by pacing needs and vascular access.

page.mentor_intro: Icosapent ethyl sits at the intersection of residual-risk medicine and trial controversy. In REDUCE-IT, high-purity EPA reduced cardiovascular events among statin-treated patients with elevated triglycerides, but the magnitude of benefit, the mineral-oil comparator question, and the failure of the DHA-containing STRENGTH trial have kept the indication debated. Clinically, the drug is not for everyone with high triglycerides: the benefit signal concentrates in statin-treated patients with established ASCVD (or high risk) and triglycerides in the 135–499 mg/dL band, making patient selection the core skill.

teaching_points.claim: REDUCE-IT established that high-purity eicosapentaenoic acid (icosapent ethyl) reduces cardiovascular events on top of statins in high-risk patients with persistent hypertriglyceridaemia.
Eligibility nuance matters: benefit concentrates in statin-treated patients with triglycerides roughly 135–499 mg/dL and LDL-C controlled, not in unselected hypertriglyceridaemia.
The neutral DHA-containing STRENGTH trial and the mineral-oil comparator debate mean EPA-specific benefit is contested and generalisation to mixed omega-3 preparations is not supported.
Adverse-effect monitoring includes atrial fibrillation and bleeding signals that weighed into regulatory and formulary decisions.

uncertainties: Whether the REDUCE-IT benefit is fully attributable to EPA versus comparator effects remains debated; biomarker mediation analyses continue.
Cost-effectiveness in lower-risk primary-prevention populations is unresolved in most health systems.

page.mentor_intro: ICU delirium is the syndrome the PADIS guidelines were built to prevent — and the 2022 SCCM update sharpened the message: routine deep sedation should be minimised, spontaneous awakening and breathing trials paired, early mobility promoted, and sleep protected. Pharmacological prevention and treatment with antipsychotics lacks outcome evidence, so management is environmental and process-based. The arc of care extends past discharge: post-intensive care syndrome bundles rehabilitation for the cognitive, physical, and psychological sequelae that outlast the ICU stay.

teaching_points.claim: The PADIS (2018) and 2022 SCCM guidelines frame delirium management around ABCDEF bundle elements: analgesia-first sedation, spontaneous awakening/breathing trials, choice of lighter sedation, delirium monitoring, early mobility, and family engagement.
Non-pharmacological prevention — reorientation, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, sensory aids — is the evidence-backed core; antipsychotics are not recommended for routine prevention or treatment.
Delirium in older persons is common, serious, and under-recognised, with lasting effects on function and cognition that justify systematic screening in at-risk populations.
Post-intensive care syndrome (physical, cognitive, psychological impairments after critical illness) warrants structured multimodal rehabilitation and follow-up after ICU discharge.

uncertainties: Whether any pharmacological agent (dexmedetomidine contexts, melatonin-agonists) improves delirium-free days is unresolved; trial signals have not translated into routine recommendations.

page.mentor_intro: ICU triage is allocation under scarcity: who benefits most from a bed, who can be managed elsewhere, and who — despite need — will not benefit. The ConICTri consensus statement operationalises these judgments with explicit prioritisation criteria, while a qualitative systematic review shows how variable real-world selection criteria are across systems. For surgical patients, 'intensive care without borders' reframes the question as matching monitored-care intensity to risk rather than geography — using prediction scores and early-warning escalation to decide who needs the unit at all.

teaching_points.claim: Structured triage frameworks (e.g. ConICTri) use explicit prioritisation criteria — diagnosis, severity, reversibility, and life expectancy — to make bed allocation auditable and consistent under scarcity.

Real-world triage and inter-facility transfer criteria vary widely across systems, with clinical judgment, bed pressure, and prognosis all influencing decisions; standardised criteria are inconsistently applied.

For surgical patients, risk prediction scores and timely recognition of postoperative deterioration can match patients to the right level of care, including high-dependency and ward-based monitoring alternatives.

ICU admission decisions rely on physiological risk stratification (assessing severe respiratory, hemodynamic, or metabolic instability requiring invasive monitoring or mechanical organ support), objective reversibility of the acute illness, and the patient's baseline functional status and advance care directives, prioritizing patients who will derive clear physiological survival benefit over those with irreversible terminal illness.

uncertainties: Whether formal scoring systems outperform structured clinical judgment for ICU admission decisions lacks definitive trial evidence.
Ethical frameworks for rationing during full-capacity crises (e.g. pandemic triage) remain contested across jurisdictions.

page.mentor_intro: Where topic 902 covers the prevention and management architecture of ICU delirium, this topic is about the instrument itself: the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU. CAM-ICU remains the most widely validated bedside tool for non-psychiatrists — an acute change in mental status with inattention, plus either altered consciousness or disorganised thinking. Psychometric synthesis confirms strong accuracy in general critically ill adults, but the tool only works when it is actually applied: most delirium in the ICU goes unrecognised without systematic screening, which is why guidelines embed CAM-ICU into hourly-to-daily assessment pathways.

teaching_points.claim: CAM-ICU is a valid, reliable instrument for delirium diagnosis in critically ill adults, including ventilated patients unable to speak, when administered by trained non-psychiatrists.

The tool's logic is an acute change or fluctuation in mental status plus inattention, disorganised thinking, or altered level of consciousness — features that distinguish delirium from dementia and depression.
Without systematic screening, the majority of ICU delirium goes undetected; routine instrument-based assessment is the prerequisite for any prevention or treatment bundle.

Delirium in intensive care is associated with increased mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and long-term cognitive impairment; routine screening using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) or Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC) alongside multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention (early mobility, sleep preservation, delirium bundle ABCDEF) represents the evidence-based standard of care.

uncertainties: Optimal screening frequency (every shift versus daily) and who should perform screening (nurses versus physicians) is institution-dependent.
Performance of CAM-ICU in deeply sedated or severely encephalopathic patients is less certain; combined instruments (e.g. with EEG correlates) are under study.

page.mentor_intro: When to start renal replacement therapy in ICU acute kidney injury has been one of nephrology's most contested questions, and the contemporary answer is restraint: large randomised trials and the Cochrane synthesis found no survival advantage to early, protocol-driven initiation over a watchful strategy that waits for absolute indications — refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema, or uraemic complications. Starting RRT is therefore a decision about concrete complications, not creatinine alone. Once started, dosing, anticoagulation, and membrane choice follow the prescription-pathway and core-curriculum frameworks that standardise delivery across ICUs.

teaching_points.claim: Randomised evidence and systematic review show no mortality benefit from early versus delayed RRT initiation in AKI; a strategy awaiting absolute indications is supported.

Traditional absolute indications remain the trigger points: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, diuretic-resistant volume overload, and uraemic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis).
Once CKRT is started, prescription quality — effluent dose, anticoagulation strategy, circuit monitoring, and drug dosing adjustment — determines delivered dose and outcomes.

Multiple landmark randomized controlled trials (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI) demonstrate that an accelerated or early strategy for initiating renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury does not reduce mortality and increases adverse catheter/electrolyte events compared to a watchful waiting strategy that initiates RRT only for conventional urgent indications (refractory hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, or pulmonary edema).

uncertainties: Whether specific phenotypes (septic AKI with fluid overload, severe hypercatabolism) benefit from earlier initiation is still being tested.
Biomarker-guided (e.g. furosemide stress test, NGAL) initiation timing has not yet changed standard practice.

page.mentor_intro: Bell's palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy, and its management hinges on two time-sensitive acts: starting corticosteroids early — ideally within 72 hours of onset, when the facial nerve is still inflamed within the fallopian canal — and protecting the eye, whose blink reflex is paralysed. Meta-analytic evidence supports adding antivirals to steroids for the best recovery rates in severe palsy, and guidelines (Japanese 2023 update among them) converge on early steroid therapy with graded add-on antivirals. The prognosis is favourable in most, but complete palsy, older age, and absent recovery by three months warrant referral for specialist assessment of synkinesis and surgical options.

teaching_points.claim: Corticosteroids started within 72 hours of onset improve facial-nerve recovery and are the cornerstone of treatment for adults with Bell's palsy.

Meta-analytic evidence indicates combination antiviral-plus-steroid therapy outperforms steroid alone in recovery, with greatest benefit in severe palsy — consistent with a likely viral (HSV) aetiology.
Eye protection is mandatory from day one: lubricating drops, ointment, and taping or patching at night to prevent corneal exposure and ulceration.

Red-flag exclusions before treating: vesicles suggest Ramsay Hunt (needs antivirals urgently), and no forehead sparing — but any atypical features (bilateral, recurrent, slow progression) demand imaging for alternative causes.

uncertainties: The incremental benefit of antivirals in mild-to-moderate palsy is modest and debated across guidelines.
Role of electrophysiology (ENoG) and surgical decompression in complete early paralysis is unresolved and specialist-dependent.

page.mentor_intro: IIH is a syndrome of raised intracranial pressure in obese women of childbearing age, diagnosed by the modified Dandy criteria: symptoms (headache, pulsatile tinnitus, visual disturbance), elevated lumbar-puncture opening pressure with normal CSF composition, and normal neuroimaging — with venous imaging to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Management is tiered: weight loss is disease-modifying, acetazolamide is first-line pharmacotherapy with modest but real benefit on vision, and escalating interventions — CSF shunting, venous sinus stenting, optic nerve sheath fenestration — are reserved for rapidly declining vision, with stenting increasingly used where venous sinus stenosis with a pressure gradient is demonstrated.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnosis requires elevated LP opening pressure (typically ≥25 cm CSF in adults, lateral decubitus) with normal CSF composition and neuroimaging excluding secondary causes, especially venous sinus thrombosis.
Weight reduction is the only disease-modifying intervention; even modest sustained loss lowers intracranial pressure and can induce remission.
Acetazolamide is first-line medical therapy; trial evidence shows modest benefit on visual field outcomes when added to diet, and it is titrated against symptom control and tolerability.

For medically refractory or rapidly declining vision, surgical options include CSF diversion (shunt), optic nerve sheath fenestration, and venous sinus stenting — the latter for patients with documented sinus stenosis and a trans-stenosis pressure gradient.

uncertainties: Optimal acetazolamide dosing and duration, and whether it alters long-term vision loss independently of weight change, remains uncertain.
Patient selection criteria for venous sinus stenting (pressure-gradient thresholds, stenosis morphology) are not standardised across centres.

page.mentor_intro: In IIH, vision is the organ at stake: papilloedema reflects axonal compromise at the optic nerve head, and the clinical mandate is early, quantitative monitoring of visual function so that decline triggers escalation before permanent field loss. Automated perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) and optic-disc photography/OCT form the monitoring backbone, interpreted alongside symptoms — transient visual obscurations are a warning sign. The nuances that distinguish expert practice include recognising atypical presentations (men, lean patients, fulminant IIH with rapid field loss), the management of IIH in pregnancy, and the discipline of urgent surgical referral when fields deteriorate despite therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Visual field testing by automated perimetry is the primary outcome measure in IIH; regular, comparable field testing detects deterioration earlier than symptoms or fundoscopy alone.
Papilloedema grading and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer complement perimetry; discordance between disc appearance and field loss is common and the field takes precedence.
Fulminant IIH — rapid, severe visual decline over days to weeks — is a neuro-ophthalmic emergency requiring urgent surgical intervention rather than medical titration.
Atypical phenotypes (male, non-obese, paediatric, or secondary pseudotumour cerebri) require scrupulous exclusion of secondary causes while applying the same vision-protection framework.

uncertainties: Optimal monitoring intervals (monthly versus three-monthly fields in stable patients) are practice-defined rather than trial-defined.
Whether optical coherence tomography can replace or triage formal perimetry in resource-limited settings is under evaluation.

page.mentor_intro: IPF is the prototypic progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease: irreversible parenchymal remodelling, honeycomb change on HRCT or UIP-pattern histology, and a median survival measured in years without treatment. Two antifibrotics — pirfenidone and nintedanib — slow forced vital capacity decline, and the progressive-pulmonary-fibrosis consensus extends the antifibrotic principle beyond IPF to other fibrosing ILDs that worsen despite management. Diagnosis is multidisciplinary, prognosis is tracked by FVC trajectory, and transplant referral is timed by risk stratification — the modern skill is recognising progression early and treating the trajectory, not the label.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnosis rests on HRCT UIP-pattern (or multidisciplinary confirmation with histology), exclusion of known causes, and recognition of the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern's prognostic weight.

The progressive-pulmonary-fibrosis framework defines worsening across symptoms, physiology, and imaging within a year of appropriate management, triggering antifibrotic therapy regardless of specific ILD label.
Monitoring relies on serial FVC and DLCO, with exacerbations — acute worsening with new ground-glass opacity — carrying high mortality and requiring aggressive management.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing and combination of antifibrotics, and treatment of acute exacerbations, lack randomised evidence.

page.mentor_intro: IgA nephropathy, the commonest primary glomerulonephritis, is now managed as a progressive-risk disease: the KDIGO 2021 guideline established risk-based surveillance, and the 2025 update adds an evidence-treatment armamentarium that has expanded rapidly — supportive care with RAS blockade and blood-pressure control remains the foundation, with SGLT2 inhibitors, targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon), sparsentan, and endothelin-receptor antagonists layered by proteinuria and eGFR trajectory. Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for high-risk patients after optimised supportive care, weighing infection and toxicity risk; tonsillectomy is considered in selected recurrent-synpharyngitic-haematuria populations.

page.mentor_intro: The sparsentan story shows how fast IgA nephropathy therapy is moving: the PROTECT trial's interim proteinuria win made the dual endothelin-A/angiotensin-receptor antagonist the first non-immunosuppressive drug with regulatory approval specifically for IgAN, built on proteinuria as a validated surrogate. Safety monitoring includes liver enzymes, pregnancy prevention (foetotoxicity), hyperkalaemia, and oedema — with structured hepatotoxicity risk-management programmes in some regions.
Network meta-analysis of RCTs now permits comparative ranking of IgAN agents by proteinuria lowering, supporting individualised sequencing as newer agents accumulate.

uncertainties: Long-term (>5 year) eGFR and ESRD outcomes for sparsentan beyond the surrogate endpoint are pending final PROTECT results.

page.mentor_intro: IgA vasculitis — Henoch-Schonlein purpura renamed — is a small-vessel IgA-dominant immune-complex vasculitis that is common and self-limiting in children but rarer, more severe, and more often renal in adults. The clinical skill is two-fold: recognising the tetrad of palpable purura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, and stratifying by organ threat, because management escalates from supportive care for skin-joint disease to immunosuppression for nephritis or severe GI disease. Adult disease behaves differently enough from paediatric disease that adult-specific evidence, though thinner, should drive treatment decisions.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnosis is clinical with characteristic IgA-dominant deposits on biopsy when needed; in adults, biopsy and secondary-cause work-up (infection, malignancy, drugs) carry more weight than in children.
Skin-limited and joint disease in adults is usually managed supportively; the systemic review evidence for immunosuppression is strongest for nephritis and severe gastrointestinal involvement.

IgAV nephritis management draws on IgA-nephropathy principles — RAS blockade for proteinuric disease, and corticosteroids/immunosuppression for higher-risk histology — extrapolated from the KDIGO framework.
Adult-onset IgAV has more frequent and more severe renal involvement than childhood-onset disease, with a higher proportion progressing to chronic kidney disease; prognosis is organ-threat dependent.

uncertainties: Randomised evidence specific to adult IgAV is scarce; most treatment recommendations are extrapolated from paediatric trials and IgA-nephropathy data.
The role of rituximab and other steroid-sparing agents in adult IgAV nephritis is not established.

page.mentor_intro: IgG4-related disease, recognised only since 2003, is a systemic fibro-inflammatory condition that can mimic malignancy, infection, and other immune disease in nearly any organ — classically autoimmune pancreatitis, sialadenitis, orbital disease, and retroperitoneal fibrosis. Pathophysiologically it is a B-cell-driven, plasmablast-rich process with characteristic histology (dense IgG4+ plasma-cell infiltrates, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis), and serum IgG4 is elevated in most but not all patients — tissue diagnosis remains the reference standard. The clinical stakes are twofold: don't miss it (steroids usually produce a dramatic response) and don't overdiagnose it (elevated IgG4 alone is non-specific, and fibrotic late-stage disease responds poorly).

teaching_points.claim: IgG4-RD is a multi-organ fibro-inflammatory disease with a characteristic histopathological signature — dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4+ plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis.
Pathophysiology centres on B cells and plasmablasts with oligoclonal expansions; this B-cell dependence explains the efficacy of B-cell depletion and informs biomarker development.
A fibrotic phenotype exists in which prominent tissue fibrosis predicts reduced glucocorticoid responsiveness — recognising it early matters for treatment selection and expectations.

Serum IgG4 concentration supports but does not establish diagnosis; tissue confirmation with IgG4/IgG ratio assessment is the reference standard, and organ-specific diagnostic criteria have been developed.

uncertainties: Whether IgG4 itself is pathogenic or an epiphenomenon of underlying B-cell dysregulation is unresolved.
Optimal glucocorticoid-sparing maintenance and relapse-prevention strategies are not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: IL-6 blockade is one of the most instructive examples of a pathway drug with dual lives. In rheumatoid arthritis, tocilizumab and sarilumab — humanised IL-6-receptor antibodies — are effective biologic DMARDs positioned by the EULAR recommendations alongside TNF inhibitors, with a distinctive side-effect signature (neutropenia, transaminitis, dyslipidaemia, bowel perforation risk). page.mentor_intro: The IRIS trial is the pivotal inflection point in modern oncology: randomising newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML between interferon-alpha plus cytarabine and imatinib, it was stopped early because imatinib produced vastly superior complete cytogenetic and major molecular responses with far better tolerability — converting CML from a fatal disease into a chronic, often near-normal-life-expectancy condition. The legacy is visible in the ELN 2020 recommendations and 2025 updates: first-line choice among imatinib and second/third-generation TKIs is now individualised by comorbidity, risk score, and treatment goal — including the modern ambition of treatment-free remission after sustained deep molecular response.

teaching_points.claim: IRIS established imatinib, the first BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor, as superior to interferon-based therapy for newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML, transforming survival.

Modern first-line choice — imatinib versus second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib) — is individualised by Sokal/ELTS risk score, comorbidities (vascular, pulmonary, hepatic), and the treatment-free-remission goal.

Response monitoring is quantitative: BCR::ABL1 transcript by international scale with milestone targets at 3, 6, and 12 months defining optimal, warning, and failure responses that trigger therapy change.

Sustained deep molecular response (typically MR4 or deeper for years) permits carefully monitored TKI discontinuation in selected patients, with the ELN recommendations defining eligibility and monitoring intensity.

uncertainties: Long-term vascular and second-malignancy signals with second-generation TKIs influence but do not settle first-line selection.
Which patients can safely attempt treatment-free remission beyond standard eligibility criteria is an active research question.

page.mentor_intro: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have made kidney injury a new frontier of onco-nephrology. The signature lesion is acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, typically presenting as abrupt creatinine rise after weeks to months of therapy, often with subnephrotic proteinuria — but the differential includes prerenal states, obstructive uropathy, and glomerular patterns such as lupus-like nephritis and podocytopathies. The ASCO-Nephrology position statement standardises the approach: hold the checkpoint inhibitor, grade the injury, biopsy for atypical or severe presentations, start corticosteroids for significant AKI, and navigate the challenge of balancing oncologic benefit against renal and immune risk.

teaching_points.claim: ICI-associated AKI most commonly reflects acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, with onset typically after several weeks of therapy; glomerular patterns (minimal change, lupus-like, ANCA) occur less often.

Diagnostic work-up excludes prerenal and obstructive causes, reviews nephrotoxin and PPI exposure, and uses biopsy when atypical features (nephrotic proteinuria, active sediment, no steroid response) are present.

Management: hold the ICI, grade severity, and treat higher-grade injury with corticosteroids (typically 0.5–1 mg/kg prednisone-equivalent, higher for severe presentations), tapering over weeks with close creatinine surveillance.
Re-challenge decisions weigh oncology urgency against relapse risk; steroid-sparing agents (mycophenolate, infliximab) are reserved for steroid-refractory or relapsing cases.

uncertainties: Optimal steroid dose and duration, and whether early biopsy-guided therapy changes outcomes, lacks randomised evidence.
ICI re-challenge after biopsy-proven nephritis: relapse rates and safety thresholds are incompletely defined.

page.mentor_intro: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is the most aggressive of the idiopathic inflammatory myopathies: severe proximal weakness, creatine kinase often in the thousands, myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammation on biopsy, and a stubborn tendency to relapse. Two antibody-defined subtypes dominate — anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR — and the HMGCR story links it to statins, creating a practical problem: how to manage dyslipidaemia when the patient's own immune system attacks the drug target. Modern management is escalating immunosuppression early (often combination therapy), intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease, and — for anti-HMGCR patients — PCSK9 inhibitors as a statin-sparing lipid strategy that sidesteps the HMGCR antigen entirely.

teaching_points.claim: IMNM presents with subacute severe proximal weakness and markedly elevated CK; biopsy shows myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammatory infiltrate, distinguishing it from polymyositis and dermatomyositis.
Anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies define the major subtypes with differing phenotypes, malignancy associations, and treatment-response profiles; antibody testing is diagnostic and prognostic.

First-line treatment is high-dose corticosteroids with early steroid-sparing immunosuppression; IVIG and combination therapy are used for refractory disease, with treatment often prolonged because relapse on tapering is common.

In statin-associated anti-HMGCR disease, statins must stop permanently; PCSK9 inhibitors provide effective cholesterol lowering without engaging the HMGCR antigen, making them a practical post-IMNM lipid strategy.

uncertainties: Optimal induction regimen (steroid monotherapy versus early combination) and IVIG dosing schedules are not standardised.
Whether prolonged remission-maintenance therapy prevents relapse better than careful tapering is unresolved.
mcq_angles: Antibody-defined subtypes and their distinguishing features.
Biopsy interpretation: necrosis with minimal inflammation.

page.mentor_intro: Immune-related adverse events are the price of unleashing T-cell immunity against cancer: any organ can be attacked, typically within weeks to months of checkpoint-inhibitor therapy, and the management grammar is now standardised by the ASCO guideline and the NCCN immunotherapy-toxicity guidelines. The core logic is immunosuppression graded to severity — hold the drug for moderate events, corticosteroids for significant events, infliximab or other steroid-sparing agents for steroid-refractory disease — with organ-specific exceptions (endocrinopathies replace rather than suppress, neurologic and cardiac events demand aggressive early treatment, and checkpoint re-challenge is individually weighed).

teaching_points.claim: irAEs can affect any organ system with characteristic patterns (colitis, pneumonitis, dermatitis, hypophysitis, thyroiditis, hepatitis, myocarditis); vigilance is required because presentations mimic infection, progression, and other toxicities.
Grading drives action: grade 1 often continues therapy with monitoring, grade 2 usually holds the drug and starts corticosteroids, grades 3–4 stop therapy and require high-dose immunosuppression.
Endocrinopathies (hypophysitis, thyroiditis, adrenalitis) are managed with hormone replacement rather than immunosuppression once the diagnosis is secure, with permanent deficits common.
High-mortality events — myocarditis and neurologic irAEs — warrant immediate high-dose steroids and multidisciplinary care; re-challenge after serious irAEs is generally avoided.

uncertainties: Whether biomarkers can predict irAE risk before checkpoint-inhibitor initiation is not clinically validated.
Optimal steroid-sparing sequencing for steroid-refractory irAEs varies by organ and lacks comparative trials.

page.mentor_intro: Immune thrombocytopenia is a diagnosis of exclusion made at any age, and modern management is built around two documents: the updated International Consensus Report and the ASH 2019 guidelines. Both shift thinking away from platelet-number reflexes toward bleeding-risk reasoning — adults with counts above 20–30 x10^9/L and no bleeding often need only observation, while treatment is warranted for bleeding, procedures, or lifestyle constraints. Corticosteroids with or without IVIG remain first line, and the guidelines explicitly resist over-treatment, favouring shorter steroid courses and shared decision-making for everything beyond.

teaching_points.claim: ITP diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes and pseudothrombocytopenia; the international consensus report standardises investigation including HIV, HCV, and Helicobacter pylori testing where appropriate.

ASH 2019 guidelines recommend observation alone for many asymptomatic adults with platelets above 20–30 x10^9/L, and short-course corticosteroids over prolonged courses or IVIG as first-line treatment when therapy is needed.

Second-line options — TPO receptor agonists, rituximab, splenectomy, fostamatinib — are selected by patient factors including durability goals, comorbidities, and surgical candidacy rather than a fixed sequence.
Emergency management of severe bleeding uses combined platelet transfusion, IVIG, and high-dose corticosteroids; thrombopoietin agonists are not emergency agents.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of second-line therapies (TPO-RAs versus rituximab versus splenectomy) lacks head-to-head trials.
Whether early TPO-RA use alters long-term natural history is unknown.

page.mentor_intro: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists changed the chronic-ITP landscape by stimulating platelet production rather than suppressing destruction: eltrombopag (oral, daily, food and chelation interactions) and romiplostim (weekly subcutaneous peptide) produce durable responses in most patients who fail first-line therapy, and a decade of use has clarified their real profile. They are not benign: arterial and venous thrombosis, paradoxical with a 'bleeding disease', is the signal that systematic review and cohort data quantify — risk concentrates with cardiovascular comorbidity, high normalised platelet counts, and portal-hypertension contexts. Dose is titrated to a safe platelet range, not to normalisation.

teaching_points.claim: TPO-RAs (eltrombopag, romiplostim) are second-line agents for persistent/chronic ITP that raise platelet counts through thrombopoietin-receptor stimulation of megakaryopoiesis, with response in a majority of patients.

Practical differences matter: eltrombopag is oral but requires separation from food and polyvalent-cation-containing medicines; romiplostim is administered weekly by injection — choice is individualised by adherence and preference.
Thrombosis is the principal serious risk: meta-analysis and observational cohorts show increased arterial and venous thrombotic events, modulated by age, comorbidity, and achieved platelet count.
Dosing targets a safe hemostatic platelet range (commonly 50 x10^9/L or above) rather than normalisation, balancing bleeding protection against thrombotic risk.

uncertainties: Whether thrombosis risk is drug-specific (eltrombopag versus romiplostim) or class-wide is unresolved.
Optimal duration and whether some patients can taper off TPO-RAs after sustained response is not established.

page.mentor_intro: Maintenance immunosuppression after solid-organ transplantation is a balancing act calibrated in milligrams and nanograms: too little invites rejection, too much delivers nephrotoxicity, infection, and malignancy. Tacrolimus — a calcineurin inhibitor with narrow therapeutic index — anchors nearly all modern regimens, combined with mycophenolate and tapered steroids; systematic-review evidence supports tacrolimus-based maintenance as the standard. The craft lies in the detail: trough-level monitoring against a steep concentration-response curve, CYP3A5 pharmacogenetics that explain much inter-patient variability, and long-term stewardship that weighs dose minimisation against the rising cardiovascular and metabolic burden of decades of therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Modern maintenance regimens centre on tacrolimus with mycophenolate and tapered corticosteroids; tacrolimus-based maintenance is supported by systematic-review evidence as the standard of care in kidney transplantation.
Tacrolimus has a narrow therapeutic window with nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity above range and rejection below; trough monitoring with dose titration is mandatory, especially early post-transplant.
Pharmacogenetics — CYP3A5 expresser status — substantially alters tacrolimus metabolism and dosing requirements, informing genotype-guided initial dosing in some centres.

Long-term management must reconcile competing harms: chronic calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity, cardiovascular and metabolic burden, infection, and malignancy risk against late rejection from over-minimisation.

uncertainties: Optimal long-term minimisation strategies (steroid withdrawal, CNI reduction with mTOR substitution) remain individualised with incomplete evidence.
Whether pharmacogenetic dosing improves hard graft outcomes versus trough-guided titration is not established.

page.mentor_intro: Inclisiran is the first siRNA to move lipid management from adherence-dependent daily pills to twice-yearly hepatocyte-directed dosing: it silences PCSK9 mRNA, lowering LDL-C by roughly 50% on top of statins — a similar magnitude to monoclonal PCSK9 antibodies but delivered in a way that solves the adherence problem that undermines chronic lipid therapy. The ORION programme established efficacy and a reassuring serious-adverse-event profile, and cardiovascular-outcome trials are maturing. Its practical appeal is healthcare-system as much as patient: administration by a clinician every six months converts a daily behaviour into a scheduled event.

teaching_points.claim: Inclisiran is a synthetic siRNA that silences hepatocyte PCSK9 production, lowering LDL-C by approximately 50% as monotherapy or on top of statins, with effects persisting between twice-yearly doses.
The twice-yearly maintenance dosing schedule (after initial and 3-month doses) addresses non-adherence, the dominant cause of suboptimal lipid control in practice.
Meta-analysis of the ORION trials found no significant increase in serious adverse events versus control, with injection-site reactions the commonest specific complaint.
Current positioning is adjunctive for patients not achieving LDL targets on maximally tolerated statins (with or without ezetimibe); cardiovascular-outcome trial evidence is still accumulating.

uncertainties: Hard cardiovascular-outcome benefit (versus the well-established LDL-C surrogate) is pending outcome-trial completion.

page.mentor_intro: Inclusion body myositis is the myopathy that refuses to behave: slowly progressive, asymmetric weakness — finger flexors and quadriceps characteristically — in older men, with rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates on biopsy, and a well-earned reputation for treatment resistance. It is frequently misdiagnosed as polymyositis and exposed only when immunosuppression fails. Modern understanding frames it as a degenerative process with inflammatory features, which explains why immunotherapies that work for other myosities disappoint here; management is therefore functional preservation, falls prevention, and honest prognostic counselling, with clinical-trial awareness the main therapeutic hope.

teaching_points.claim: IBM presents in older adults with slowly progressive, often asymmetric weakness with early finger-flexor and quadriceps involvement; falling and grip loss are characteristic functional clues.
Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and protein aggregates (including TDP-43 and p62); the degenerative-plus-inflammatory signature underlies treatment resistance.
Immunosuppression lacks robust efficacy in IBM — a key discriminator from polymyositis and dermatomyositis; misdiagnosis as treatment-refractory polymyositis should prompt re-evaluation for IBM.
Management centres on exercise and rehabilitation to preserve function, falls prevention, dysphagia surveillance, and enrolment into clinical trials; no disease-modifying therapy is established.

uncertainties: Whether targeted anti-inflammatory or anti-degenerative strategies can modify progression is untested at scale.
Optimal role of corticosteroids or IVIG in selected subsets (e.g. rapidly progressive or dysphagia-predominant) remains individualised.

The result, codified in the EULAR 2022 recommendations, is that rituximab is now preferred first-line induction for most new and relapsing patients, with cyclophosphamide retained for organ-threatening emergencies and cost-constrained settings. The nuance examiners love: rituximab's advantage is strongest at relapse and in PR3-ANCA disease, and glucocorticoid-sparing regimens (avacopan era) now accompany both arms.

teaching_points.claim: RAVE established rituximab as non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for remission induction in early severe GPA/MPA, with superiority in relapsing disease.
RITUXVAS confirmed non-inferiority of rituximab-based induction in severe AAV with renal involvement, cementing B-cell depletion as a standard induction option.

EULAR 2022 recommendations position rituximab as preferred induction for new and relapsing GPA/MPA, reserving cyclophosphamide for selected organ-threatening presentations and specific contraindications.
Relapse prediction guides intensity: PR3-ANCA positivity and prior relapse favour rituximab, which also serves as maintenance with repeat dosing.

uncertainties: Optimal glucocorticoid taper speed and the integrating role of C5a-receptor inhibition (avacopan) with either induction arm continue to evolve.

page.mentor_intro: Infections in pregnancy demand dual-patient thinking: the mother, the fetus, and the drugs that must be safe for both. Group B streptococcus is the organised success story — universal late-gestation screening with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for colonised mothers has slashed early-onset neonatal disease, with ACOG's Committee Opinion defining screening timing, risk-based alternatives, and prophylaxis regimens. Beyond GBS, the clinician must hold the less algorithmic territory: listeriosis and toxoplasmosis as foodborne and cat-associated risks managed by prevention and targeted testing, antiviral safety questions in influenza and herpes infections, and the recognition that sepsis remains a leading cause of maternal mortality with modified (pregnancy-appropriate) early-warning criteria.

teaching_points.claim: Universal antenatal GBS screening at 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin first-line) for colonised or high-risk mothers is the standard for preventing early-onset neonatal disease.

Approximately half of women colonised with GBS transmit to the newborn; intrapartum prophylaxis reduces early-onset disease transmission, with risk-based prophylaxis for untested women with obstetric risk factors.

Maternal sepsis is a leading cause of maternal mortality; major guidelines emphasise early recognition with pregnancy-adjusted warning scores, source control, and foetal surveillance alongside maternal resuscitation.

Prevention education remains central for listeriosis (food hygiene) and toxoplasmosis (cat-litter and undercooked-meat avoidance); serological testing and treatment decisions follow exposure-risk assessment.

uncertainties: Optimal management of penicillin-allergic GBS-colonised mothers (clindamycin resistance concerns) varies by region and testing availability.
Toxoplasmosis treatment regimens in pregnancy (spiramycin versus pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine timing) follow regional protocols with limited trial evidence.

page.mentor_intro: Infection after solid-organ transplantation is predictable by clock and immunosuppression intensity: the first month brings nosocomial and surgical complications, months one to six bring the opportunists — CMV above all, plus Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, and BK virus — and beyond six months, community-acquired infections dominate with immune-deficiency patterns in over-immunosuppressed patients. CMV is the single most consequential pathogen: direct disease (colitis, pneumonitis) and indirect effects (rejection, graft injury) are addressed by universal or targeted prophylaxis with valganciclovir and preemptive strategies guided by viral-load monitoring, with maribavir now available for refractory disease. PCP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is standard for the early period — one prescription that prevents the most preventable transplant death.

teaching_points.claim: The post-transplant infection timeline structures the differential: healthcare-associated infections in month one, opportunistic infections (CMV, PCP, moulds, BK) in months 1–6, and community-acquired infections thereafter.
CMV is the most common significant post-transplant infection; D+/R- serostatus defines highest risk, and direct (tissue-invasive) plus indirect (rejection-linked) effects both demand prevention.

Prevention strategies are prophylaxis (valganciclovir for high-risk recipients) versus preemptive therapy guided by quantitative PCR monitoring — both effective, selection depends on serostatus, organ, and logistics.
Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is standard for at least 6–12 months post-transplant; alternatives (atovaquone, dapsone, pentamidine) serve sulfa-allergic patients.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of CMV prophylaxis and the long-term value of extending beyond six months in high-risk recipients are debated.

page.mentor_intro: Infection prevention and control is the highest-yield low-technology discipline in medicine: healthcare-worker hands are the dominant transmission vehicle for hospital-acquired infection, and hand hygiene at the WHO five moments remains the single most effective intervention — systematic review confirms compliance reduces HAI, while behaviour-change literature shows multimodal programmes (education, feedback, cues, leadership) outperform posters alone. Above standard precautions, contact precautions (gowns, gloves, single rooms) for multidrug-resistant organisms are standard practice despite contested effectiveness data — the systematic-review evidence is conflicted, and the modern debate centres on targeted versus universal application, balancing transmission prevention against isolation's harms to patients and care processes.

teaching_points.claim: Hand hygiene is the cornerstone of standard precautions; systematic-review evidence links healthcare-worker hand-hygiene compliance with reduced hospital-acquired infection rates.

Multimodal interventions — education, performance feedback, reminders, environmental cues, and administrative support — improve and sustain hand-hygiene compliance better than single-strategy approaches.

Contact precautions (gown, gloves, single room) for MDRO-colonised patients are guideline-standard, but systematic-review evidence of their incremental effectiveness over standard precautions shows conflicting results.
Isolation carries measurable downsides — fewer clinician visits, adverse events, patient experience harm — informing the shift toward targeted precautions and universal gloving in endemic settings.

uncertainties: Whether contact precautions add transmission protection beyond good standard precautions and terminal cleaning is unresolved in endemic settings.
Optimal isolation discontinuation criteria (clearance cultures versus time-based) are not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: Biologic and targeted therapies have transformed immune-mediated disease, but each mechanism opens a specific infection door: TNF inhibitors reactivate latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B, B-cell depletion disarms long-term humoral immunity, JAK inhibitors carry herpes-zoster and opportunist signals, and IL-6 blockade masks fever and CRP — the inflammatory alarms that normally announce infection. The ESGICH consensus documents systematise the safety profile agent-by-agent, while the EULAR 2022 recommendations (built on systematic review) define the screening and prophylaxis grammar: latent-TB testing and HBV serology before starting, antiviral prophylaxis for HBV carriers, and PJP prophylaxis when compounded immunosuppression crosses defined thresholds.

teaching_points.claim: Screening before biologic initiation: latent-TB testing (IGRA/tuberculin) and HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc) are standard across drug classes, with reactivation risk drug- and regimen-dependent.

HBV reactivation in resolved or chronic carriers on B-cell-depleting or TNF therapy requires antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir/tenofovir) or intensified monitoring, per EULAR-informed risk stratification.

PJP prophylaxis is recommended when high-dose steroids combine with biologic immunosuppression crossing defined thresholds (e.g. prolonged ≥20–30 mg prednisone-equivalent with second immunosuppressant).

Drug-specific infection signatures matter clinically: TNF inhibition raises TB, HBV, and deep fungal risk; IL-6 blockade blunts fever/CRP responses to infection; JAK inhibitors carry zoster and opportunist signals.

uncertainties: Optimal PJP prophylaxis thresholds for newer agents (JAK inhibitors, IL-23 blockade) are extrapolated rather than trial-defined.
Whether HBV screening paradigms need updating for lower-risk agents is debated.

page.mentor_intro: Acute diarrhoea is one of the commonest presentations in any setting — and one where restraint is the evidence-based skill. Most adult infectious diarrhoea, traveller's included, is viral or self-limiting bacterial disease managed with rehydration alone; the art is identifying who needs stool testing, who needs antibiotics, and who needs admission. Inflammatory features (blood, mucus, fever, severe pain) predict bacterial aetiology and shape empiric choices, while the pretravel consultation adds prevention: food and water precautions, and standby antibiotics for high-risk itineraries. Norovirus remains the commonest overall cause — a diagnosis of clinical and infection-control consequence.

teaching_points.claim: Most acute diarrhoea in adults is self-limiting; oral rehydration is the foundation of therapy, with antibiotics reserved for suspected bacterial dysentery, severe disease, or specific risk factors.
Inflammatory features (bloody stool, fever, tenesmus, severe abdominal pain) distinguish dysentery from watery diarrhoea and drive stool-culture and empiric-antibiotic decisions.
Norovirus is the commonest cause of gastroenteritis overall; recognition matters for infection control and because antibiotics have no role.

Traveller's diarrhoea management combines rehydration, loperamide for non-bloody cases, and standby antibiotics (fluoroquinolone or azithromycin) for moderate-to-severe cases on high-risk itineraries.

page.mentor_intro: Where topic 931 covers the general management of diarrhoea, this topic is about the organism-level decision that catches clinicians out: whether to give antibiotics. Campylobacter and non-typhoidal Salmonella mostly need no antibiotics in the well adult; suspected Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli (STEC O157) is the dangerous exception in reverse — antibiotics increase haemolytic uraemic syndrome risk and must be avoided. Norovirus needs neither antibiotics nor testing in most settings, but strict infection control. The single most testable pearl: bloody diarrhoea plus exposure to undercooked beef equals no antibiotics, and HUS surveillance — the syndrome that defines thrombotic microangiopathy in this context.

teaching_points.claim: Antibiotics are indicated for severe suspected bacterial gastroenteritis, dysentery in specific groups, and confirmed treatable pathogens; most Campylobacter and non-typhoidal Salmonella infections in healthy adults resolve without them.

In suspected or confirmed STEC (E. coli O157) infection, antibiotics are contraindicated because they increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome; management is supportive with vigilant renal monitoring.

HUS is defined by the triad of non-immune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury from thrombotic microangiopathy; STEC is the dominant trigger and TTP the key differential within the TMA spectrum.
Norovirus, the commonest gastroenteritis cause, requires no antibiotics and no specific testing in sporadic adult cases; outbreak settings demand environmental disinfection and exclusion policies.

uncertainties: Whether antibiotics benefit bloody Campylobacter dysentery in otherwise healthy adults is debated; practice varies.
Optimal HUS management (hydration strategy, plasma exchange indications versus TTP) follows centre protocols rather than randomised evidence.

page.mentor_intro: Two numbers govern infective endocarditis treatment: the weeks of antibiotics and the timing of surgery. Duration is set by organism and valve — viridans streptococci on a native valve can be cured in two weeks with combination therapy, while staphylococci on prosthetic material demand six — and reviews of the ESC framework examine where shorter, equally effective courses can replace tradition. Surgery is lifesaving but high-risk: perioperative optimisation, the classic indications (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetations with embolic risk), and the modern operative challenges of extensive root destruction and device extraction define the contemporary craft.

teaching_points.claim: Antibiotic duration in IE is pathogen- and valve-specific: 2 weeks is possible for selected viridans-group streptococcal native-valve disease with suitable agents, while staphylococcal and prosthetic-valve infection typically requires 4-6 weeks.
Reviews of the ESC treatment framework examine strategies to treat more effectively — shorter total courses and early oral switch in stable, selected patients — without loss of cure rates.

Surgical indications remain heart failure from valvular dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent sepsis, prosthetic dehiscence), and embolism prevention for large/mobile vegetations, particularly with staphylococci.
