page.mentor_intro: The POET trial broke the oldest rule in endocarditis treatment: that cure demands six weeks of intravenous antibiotics. In stable, non-septic patients on effective IV therapy with susceptible organisms, switching to oral combination therapy was non-inferior — transforming an inpatient doctrine into an outpatient pathway. The modern literature formalises who qualifies: clinical stability, documented susceptibility, suitable oral-agent bioavailability, no uncontrolled foci or high-resistance organisms, and a reliable patient with follow-up. Not every endocarditis qualifies — but the default of 'IV until week six' is now a choice, not a law.

teaching_points.claim: Partial oral treatment (POET) is non-inferior to continued IV therapy in stable left-sided endocarditis caused by susceptible streptococci, enterococci, and S. aureus, after an initial effective IV period.
Eligibility for oral step-down demands clinical stability, organism susceptibility, high-bioavailability oral agents, absence of uncontrolled infection foci or abscess, and reliable follow-up.
Oral regimens typically use combination therapy (two agents with different mechanisms) to protect against resistance emergence given sub-therapeutic tissue levels risk.

Exclusions for oral switch include prosthetic-valve infection in the early post-operative period, uncontrolled sepsis, heart failure awaiting surgery, and organisms with reduced oral-susceptibility options.

uncertainties: Whether oral step-down applies to prosthetic-valve IE beyond selected low-risk cohorts is unresolved.
Optimal duration of the initial IV period before switching (2 versus 4 weeks) by organism remains centre-defined.

page.mentor_intro: The diagnostic spine of infective endocarditis is procedural discipline: at least three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before any antibiotics, followed by echocardiography — transthoracic first, transoesophageal when suspicion persists or prosthetic material is involved. The modified Duke criteria organise the result into definite, possible, and rejected, but their known weakness is sensitivity in the era of device infection and culture-negative disease, which is where advanced imaging earns its place. This topic is the instrument-focused view of the endocarditis cluster: get the cultures right, get the echo right, and the diagnosis usually declares itself.

teaching_points.claim: Blood-culture discipline: at least three sets from separate venepunctures over 12-24 hours before antibiotics, with cultures held for extended incubation when prior antibiotics were given.
Echocardiography follows a TTE-then-TEE logic: TEE is mandatory for prosthetic valves, persistent suspicion after negative TTE, and assessment of complications such as abscess and fistula.

The modified Duke criteria classify definite/possible/rejected endocarditis using major (positive echocardiogram, typical organism) and minor criteria; sensitivity limitations are increasingly recognised.

Surgical indications detected on imaging — heart failure from valve destruction, abscess/fistula formation, and persistent vegetations after emboli — convert the diagnostic pathway into an urgent surgical referral.

uncertainties: How to integrate PET/CT and cardiac CT into the Duke framework beyond prosthetic valves and devices is evolving.
Optimal echocardiographic vegetation-size threshold for surgery is informed by trial subgroup data rather than absolute rules.

page.mentor_intro: Empiric antibiotics in infective endocarditis are a narrowing problem: the 2015 AHA and ESC guidelines converge on organism-driven choices — antistaphylococcal cover for acute community or healthcare presentation, penicillin/ceftriaxone for subacute native-valve disease — while explicitly disagreeing in places that examiners probe. Two modern refinements: aminoglycoside synergism, long dogma for enterococcal and streptococcal IE, now carries documented nephrotoxicity without proven outcome benefit, and guidelines increasingly say goodbye; and enterococcal disease — increasingly ampicillin-resistant — forces regimen individualisation where bacteraemia and endocardia merge clinically.

teaching_points.claim: The 2015 AHA and ESC guidelines agree on organism-directed empiric therapy: cover S. aureus for acute presentations and healthcare-associated disease, and streptococcal cover with ceftriaxone/penicillin for subacute native-valve presentations pending cultures.

Enterococcal bacteraemia and endocarditis management requires source assessment, susceptibility-guided regimens (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone for susceptible strains, daptomycin or linezolid for resistant), and infectious-disease input.

page.mentor_intro: Inflammatory bowel disease — Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis — is managed at a genuinely modern pace: the 2025 British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines codify treat-to-target medicine with early biologic escalation, biomarker-guided monitoring, and an expanding small-molecule armamentarium. The core skill is no longer memorising drugs but running the disease: objective assessment (endoscopy, faecal calprotectin, CRP) rather than symptom guesswork, escalation before damage accumulates, and complication surveillance that changes with disease duration and extent. IBD is now a specialty where induction speed and monitoring discipline determine long-term outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: IBD management is treat-to-target: the BSG 2025 guidelines emphasise objective remission targets (mucosal healing, biomarker normalisation) with regular re-assessment rather than symptom-based adjustment.
Faecal calprotectin and CRP are the workhorse biomarkers for activity monitoring and relapse prediction, reducing but not replacing endoscopic assessment.

Therapy spans 5-ASA and steroids for UC, immunomodulators, biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab), and small molecules (JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators), selected by disease phenotype, severity, and prior response.

Complication surveillance — colorectal cancer screening by disease duration/extent in colitis, osteoporosis from repeated steroids, and vaccination before immunosuppression — is part of every IBD treatment plan.

uncertainties: Optimal first-line biologic selection (anti-TNF versus integrin versus IL-12/23) for individual phenotypes is partially answered by head-to-head data.
Whether biomarker-normalisation alone can substitute for scheduled endoscopy in sustained remission is being tested.

page.mentor_intro: Biologic therapy in IBD is a story of expanding options and sharpening precision. Five biologics are approved for ulcerative colitis with differing efficacy and positioning; after anti-TNF failure in Crohn's, indirect-comparison meta-analysis informs the vedolizumab-versus-ustekinumab choice that lacks a head-to-head trial; dual biologic therapy pushes the frontier for refractory disease at accepted infection-cost. And therapeutic drug monitoring has converted biologic prescribing from 'intensify and hope' to pharmacokinetic reasoning — low drug levels with antibodies point to switching class, low levels without antibodies to dose escalation. Modern IBD biologic care is applied pharmacology.

teaching_points.claim: Five biologics are approved for UC (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) with differing efficacy and positioning; selection weighs disease severity, extraintestinal manifestations, and patient factors.

After anti-TNF failure in Crohn's disease, meta-analytic indirect comparison supports ustekinumab and vedolizumab as effective next-line options, with selection informed by phenotype and safety profile.

Dual biologic therapy (anti-TNF plus vedolizumab or ustekinumab) is an emerging strategy for refractory IBD with encouraging short-term outcomes in systematic review, at the cost of increased infection risk.

Therapeutic drug monitoring distinguishes mechanistic loss of response: low drug levels with anti-drug antibodies indicate switching class; low levels without antibodies indicate intensification — applying this prevents inappropriate escalation.

uncertainties: Whether dual biologics offer durable remission beyond small series, and their long-term safety, is unknown.
Optimal TDM thresholds and proactive-versus-reactive monitoring strategies are not fully standardised.

page.mentor_intro: The idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are a heterogenous family unified by proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase but divided by skin, lung, antibody, and histology — and the modern classification (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, anti-synthetase syndrome, inclusion body myositis) directly drives treatment. Dermatomyositis brings its cancer-surveillance duty and characteristic rashes; anti-synthetase syndrome brings the mechanic's-hands, fever, and interstitial lung disease that can dominate the prognosis; IBM (topic 925) resists immunotherapy by its degenerative core. First-line treatment remains high-dose corticosteroids with early steroid-sparing agents, with myositis-specific antibodies now guiding both prognosis and escalation choices.

teaching_points.claim: Modern classification divides IIM into dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, anti-synthetase syndrome, and inclusion body myositis — categories with distinct treatment responses and prognoses.
Dermatomyositis carries a malignancy association warranting age-appropriate cancer screening at diagnosis; characteristic cutaneous signs (heliotrope, Gottron papules) complement proximal weakness.

Anti-synthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1 and others) presents with myositis, mechanic's hands, fever, Raynaud, and interstitial lung disease; ILD severity often dictates the prognosis and escalation intensity.

First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids with early addition of steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate, IVIG); myositis-specific antibodies increasingly inform prognosis and treatment selection.

page.mentor_intro: Most low back pain is mechanical and self-limiting; the clinician's job is to find the small fraction that is not. Red flags — cancer history, fever, weight loss, night pain, neurological deficit, bowel/bladder dysfunction — are the screening grammar, and guideline reviews show which flags are actually endorsed and with what strength. The sobering evidence: individual red flags have weak diagnostic accuracy, so clustering and judgment matter more than any single question. Inflammatory back pain suggests axial spondyloarthritis — age under 40-45, insidious onset, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, alternating buttock pain — where early MRI and rheumatology referral change outcomes, while MRI for uncomplicated mechanical pain correlates poorly with symptoms and invites overtreatment.

teaching_points.claim: Most low back pain is mechanical/nonspecific; red flags are the screening tool for serious pathology (malignancy, infection, fracture, cauda equina), and their presence — not pain severity — drives imaging and referral.

Guideline reviews show variable endorsement of red flags; individual flags have limited diagnostic accuracy in emergency-department cohorts, so clusters of findings and clinical context must guide decisions.

Inflammatory back pain (insidious onset before 40-45, morning stiffness >30-60 minutes, improvement with exercise not rest, alternating buttock pain, night waking) suggests axial spondyloarthritis and warrants inflammatory work-up and appropriate imaging.

MRI is indicated for red flags, suspected cauda equina, infection, or inflammatory disease — not for uncomplicated mechanical pain, where degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic people and correlate poorly with symptoms.

uncertainties: Optimal combinations and weighting of red flags for screening rules is not settled across guidelines.
When to refer possible axial spondyloarthritis with negative imaging (non-radiographic disease) follows expert frameworks rather than trial evidence.

page.mentor_intro: Antiviral treatment of influenza is a timing and selection problem. Oseltamivir remains the workhorse neuraminidase inhibitor, ideally started within 48 hours of symptom onset, with benefit extending beyond that window in severe or progressive disease; baloxavir added a single-dose polymerase-acid-inhibitor option. The 2024 network meta-analyses for WHO guidance rank the options separately for severe and nonsevere influenza — an important distinction because evidence and effect sizes differ by severity. Hospitalised and high-risk patients should be treated regardless of illness duration; the '48-hour rule' is a community outpatient rule, not a hospital one.

teaching_points.claim: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir oral, zanamivir inhaled, peramivir IV) and the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir are the available classes; oseltamivir is the standard for most patients.
Treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset maximises benefit in outpatient influenza; hospitalised, severe, or high-risk patients should be treated even beyond 48 hours.
Network meta-analysis for severe influenza supports oseltamivir-based regimens as the evidence-backed choice, with other classes positioned by severity and resistance patterns.
For nonsevere influenza, comparative effectiveness across agents is modest; single-dose baloxavir offers adherence advantages in selected patients.

uncertainties: Whether combination antiviral therapy adds benefit in severe influenza is untested adequately.
Baloxavir resistance (PA/I38 substitutions) and its clinical significance are evolving concerns.

page.mentor_intro: This topic pairs the two halves of influenza control: vaccination as prevention, and neuraminidase-inhibitor prophylaxis as the pharmacological bridge. Annual vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups — older adults, chronic disease, pregnancy, immunosuppression — and meta-analysis confirms effectiveness against laboratory-confirmed illness, though effectiveness varies by season, match, and group. Chemoprophylaxis with oseltamivir after exposure reduces symptomatic influenza in the unvaccinated and outbreak settings; it complements, never replaces, vaccination. The mature clinical skill is timing: vaccinate before the season, treat within 48 hours, and prophylax only where guidelines indicate.

teaching_points.claim: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups (age 65+, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, pregnancy, immunosuppression, healthcare workers); healthy-adult benefit is mainly work-loss reduction.

page.mentor_intro: SMART — single maintenance and reliever therapy — is the most important asthma strategy shift of the GINA era: one inhaler, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol, serves as daily preventer and as-needed reliever, guaranteeing an anti-inflammatory dose with every reliever use. Evidence shows fewer severe exacerbations than traditional separate SABA reliever strategies, and real-world network meta-analysis confirms the benefit in populations trial criteria exclude. Implementation demands patient education — the inhaler counts as both preventer and reliever — but converts asthma care from two-inhaler complexity to a single consistent message: treat symptoms early, and every treatment is treatment.

teaching_points.claim: SMART uses a single ICS-formoterol inhaler for daily maintenance and as-needed relief, embedding anti-inflammatory treatment in every reliever dose.
ICS-formoterol as controller-and-reliever is associated with significantly fewer severe asthma exacerbations than SABA-reliever-based regimens across severity strata.
Network meta-analysis of real-world populations (often trial-ineligible) confirms SMART's exacerbation benefit beyond RCT settings.

The as-needed-ICS principle generalises: anti-inflammatory reliever therapy (SMART or ICS-containing reliever variants) treats the underlying inflammation, not just bronchospasm — a conceptual break from SABA-only rescue.

page.mentor_intro: The inherited arrhythmia syndromes — long QT, Brugada, CPVT, ARVC — are rare conditions where a single missed diagnosis is a young sudden death, and a single over-diagnosis is a lifetime of restriction. Each has a signature trigger: exertion and emotion for long QT and CPVT, rest and fever for Brugada, competitive sport for ARVC. Diagnosis blends ECG patterns, exercise testing, drug challenge, and genetics — where modern panels increasingly identify pathogenic variants, though variants of uncertain significance complicate counselling. Management combines trigger avoidance, beta-blockade (long QT, CPVT), ICD decisions weighted by risk scores, and family cascade screening.

teaching_points.claim: Each syndrome has characteristic triggers — exertion/emotion in long QT and CPVT, rest/sleep/fever in Brugada, sustained exercise in ARVC — and trigger-specific history-taking drives diagnosis.

Diagnostic work-up combines ECG (including recovery-phase and high-lead recordings), exercise testing, ajmaline/flecainide challenge for Brugada, imaging for ARVC, and genetic testing with informed counselling.
Beta-blockade (preferably non-selective, e.g. nadolol/propranolol) is foundational for long QT and CPVT; ICDs are reserved for high-risk profiles given device-related harms in young patients.
Exercise recommendations are syndrome-specific and increasingly individualised; blanket sport bans are giving way to shared decisions weighing relative risk and psychological benefit.

uncertainties: Risk-stratification for ICD in Brugada and ARVC remains imprecise; programme-shock trade-offs in the young are actively debated.
Management of variants of uncertain significance and genotype-positive/phenotype-negative relatives follows expert consensus rather than trial evidence.

page.mentor_intro: The COURAGE-era question — should stable coronary disease get stents first or medicine first? — was substantially answered by ISCHEMIA: in stable patients without left-main disease, an initial invasive strategy did not reduce hard events compared with conservative management with optimal medical therapy, though symptom relief favoured revascularisation in angina-heavy patients. The clinical translation is a triage skill: left-main, severe proximal multivessel with impaired function, and refractory symptoms despite medical therapy point to the cath lab; everything else starts with optimal medical therapy — antiplatelets, statins, beta-blockade, risk-factor control — and escalates by symptoms, not by stenosis percentages alone.

teaching_points.claim: In stable coronary disease without left-main or equivalent anatomy, an initial conservative strategy with optimal medical therapy is event-equivalent to routine invasive management (ISCHEMIA-era evidence).
Revascularisation retains clear roles: left-main disease, proximal multivessel disease with reduced function, and symptom relief when angina persists despite medical therapy.

Optimal medical therapy is itself prognostic: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, blood-pressure and glycaemic control, beta-blockers for angina, and smoking cessation modify outcomes independent of revascularisation.
Symptom burden, not stenosis percentage alone, should drive escalation decisions in stable disease; ischaemia-guided selection refines who benefits from the cath lab.

uncertainties: Long-term (>10 year) outcomes of initial conservative versus invasive strategies are still accumulating.

page.mentor_intro: Inotropes buy time in shock at a price: increased myocardial oxygen demand, arrhythmias, and — in the dopamine tradition — harm shown in trials. The modern grammar: norepinephrine is the vasopressor backbone of cardiogenic shock (renin-angiotensin support with the least tachyarrhythmia), dobutamine adds inotropy when output remains inadequate, and levosimendan or milrinone offer phosphodiesterase/calcium-sensitising alternatives without catecholamine load. Epinephrine and dopamine are de-emphasised after outcome signals. Inotropes are a bridge — to revascularisation, recovery, or temporary mechanical support — not a destination; the toughest modern skill is recognising when they merely prolong dying.

teaching_points.claim: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock, providing peripheral vascular support with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine or epinephrine.

Dobutamine is the standard inotrope add-on for low cardiac output; its beta-agonism increases contractility at the cost of oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk, warranting ECG and filling-pressure monitoring.

Non-catecholamine options — levosimendan (calcium sensitiser, active metabolites) and milrinone (PDE-3 inhibitor) — suit catecholamine-resistant or beta-blocked patients but cause vasodilatation and hypotension.
Inotropes and vasopressors bridge to definitive therapy — revascularisation, recovery, or escalation to temporary mechanical circulatory support in refractory shock.

uncertainties: Whether levosimendan improves outcomes over dobutamine in cardiogenic shock remains unproven at trial level.
Optimal timing and patient selection for mechanical support escalation is centre-dependent and incompletely evidence-based.

page.mentor_intro: Fasting hypoglycaemia with endogenous hyperinsulinaemia is insulinoma until proven otherwise: the classic diagnostic triad (Whipple's) of symptoms with low glucose, relief with glucose, and — from the supervised 72-hour fast — inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin during hypoglycaemia. The C-peptide is the discriminator that splits the differential: endogenous hyperinsulinaemia (insulinoma, sulfonylurea use) versus exogenous insulin (C-peptide suppressed) and IGF-2-mediated hypoglycaemia. Definitive treatment is surgical resection after localisation — the majority are benign solitary adenomas — with medical bridging (diazoxide, frequent feeds) for the unresectable minority.

teaching_points.claim: The supervised 72-hour fast is the reference diagnostic test: symptomatic hypoglycaemia with inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin confirms endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycaemia.

C-peptide and insulin antibodies discriminate the causes: elevated C-peptide indicates insulinoma or sulfonylurea ingestion; suppressed C-peptide indicates exogenous insulin; insulin antibodies suggest autoimmune hypoglycaemia.
Sulfonylurea screen (blood or urine) is essential before attributing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia to insulinoma; the biochemical profiles overlap.
Treatment of choice is surgical resection of the localised lesion (most insulinomas are benign and solitary); preoperative localisation and intraoperative glucose monitoring guide the operation.

uncertainties: Localisation strategy for occult insulinomas (multiphasic CT, MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, selective arterial calcium stimulation) follows centre algorithms without comparative-trial evidence.
Management of malignant or metastatic insulinoma (diazoxide, everolimus, peptide-receptor therapy) is individualised.

page.mentor_intro: Insulin prescribing is applied pharmacokinetics: the basal insulins (glargine, detemir, degludec) provide flat, peakless coverage tuned by duration — degludec's ultra-long profile smoothing day-to-day variability — while prandial analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) peak fast and clear quickly to match meals. Premixed and co-formulated products trade flexibility for simplicity: fixed ratios suit predictable routines and limited self-management capacity, at the cost of adjustment granularity. Switching between types — the commonest real-world manoeuvre — requires attention to unit-for-unit conversion caveats, overlap timing, and hypoglycaemia vigilance in the transition window.

teaching_points.claim: Basal analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec) provide flat 24-hour-plus coverage; degludec's duration beyond 42 hours confers the lowest day-to-day glucose variability and some dosing-time flexibility.
Prandial analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) mimic physiologic meal peaks with rapid onset and short duration; they are dosed with meals and allow flexible carbohydrate matching.

Co-formulations such as insulin degludec/insulin aspart (70/30) combine basal stability with prandial coverage in a single injection — the two components retain their individual pharmacokinetic profiles.

Premixed insulins suit patients with regular meals and limited self-management capacity, but the fixed ratio prevents independent titration of basal versus prandial components — a key switching consideration.

uncertainties: Whether ultra-long basal analogues reduce severe hypoglycaemia enough to justify cost over glargine varies by population and setting.
Optimal conversion ratios when switching between basal analogues or to co-formulations are partly empiric.

page.mentor_intro: Insulin pump therapy — continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion — delivers basal-bolus physiology without injections, and its modern form is converging with continuous glucose monitoring into hybrid closed-loop systems that algorithmically adjust delivery. Candidate selection matters more than the hardware: motivated patients (or parents) able to count carbohydrates, troubleshoot occlusions, and manage the device unlock the benefit; system complexity without skills produces the same glycaemia with more failure modes. Sick-day rules complete the picture: illness, ketones, and pump interruption demand proactive sick-day insulin strategies and never omitting basal insulin — pump suspension plus illness is the classic route to DKA.

teaching_points.claim: CSII provides continuous basal infusion with bolus dosing for meals, enabling precise insulin delivery matched to lifestyle; systematic-review evidence supports glycaemic benefit over multiple daily injections in appropriate patients.

Hybrid closed-loop systems link CGM to algorithm-driven basal adjustment, reducing hypoglycaemia and improving time-in-range; systematic review and economic analysis support adoption in type 1 diabetes.
Patient selection is the rate-limiting step: carbohydrate-counting ability, device-competence, motivation, and support structure predict success better than any device feature.

Sick-day rules are safety-critical: never omit insulin during illness, monitor glucose and ketones frequently, have an injection backup plan for pump failure, and seek urgent care for vomiting with ketones.

uncertainties: Fully closed-loop (unannounced-meal) systems and their real-world performance are maturing.
Cost-effectiveness thresholds for hybrid closed-loop across health systems are still being established.

page.mentor_intro: UKPDS taught endocrinology its defining lesson: in type 2 diabetes, early intensive glycaemic control with sulphonylureas or insulin does more than lower glucose — it prevents microvascular complications, and its benefits persist for years after the trial ended (the 'legacy effect'). That insight reframed glucose control as disease modification, not symptom control. The modern nuance: glycaemic control remains central but now shares the stage with cardiovascular-risk-directed therapy (statins, BP control, and newer agents with proven CV benefit) — the UKPDS lesson is necessary, not sufficient.

teaching_points.claim: UKPDS established that intensive glycaemic control with sulphonylureas or insulin reduces microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy) in type 2 diabetes, with no excess cardiovascular harm.

The legacy effect describes durable long-term benefit from early intensive therapy observed years after trial completion — early glycaemic control 'banks' protection (UKPDS, and analogous findings in hypertension and lipids).

Sulphonylurea- and insulin-based intensification remain evidence-based for microvascular protection, though modern guidelines prioritise agents with cardiovascular benefit (GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors) for patients with established disease.
Glucose control sits within a hierarchy: glycaemia management is necessary but must be integrated with blood pressure, lipid, and weight management for maximal cardiovascular prevention.

uncertainties: Whether sulphonylureas retain a role versus newer agents in early intensive therapy is contested by cardiovascular-outcome data.
The durability of legacy effects with modern agents is untested at UKPDS timescales.

page.mentor_intro: High-yield ICU guidelines share a signature: they convert physiology into checklists that change outcomes. Ventilator care bundles — head-of-bed elevation, sedation breaks, spontaneous breathing trials, oral care, prophylaxis — reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia in meta-analysis, and implementation science shows the bundle matters less than the strategy that embeds it. The ESICM fluid therapy guideline restricts resuscitation fluids to balanced crystalloids as default and questions starches; the ERS/ATS NIV guideline defines which acute respiratory failure phenotypes (COPD exacerbation with acidosis, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema) benefit from noninvasive ventilation and which need intubation. teaching_points.claim: Ventilator-associated pneumonia care bundles reduce VAP incidence in meta-analysis; bundle elements (positioning, sedation interruption, oral care, prophylaxis) are the highest-yield preventive practice in the ventilated patient.

page.mentor_intro: Where topic 951 covers what intensive control can achieve, this topic covers what it can cost. The modern synthesis of intensive-versus-standard trials finds a consistent pattern: intensive lowering reduces microvascular events but its effect on macrovascular outcomes and mortality depends on context — with ACCORD's excess mortality in aggressively targeted patients as the cautionary counterweight. Regional meta-analysis adds the generalisability caveat: benefits and harms vary with baseline care quality. The clinical rule that emerges: intensive targets earn their risk in younger, healthier, recently diagnosed patients with support systems; they pay it out in the frail, the elderly, and the long-diagnosed.

teaching_points.claim: Systematic review of intensive versus conventional glucose targets confirms microvascular benefit while showing macrovascular and mortality effects are context-dependent rather than uniformly favourable.

The ACCORD-era lesson stands: aggressive intensification in higher-risk, longer-diagnosed patients increased mortality and severe hypoglycaemia — patient selection, not the number itself, drives safety.
Meta-analysis across regions shows intensive-versus-standard effects vary with baseline control quality, implying diminishing returns where baseline care is already good.

Severe hypoglycaemia is the central harm of intensification — it drives cardiovascular events, falls, and cognitive decline — and its risk must be weighed against microvascular benefit in every target decision.

uncertainties: Whether modern agents (GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i) change the risk-benefit of intensive targets independent of glycaemia is an active research area.
Optimal de-intensification criteria for older patients are guideline-inferred rather than trial-proven.

page.mentor_intro: The HbA1c number is now a shared decision, not an order: guidelines systematically individualise targets by life expectancy, comorbidity burden, hypoglycaemia risk, and patient preference. Younger, healthier patients aim for near-normal glycaemia (6.0-6.5%); healthy older adults relax modestly (7.0-7.5%); frailty, dementia, limited life expectancy, or severe hypoglycaemia history justify 8.0% or higher — where comfort and safety outrank the microvascular arithmetic. The systematic review of guideline recommendations shows this individualisation is now explicit and consistent across major societies; the craft is matching the target to the person, then matching the therapy's hypoglycaemia risk to the target.

teaching_points.claim: Major guidelines individualise HbA1c targets: approximately <6.5-7.0% for healthy younger patients, 7.0-7.5% for healthy older adults, and 8.0%+ for frail patients or limited life expectancy.
In older patients, intensive control's benefit-harm balance shifts: microvascular gains shrink while hypoglycaemia, falls, and treatment burden grow, driving relaxed targets with advancing frailty.
Guideline recommendations consistently frame targets around patient characteristics (life expectancy, comorbidity, hypoglycaemia risk, preference) rather than a single population number.

Therapy selection must match the target: agents with low hypoglycaemia risk (metformin, GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i, DPP-4i) support intensive targets safely; sulphonylureas and insulin require target relaxation or enhanced monitoring in vulnerable patients.

uncertainties: Exact HbA1c cut-offs by frailty category vary between guidelines; local protocols differ.
How to operationalise individualisation in busy clinics (frailty scoring uptake) is an implementation, not efficacy, question.

page.mentor_intro: The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' meta-analyses established the foundational rule of lipid medicine: cardiovascular benefit is proportional to the absolute LDL-C reduction, in every group studied — men and women, primary and secondary prevention — and there is no threshold below which benefit stops. Intensive lowering therefore means driving LDL as low as practically achievable with tolerated therapy. The modern implementation question: whether moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe matches high-intensity statin alone — meta-analytic evidence now suggests comparable LDL lowering with better tolerability, reshaping the escalation ladder.

Intensive LDL targets in very-high-risk ASCVD (e.g. <1.4 mmol/L or <55 mg/dL per ESC) operationalise the proportional-benefit rule with combination therapy as needed.
Tolerability drives adherence: switching to combination moderate-intensity therapy is preferable to statin discontinuation when high-intensity doses cause adverse effects.

uncertainties: Whether combination moderate-intensity therapy reduces hard cardiovascular outcomes identically to high-intensity monotherapy awaits dedicated outcome trials.
Optimal LDL floors and very-long-term safety of very low LDL remain reassuring but observational.

page.mentor_intro: Intermediate-risk (submassive) pulmonary embolism — haemodynamically stable but with RV dysfunction or troponin elevation — is the discipline's judgement call: anticoagulation alone has a low but real early mortality, while systemic thrombolysis prevents haemodynamic collapse but at a cost of major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage. PEITHO quantified the trade: thrombolysis averted deterioration but with roughly 2% intracranial bleeding. Meta-analyses frame the modern answer: anticoagulation for most, rescue thrombolysis for the 5-10% who deteriorate, and catheter-directed therapy as the evolving middle path — promising lower bleeding, still awaiting definitive outcome trials.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis of intermediate-risk PE shows thrombolysis reduces early clinical deterioration and recurrent PE compared with anticoagulation alone, at the cost of significantly more major bleeding.
The PEITHO-era trade-off defines practice: most intermediate-risk patients are managed with anticoagulation plus close monitoring, with rescue thrombolysis reserved for haemodynamic deterioration.
Network and pairwise meta-analyses position catheter-directed thrombolysis between systemic lysis and anticoagulation — lower bleeding than systemic lysis, but without definitive outcome superiority.
Risk markers (RV dysfunction on echo/CT, elevated troponin/BNP, PESI class) identify the intermediate-risk category but do not yet reliably identify who benefits from upfront reperfusion.

uncertainties: Whether catheter-directed therapy improves hard outcomes versus anticoagulation alone is the subject of ongoing trials.
Optimal selection of intermediate-high-risk patients ('the grey zone') for upfront reperfusion is unresolved.

page.mentor_intro: Intermittent haemodialysis works by the physics of diffusion and convection: blood and dialysate flow past a semipermeable membrane in counter-current, clearing small solutes in proportion to time, surface area, and concentration gradient. Adequacy is measured — Kt/V (clearance x time over volume) targeting around 1.2-1.4 per session thrice-weekly, supplemented by the uraemic-solute view that phosphate and middle molecules clear differently from urea. The modern refinement is individualisation: incremental regimens for residual renal function and session tolerance, recognising that the number is a guide, not a verdict. And the commonest session-level complication, intradialytic hypotension, reflects the fine balance between ultrafiltration demand and cardiovascular compensation.

teaching_points.claim: IHD adequacy is quantified by Kt/V (spKt/V target ≥1.2 per session, with minimum delivered dose-equivalent of 1.4 by single-pool measures), supplemented by assessment of phosphate, fluid, and middle-molecule clearance.

Uremic solute kinetics differ by size and protein-binding: small solutes like urea clear readily, while phosphate and larger 'middle molecules' need longer or more frequent sessions — the rationale for individualised prescriptions.
Incremental haemodialysis — starting with fewer/shorter sessions when residual kidney function remains — is supported as an individualised adequacy strategy rather than a fixed thrice-weekly default.

Intradialytic hypotension results from the interaction of ultrafiltration rate, refilling capacity, and autonomic/vascular compensation; it associates with adverse long-term outcomes and requires active prevention (dialysate temperature, UF profiling, sodium modelling, midodrine).

uncertainties: Whether higher session frequency (short daily) improves hard outcomes beyond adequacy numbers is debated.
Optimal incremental-dialysis protocols and their long-term safety are under study.

page.mentor_intro: The IHD-versus-CRRT debate has matured from ideology to physiology: meta-analyses show no mortality difference between modalities in critically ill AKI, so the choice rests on the patient's haemodynamic tolerance, metabolic burden, and practical constraints. CRRT offers slow, continuous solute and fluid removal — kinder to unstable circuits, better for severe catabolism and raised intracranial pressure, but resource-heavy and anticoagulation-hungry. IHD is efficient, available, and frees the patient between sessions, but tolerates less instability. Hybrid extended-daily dialysis splits the difference, and meta-analysis finds it comparable to CRRT — a legitimate middle path.

teaching_points.claim: No mortality difference between IHD and CRRT has been shown in meta-analyses of critically ill AKI; modality selection is therefore physiological and practical, not evidence-dictated.

CRRT is favoured for haemodynamic instability, severe fluid overload needing gentle removal, high catabolic states, and raised intracranial pressure; IHD suits stable patients and resource-constrained settings.
Extended daily (hybrid) dialysis shows comparable outcomes to CRRT in meta-analysis, offering slower clearance with intermittent logistics — a legitimate alternative where expertise exists.
Practical factors — anticoagulation needs, nursing ratio, vascular access, cost, and the ability to interrupt for procedures — legitimately shape modality choice alongside physiology.

uncertainties: Whether CRRT's haemodynamic gentleness translates to renal-recovery benefit is unproven.
Optimal modality-switching protocols during a single AKI episode are not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: Interstitial lung disease is an umbrella, not a diagnosis: the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, connective-tissue-disease-related ILD, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and drug-induced disease share radiological patterns but diverge in treatment and prognosis. The modern craft is pattern recognition followed by an aetiology hunt — exposures, autoimmunity, drugs — because the HRCT pattern organises everything: UIP suggests IPF after cause exclusion, while NSIP, organising pneumonia, and HP patterns point to specific treatable entities. Two contemporary frames matter: interstitial lung abnormalities on incidental CT, common and mostly indolent but a marker of future progression; and interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features, the research category for patients who fall between rheumatology and respiratory clinics.

teaching_points.claim: ILD requires a systematic aetiology work-up — exposures (hypersensitivity pneumonitis), connective tissue disease serology, drug history, and family history — because treatment is cause-specific.
HRCT patterns organise ILD diagnosis: UIP pattern strongly suggests IPF (after cause exclusion), while NSIP, organising pneumonia, and hypersensitivity patterns point to specific treatable entities.

The progressive-pulmonary-fibrosis concept unites fibrosing ILDs by trajectory rather than label: worsening symptoms, physiology, or imaging within a year on appropriate therapy triggers antifibrotic treatment (see topic 909).
Non-IPF ILDs with inflammatory phenotypes — CTD-ILD and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis — have immunomodulatory options (mycophenolate, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) that IPF lacks.

uncertainties: Surveillance intervals and treatment thresholds for ILAs are not standardised.
Whether IPAF should be treated as inflammatory or fibrotic disease (or both sequentially) is unresolved.

page.mentor_intro: Acute interstitial nephritis is the great mimic of AKI: an idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reaction arriving 7-10 days after exposure to the culprit — antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs the commonest — with a sterile pyuria, modest proteinuria, and often systemic allergic features. The diagnostic trap is that the classic triad (fever, rash, eosinophilia) is frequently absent; eosinophiluria has fallen from favour, and biopsy remains the reference standard when suspicion is high and improvement does not follow drug withdrawal. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis is its insidious counterpart: progressive fibrosis from persistent insults — including long-term PPI exposure, analgesics, or aristolochic acid — presenting with concentrating defects and slowly progressive CKD.

teaching_points.claim: Drug-induced AIN is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction appearing 7-10 days after culprit exposure; drugs account for the overwhelming majority of AIN cases, with antibiotics, PPIs, and NSAIDs the leading causes.

The classic allergic triad is frequently absent; diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion (AKI after a new drug, sterile pyuria, modest non-nephrotic proteinuria), and biopsy is the reference standard when suspicion persists.

First-line treatment is withdrawal of the culprit drug with corticosteroids for persistent or biopsy-severe disease; early steroid responsiveness is the rule and delayed treatment risks incomplete recovery.

Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis — from prolonged PPI use, analgesics, toxins, or previous AIN — presents with tubular dysfunction (concentrating defects, acidosis, salt wasting) and progressive CKD requiring culprit withdrawal and supportive care.

uncertainties: Optimal steroid dose, duration, and whether early biopsy-guided therapy improves renal recovery lacks randomised evidence.
The causal contribution of PPIs to CKD progression at population level remains debated despite consistent observational signals.

page.mentor_intro: The small bowel is the longest segment of the gut and the rarest site for cancer — but primary gastrointestinal lymphoma is the exception, the GI tract being the commonest extranodal site of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The subtypes each carry a signature: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma as the dominant aggressive form; MALT lymphoma linked to Helicobacter in the stomach; enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (now MEITL) as the feared complication of coeliac disease; and Burkitt-type disease in the immunocompromised. Presentation is non-specific — pain, obstruction, bleeding, weight loss — so the diagnostic route runs through CT enterography, capsule endoscopy, and deep biopsy, with specialised cross-sectional imaging for staging.

teaching_points.claim: The GI tract is the most common extranodal site of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, though primary GI lymphoma remains a minority of all NHL; small-bowel primaries are disproportionately lymphomatous among small-bowel malignancies.
Principal subtypes: DLBCL (dominant aggressive form), MALT (gastric, H. pylori-associated), enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (coeliac-linked), and immunodeficiency-associated lymphomas.
Diagnosis requires endoscopic or surgical deep biopsy with immunophenotyping; cross-sectional imaging (CT/PET) and bone-marrow assessment stage the disease.

Treatment is subtype- and stage-directed: H. pylori eradication for early gastric MALT, chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP-type) for DLBCL, and surgery reserved for complications (perforation, obstruction, bleeding) rather than routine therapy.

uncertainties: Optimal management of refractory/relapsed enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is unsatisfactory and individualised.
The role of surgery versus endoscopic management for small-bowel obstruction in lymphoma is case-based.

page.mentor_intro: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction is dysmotility masquerading as obstruction: coordinated propulsive activity fails without a mechanical blockage, producing recurrent distension, pain, vomiting, and malnutrition. Diagnosis is one of exclusion — imaging to rule out obstruction, then manometry, scintigraphy, and full-thickness biopsy when available to characterise the neuromuscular pathology. Secondary causes (scleroderma, amyloid, opioids, paraneoplastic) must be hunted. Management combines nutritional support, prokinetic trials, and small-bowel transplantation for intestinal failure; pyridostigmine's systematic-review evidence makes it a first-line pharmacological option.

teaching_points.claim: CIPO is a severe gastrointestinal dysmotility mimicking mechanical obstruction; diagnosis requires exclusion of mechanical causes followed by physiological testing (manometry, transit studies) and consideration of full-thickness biopsy.

Aetiology is primary (visceral myopathy or neuropathy) or secondary — scleroderma, amyloidosis, endocrine disease, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), paraneoplastic syndromes; identifying secondary causes redirects therapy.

Management is multimodal: dietary modification and enteral/parenteral nutrition, prokinetic agents (pyridostigmine supported by systematic review), treatment of secondary causes, and decompressive or transplant surgery for intestinal failure.
Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor enhancing cholinergic drive, has systematic-review support as a treatment option for CIPO directed at improving colonic and gut motility.

uncertainties: The evidence base for most prokinetics and novel agents (prucalopride, mosapride) in CIPO is small and heterogeneous.
Optimal timing and candidacy for intestinal transplantation in CIPO-related intestinal failure is individualised.

page.mentor_intro: Intestinal tuberculosis returns wherever tuberculosis returns: the ileocaecal region is its favoured site, and the challenge is twofold — diagnosing a disease whose presentation (chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, ileocaecal ulceration, strictures) is near-identical to Crohn's disease, and treating it with a regimen proven for pulmonary TB but applied to sites where drug penetration and duration questions persist. The diagnostic modernisation is molecular and endoscopic: tissue PCR, biopsy culture, and endoscopic-ultrasound guided sampling raise the yield over old serology. Mistaking Crohn's for TB commits patients to unnecessary immunosuppression; mistaking TB for Crohn's delays effective therapy — the differentiating review is the clinical lifeline.

teaching_points.claim: The ileocaecal region is the commonest site of intestinal TB; abdominal involvement accounts for about 11% of extra-pulmonary disease, with peritoneal and gastrointestinal forms predominating.

Diagnosis combines clinical-radiological suspicion with tissue confirmation: endoscopic biopsy for caseating granulomas, culture, and molecular (PCR) testing; peritoneal fluid analysis and ultrasound/CT-guided sampling assist in peritoneal disease.

The Crohn's-disease mimic is the central diagnostic trap; features favouring TB include pulmonary involvement, night sweats, ascites, patulous ileocaecal valve, and transverse ulcers, while longitudinal ulcers and perianal disease favour Crohn's.
Treatment follows standard anti-tubercular therapy (rifampicin-based multi-drug regimens); surgery is reserved for complications — obstruction, perforation, fistula, or bleeding.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of therapy for intestinal versus pulmonary TB, and the role of therapeutic trials, varies by guideline.
Diagnostic-test accuracy of individual modalities (PCR versus culture versus histology) varies with prevalence and technique.

page.mentor_intro: Intra-abdominal infection is a two-front war: source control and antimicrobials, with source control the non-negotiable first front — no antibiotic regimen rescues an uncontrolled leak. The principles are physical: drain the pus, control the leak, restore anatomy, often staged with damage-control surgery in the unstable. Antimicrobial therapy covers the polymicrobial flora of secondary peritonitis (enteric gram-negatives, anaerobes, enterococci) with a source-appropriate, narrowable regimen; observational ICU cohorts show outcomes are dominated by severity, source control adequacy, and resistance patterns rather than agent choice alone.

teaching_points.claim: Source control — drainage of infected collections, definitive control of contamination, and restoration of anatomy — is the foundation of intra-abdominal infection management; antibiotics cannot compensate for inadequate source control.

Secondary peritonitis is polymicrobial; empirical regimens must cover enteric gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, with anti-enterococcal cover for healthcare-associated and high-risk cases, then de-escalate on culture.
Large ICU cohorts show mortality is driven by severity at onset, anatomical disruption extent, and inadequate source control — reinforcing early intervention and reassessment.
Duration of therapy shortens dramatically with adequate source control: 4-7 days is supported for most controlled intra-abdominal infections, extending only for persistent foci or inadequate control.

uncertainties: Optimal duration (short versus standard) in specific sources (pancreatic, biliary) continues to evolve.
The role of routine enterococcal and antifungal cover in community-acquired peritonitis is debated.

page.mentor_intro: Two devices carry most of the short-term mechanical-circulatory-support load. The intra-aortic balloon pump is the elder: counterpulsation inflating in diastole augments coronary perfusion and deflating in systole offloads the ventricle — modest support, easy to insert, but with the weakest outcome evidence (IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in post-MI shock). The Impella transvalvular axial-flow pump provides far greater flows and true ventricular unloading, at the cost of vascular complications, haemolysis, and bleeding. Combined IABP-plus-Impella strategies appear in systematic review as an escalation option; complications surveillance — access-site, haemolysis, limb ischaemia — is the defining ICU management skill.

teaching_points.claim: IABP counterpulsation augments diastolic coronary perfusion and reduces afterload; it provides modest haemodynamic support but IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in post-MI cardiogenic shock.

Impella axial-flow pumps deliver higher flows with active ventricular unloading across the aortic valve; they suit higher-severity shock but carry vascular-access, bleeding, and haemolysis complications.
Combined IABP-plus-Impella support is described in systematic review as an escalation strategy for refractory cardiogenic shock, adding pulsatility and afterload reduction to axial-flow output.

ICU management centres on complications surveillance: access-site bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis (plasma-free haemoglobin monitoring), device position (echo surveillance), and anticoagulation titration.

uncertainties: Whether Impella-based strategies improve mortality in cardiogenic shock (versus IABP or medical therapy alone) awaits definitive trials.
Optimal anticoagulation intensity and device-weaning protocols are centre-specific.

page.mentor_intro: Intra-articular injections for osteoarthritis sit on contested evidence: guideline recommendations diverge by region and economics, and the placebo-controlled literature is humbling — intra-articular saline performs comparably to corticosteroid, PRP, and hyaluronic acid in hip-OA network meta-analysis, reminding clinicians that much of the injection benefit is contextual. teaching_points.claim: Clinical-practice-guideline systematic review shows divergent regional recommendations for IA corticosteroid, hyaluronic acid, and PRP in knee OA — reflecting evidence uncertainty and economic context rather than clear efficacy differences.

Placebo-controlled network meta-analysis in hip OA found intra-articular saline as effective as corticosteroid, PRP, and hyaluronic acid — a powerful demonstration of contextual and placebo effects in injection trials.

In knee-OA comparative meta-analysis, PRP, bone-marrow aspirate concentrate, and hyaluronic acid outperformed corticosteroids for symptom outcomes, though heterogeneity and commercial bias temper the conclusions.

AAOS guidance supports corticosteroid use for short-term knee-OA symptom relief while not recommending routine hyaluronic-acid injection; repeated steroid injections carry diminishing returns and theoretical cartilage-harm concerns.

uncertainties: Whether PRP's comparative benefit survives rigorous placebo-controlled standardised-protocol trials is unresolved.

page.mentor_intro: Two interventions dominate the first hours of intracerebral haemorrhage, and both are about stopping the bleed. Blood-pressure lowering — the INTERACT2/ATACH lineage refined to a target around 130-140 mmHg systolic, achieved smoothly and early — reduces haematoma expansion, the strongest modifiable predictor of outcome. Anticoagulant reversal is the second: warfarin reversed with PCC plus vitamin K, the DOACs with specific reversal agents (idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors), alongside platelet-transfusion caution — the PATCH lesson that indiscriminate platelet transfusion in antiplatelet-associated ICH may worsen outcome.

teaching_points.claim: Early, smooth systolic blood-pressure lowering to approximately 130-140 mmHg limits haematoma expansion, the strongest modifiable predictor of poor functional outcome.
Haematoma expansion is common within the first hours; blood-pressure variability and peaks are as important as the absolute achieved level — smooth control matters.

Anticoagulant reversal is urgent: vitamin K plus four-factor PCC for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors — with the agent's last-dose timing guiding urgency.
Platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH is not routine: the PATCH trial signal of harm without surgical indication cautions against indiscriminate transfusion.

uncertainties: How low to target systolic BP (intensive <130 versus 140-150) and the role of ultra-early aggressive lowering are refined but unsettled.
The ideal reversal strategy for factor-Xa inhibitor ICH when andexanet is unavailable follows PCC-based protocols.

page.mentor_intro: Acute ICH management beyond BP and reversal is a choreography of neuroprotection, surveillance, and escalation. The World Stroke Organization's synthesis of global guidelines provides the consensus frame: rapid CT, reversal of coagulopathy, BP control, and early neurosurgical assessment for cerebellar haemorrhage or deterioration — with inter-hospital transfer protocols for centres lacking neurosurgery. Raised intracranial pressure is managed with head positioning, osmotherapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol), and decompressive craniectomy for malignant MCA-pattern swelling; the cerebral-oedema guideline formalises selection and monitoring of these therapies. The through-line is organised systems — 'Code ICH' pathways compressing time-to-CT, time-to-reversal, and time-to-decision.

teaching_points.claim: Global stroke-guideline synthesis supports the core acute-ICH bundle: rapid neuroimaging, coagulopathy reversal, controlled BP lowering, structured observation, and early surgical assessment for cerebellar or deteriorating haemorrhage.

Intracranial-pressure management uses tiered escalation: head-of-bed elevation, sedation, osmotherapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol), CSF diversion where indicated, and decompressive craniectomy for refractory malignant swelling.
The cerebral-oedema guideline provides practical recommendations for selecting and monitoring osmotherapy and ICP-directed therapies in neurocritical care.
Cerebellar haemorrhage with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus is a surgical emergency for decompression and/or ventricular drainage — early recognition and transfer protocols determine outcome.

uncertainties: Whether ICP-monitoring-guided therapy improves functional outcome in ICH is unproven.
Optimal timing and selection for minimally-invasive haematoma evacuation remain under active trial evaluation.

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous-fluid prescribing is the commonest inpatient intervention and among the least audited: fluids are drugs with indications, contraindications, and toxicity — yet they are often prescribed 'to keep the vein open' by the most junior team member. The modern evidence frame is the four Ds and the harm narrative: the evidence base for exactly when and how much resuscitation fluid remains thin in multimorbid acute medicine, while harm accrues quietly through fluid accumulation — positive balance drives oedema, AKI, and delayed recovery even when each bolus looked reasonable. Perioperative and thoracic-surgery data anchor the optimisation principle: goal-directed, moderate-volume strategies beat both liberal flooding and dogmatic restriction.

teaching_points.claim: Fluid prescribing should follow drug-prescribing logic: assess need (hypovolaemia versus euvolaemia), choose fluid type deliberately (crystalloid default), define volume and endpoint, and review daily with a stop date.

The evidence base for exactly when and how much resuscitation fluid to give in acute medicine is limited; uncertainty should translate into small aliquots with reassessment rather than large empirical boluses.

Cumulative positive fluid balance is an independent harm driver: 'zero fluid accumulation' is the therapeutic goal in critical illness, with deresuscitation (fluid removal) a deliberate phase of care.
Perioperative evidence supports optimised, goal-directed moderate-fluid strategies over liberal administration; thoracic-surgery data show excess fluid drives respiratory complications.

uncertainties: Which dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, echo) best guide fluid responsiveness at the bedside remains practice-variable.
Optimal deresuscitation timing and triggers in established positive balance are not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: In acute decompensated heart failure with a low-output state — hypoperfusion, rising lactate, cool extremities despite adequate filling pressures — intravenous inotropes are the temporary scaffold while the cause is treated. Dobutamine, the beta-agonist workhorse, increases contractility and output at the price of tachyarrhythmia and myocardial oxygen demand; milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, adds vasodilation and lusitropy but accumulates in renal dysfunction and causes hypotension; levosimendan, the calcium-sensitising agent with active metabolites, offers catecholamine-independent inotropy suited to the beta-blocked patient. None improve hard outcomes — they are a bridge to recovery, device, or decision.

teaching_points.claim: Inotropes in acute heart failure are indicated for the hypoperfused low-output state (end-organ dysfunction with low cardiac output), not for routine decongestion; they are a bridge to definitive therapy.
Dobutamine provides inotropy and mild vasodilation through beta-agonism, with tachyarrhythmia and increased oxygen demand as principal limitations.

Milrinone offers inotropy plus vasodilation and is useful in pulmonary hypertension contexts, but causes hypotension and requires renal dose adjustment; levosimendan provides calcium-sensitising, catecholamine-independent inotropy with utility in beta-blocked patients.
No inotrope has improved survival in acute heart failure; therapy is temporising, with arrhythmia, ischaemia, and hypotension as the costs that must be monitored.

uncertainties: Whether levosimendan improves outcomes over dobutamine in specific phenotypes (beta-blocked, septic-cardiomyopathy) is unproven.
Optimal weaning sequences and inotrope-free intervals are protocolised rather than evidence-defined.
mcq_angles: Low-output-state recognition and inotrope indications.
Agent selection by phenotype and renal function.
The no-mortality-benefit principle.
Monitoring: arrhythmia, ischaemia, hypotension.

page.mentor_intro: Intrinsic acute kidney injury is parenchymal failure: the kidney itself is injured, whether by ischaemia-reperfusion (the ischaemic ATN of shock and sepsis), nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, cisplatin), pigment (rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis), or interstitial inflammation (drug AIN). It is distinguished from pre-renal azotaemia by its failure to respond to volume and by urinary sediment — muddy-brown casts the classic signature of ischaemic ATN. Management is largely supportive: haemodynamic optimisation without fluid overload, nephrotoxin withdrawal, dose adjustment, and the recognition that recovery, when it comes, takes weeks.

teaching_points.claim: AKI is defined by rising creatinine or falling urine output over hours to days; categorising the cause as pre-renal, intrinsic, or post-renal structures the diagnostic work-up.

Intrinsic AKI subtypes include ischaemic/toxic acute tubular necrosis, pigment nephropathy, and interstitial nephritis; the urinary sediment (muddy-brown granular casts in ATN) and failure to respond to volume help distinguish intrinsic from pre-renal disease.
Management is supportive: treat the cause, withdraw nephrotoxins, adjust drug doses, optimise haemodynamics while avoiding fluid overload, and institute RRT only for absolute indications.
Recovery from intrinsic AKI is slow — tubular regeneration takes weeks — and incomplete recovery leaves CKD, the rationale for nephrotoxin vigilance and follow-up.

uncertainties: No pharmacological therapy (dopamine, fenoldopam, mannitol) has improved outcomes in intrinsic AKI.
Biomarker-guided early differentiation of pre-renal from intrinsic AKI is promising but not practice-changing.
mcq_angles: Pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal categorisation.
Sediment and diagnostic clues by subtype.
Supportive management and nephrotoxin withdrawal.
Recovery timeline and CKD transition.

page.mentor_intro: Antifungal therapy for invasive aspergillosis is anchored by the ESCMID-ECMM-ERS guideline: voriconazole is first-line for most invasive disease, with isavuconazole an equal-alternative and liposomal amphotericin B the alternative when azoles fail or are contraindicated. The pharmacology makes or breaks outcomes: voriconazole's nonlinear kinetics, CYP2C19 genetic variability, and narrow therapeutic window demand therapeutic drug monitoring; posaconazole and itraconazole absorption is erratic without formulations optimised. Resistance surveillance — azole-resistant A. fumigatus — is now a first-order concern shaping empiric choices and requiring susceptibility data.

teaching_points.claim: Voriconazole is first-line therapy for invasive aspergillosis per ESCMID-ECMM-ERS guidance, with isavuconazole an equal alternative and liposomal amphotericin B reserved for intolerance, failure, or resistance.

Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for voriconazole (nonlinear kinetics, CYP2C19 variability, neurotoxicity at high levels) and recommended for posaconazole/itraconazole; trough-guided dosing improves exposure-target attainment.
Combination antifungal therapy (voriconazole plus an echinocandin) is considered in selected high-risk or refractory cases but lacks definitive outcome superiority.
Azole resistance in A. fumigatus is an escalating threat; susceptibility testing and local-resistance patterns should inform empiric and salvage therapy.

uncertainties: The optimal role and timing of combination antifungal therapy remains unresolved.
Whether newer agents (rezafungin, olorofim) displace current first-line therapy awaits comparative outcome data.

page.mentor_intro: Candidemia is the commonest invasive fungal disease in hospitals, and its management has two non-negotiables: an echinocandin is first-line empiric therapy (fluconazole reserved for stable, susceptible isolates), and central-line removal plus fundoscopic examination are part of the treatment, not adjuncts to it. The IDSA 2016 update codifies therapy by syndrome — candidemia, candidaemia with neutropenia, and organ-specific disease each have distinct durations and agents. The challenges review frames the modern threats: non-albicans species with reduced azole susceptibility, echninocandin resistance emerging in C. glabrata, and the difficulty of diagnosing deep-seated foci without candidemia.

teaching_points.claim: An echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) is recommended first-line empiric therapy for candidemia; fluconazole is an option for stable patients with susceptible isolates, and step-down to oral fluconazole follows susceptibility.
Source control is integral: central-venous-catheter removal where feasible, and ophthalmological examination to exclude endophthalmitis, are parts of standard candidemia management.
Non-albicans species (C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis) now dominate many series with reduced azole susceptibility, driving species-level therapy selection and susceptibility testing.
Treatment duration is typically 14 days from first negative blood culture for candidemia without metastatic foci; longer with endophthalmitis, osteoarticular, or other deep-seated disease.

uncertainties: The optimal role of rapid species-identification and resistance-marker testing in directing early therapy is evolving.
Management of persistent candidemia despite therapy (source exclusion, resistance, immune reconstitution) is individualised.

page.mentor_intro: In the immunocompromised host, invasive fungal infection is a race between diagnostic certainty and disease progression — and the modern strategy treats early. Serum and bronchoalveolar galactomannan, beta-D-glucan, and high-resolution CT's halo sign provide pre-culture evidence; the host's net state of immunosuppression (neutropenia duration, corticosteroid dose, transplant type) sets the pre-test probability. The ICU adds a diagnostic wrinkle: invasive aspergillosis now occurs in non-neutropenic patients — COPD on steroids, cirrhosis, post-influenza — where the classic frameworks fit poorly. Therapy is empiric-to-preemptive, anchored on voriconazole with the echinocandins and the newer agents filling defined niches.

Non-culture diagnostics — galactomannan (serum and BAL), beta-D-glucan, and CT halo/infarct patterns — enable earlier diagnosis and preemptive therapy before culture or histology.
Invasive aspergillosis increasingly affects non-neutropenic ICU patients (COPD on steroids, post-influenza, liver failure), challenging classical diagnostic frameworks built on neutropenia.
Voriconazole anchors therapy; echinocandins serve as first-line in selected candidiasis contexts and salvage in aspergillosis, with newer agents expanding the armamentarium.

page.mentor_intro: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is the clinical entity — fever, cough, pleuritic pain, and progressive infiltrates in an immunocompromised host — that the antifungal guidelines (topic 973) treat. Diagnosis is probabilistic, staged from possible to probable to proven on host factors, radiology, and mycology; the halo sign on early CT is the radiological signature, later giving way to the air-crescent of recovering lesions. Refractory disease — failure on adequate voriconazole — demands systematic reassessment: adherence and troughs first, resistance and imaging progression next, then salvage with a lipid amphotericin, isavuconazole, or combination approaches, with surgical resection considered for localised disease in fit patients.

teaching_points.claim: IPA diagnosis is staged (possible/probable/proven) combining host factors, radiological features (halo sign, infarct-shaped consolidation), and mycological evidence (galactomannan, culture, BAL microscopy).
Invasive aspergillosis increasingly involves non-fumigatus species with variable antifungal susceptibility; identification to species level and susceptibility testing inform management.

Refractory IPA management follows a sequence: confirm exposure (adherence, trough levels), assess resistance and progression, then salvage with alternative agents (liposomal amphotericin B, isavuconazole), combination therapy, or surgical resection for localised disease.

Severe respiratory infection in the immunocompromised demands systematic identification of the cause — invasive diagnostics (BAL with galactomannan, multiplex PCR) improve targeted therapy in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

uncertainties: The contribution of surgical resection to outcomes in localised IPA is based on case series rather than trials.
Optimal salvage-therapy sequencing for refractory disease is expert-guided.

page.mentor_intro: Suspected stable angina in women runs on a different track: women present later, with atypical and microvascular-predominant disease, and carry a higher burden of angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries — ANOCA/INOCA affecting nearly half of women undergoing angiography for suspected ischemia. The 2021 AHA/ACC chest-pain guideline explicitly addresses sex-specific pathways: functional testing and CT-angiography selection perform differently by sex, and a negative anatomical test does not end the work-up when microvascular disease is plausible. The modern skill is resisting both errors: dismissing women's chest pain as non-cardiac, and stop investigating once the epicardial arteries look clean.

teaching_points.claim: Women with suspected CAD present with atypical symptoms more often, develop more nonobstructive and microvascular disease, and are under-investigated relative to men — the 2021 AHA/ACC guideline codifies sex-specific diagnostic pathways.

ANOCA/INOCA — angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries — may affect nearly half of patients undergoing invasive angiography for suspected ischemia and encompasses coronary microvascular dysfunction and vasospasm.

Diagnostic-test performance differs by sex; CTA subgroup analysis informs appropriate-use, and a clean epicardial angiogram should prompt functional/microvascular assessment (stress imaging, CFR/IMR where available) rather than reassurance alone.
Investigating women requires the dual framework: exclude obstructive disease with appropriate testing, then actively pursue microvascular and vasospastic mechanisms when symptoms persist.

uncertainties: Optimal diagnostic thresholds and test-selection algorithms for women remain refined by ongoing sex-specific outcome data.
Treatment of confirmed microvascular angina improves symptoms more consistently than outcomes.

page.mentor_intro: Iron deficiency anaemia is a sign before it is a diagnosis: in men and postmenopausal women the mandate is finding the blood loss, which is gastrointestinal until proven otherwise. The BSG guideline structures the work-up — coeliac serology with the ferritin, faecal occult blood and endoscopic evaluation by risk, and small-bowel investigation when upper-and-lower endoscopy is negative — while ferritin thresholds (with transferrin saturation where inflammation blurs the picture) anchor the laboratory diagnosis. Treatment restores the deficit (oral first for most, intravenous when oral fails or urgency dictates — see topic 979) but never substitutes for finding the cause.

teaching_points.claim: In adults without inflammation, ferritin below 45 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency; ferritin 46-99 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 20% also confirms deficiency — inflammation raises ferritin and masks deficiency.

Men and postmenopausal women with IDA require gastrointestinal evaluation for occult blood loss; coeliac serology is part of the first-line work-up, and small-bowel investigation follows negative bidirectional endoscopy in ongoing-deficiency cases.
Oral iron is first-line for most stable patients; intravenous iron is reserved for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing losses exceeding oral absorption, or clinical urgency.
Response is monitored by reticulocyte haemoglobin and haemoglobin rise at 2-4 weeks; failure to respond prompts re-evaluation of adherence, absorption, continued loss, and the original diagnosis.

uncertainties: Optimal small-bowel-imaging pathways (capsule versus MR-enterography versus device-assisted enteroscopy) follow local expertise.
The threshold for IV-first strategies in non-urgent IDA is evolving (see topic 979).
mcq_angles: Ferritin/TSAT diagnostic thresholds and inflammation caveats.
GI work-up sequence by sex and risk.

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous iron has moved from rescue to routine: modern formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, iron derisomaltose, ferumoxytol) deliver a gram of iron in 15-60 minutes with reaction rates that no longer justify inpatient observation. The indications are intolerance or non-response to oral iron, malabsorption, ongoing losses outpacing oral absorption, and urgency — but increasingly also convenience and guaranteed delivery. The distinctive modern safety signal is hypophosphatemia: FCM's FGF-23-mediated phosphate wasting is common, usually transient and subclinical, but symptomatic cases with osteomalacia risk warrant monitoring in high-risk and repeated-dose patients.

teaching_points.claim: IV iron indications: oral intolerance or non-response, malabsorption (IBD, bariatric, coeliac), ongoing losses exceeding oral replacement, and clinical urgency; modern formulations allow rapid high-dose repletion in single or split doses.
Oral iron remains first-line for stable, tolerant patients; IV iron achieves faster and more complete repletion and is increasingly used first-line where speed, certainty, or tolerance favour it.

Ferric carboxymaltose is associated with hypophosphatemia through FGF-23-mediated renal phosphate wasting; systematic review quantifies the risk as frequent, usually transient, but occasionally symptomatic.

Hypophosphatemia risk is higher with repeated doses, low baseline phosphate, and certain formulations; monitoring phosphate in at-risk patients and choosing lower-risk formulations (e.g. derisomaltose) are practical mitigations.

uncertainties: Long-term clinical consequences of repeated FCM-associated hypophosphatemia (bone health) are incompletely defined.
Optimal IV-first versus oral-first strategies by phenotype and health-system cost are evolving.

page.mentor_intro: Blood-component modifications exist because transfusions can harm in specific hosts: irradiation prevents the rare and fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in recipients whose immune systems cannot clear donor lymphocytes — congenital immunodeficiency, haematologic malignancy, stem-cell transplant, directed donations from relatives, and HLA-matched platelets. Leukoreduction reduces febrile non-haemolytic reactions, CMV transmission risk, and HLA-alloimmunisation — near-universal in many systems. Washing removes plasma for the rare severe allergic or IgA-deficiency recipient. Each modification adds cost and delay, so the discipline is matching modification to indication, not applying them by default.

teaching_points.claim: Irradiated cellular components prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD), a rare but near-universally fatal complication in recipients who cannot reject donor lymphocytes.

Irradiation indications include congenital cellular immunodeficiency, haematologic malignancy and its treatment, haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, directed donations from blood relatives, and HLA-matched platelets.
Leukoreduction reduces febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions, CMV transmission risk, and HLA-alloimmunisation; many jurisdictions apply it universally while others target by indication.

Washed components (removing plasma) are reserved for severe allergic transfusion reactions and IgA-deficiency with anti-IgA — the modification must match a defined indication because each adds cost and delay.

uncertainties: Whether pathogen-reduction technology will consolidate or replace component-modification strategies is system-dependent.
The precise threshold of immunosuppression warranting irradiation in non-classical indications follows expert consensus.

The irradiation indication list.

page.mentor_intro: Irritable bowel syndrome affects roughly 4-10% of the population (estimates range up to 21% depending on criteria) and is defined by abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits rather than being a diagnosis of exclusion. Modern management is positive and subtype-directed: classify as IBS-C, IBS-D, or mixed, then step through diet and lifestyle measures, fibre and probiotics, targeted pharmacotherapy by subtype, and gut-directed psychological therapy for refractory symptoms. This page anchors the general strategy; the paired diet/microbiome topic (982) details dietary intervention.

teaching_points.claim: IBS is a positive clinical diagnosis based on symptom criteria (Rome IV): recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation with altered stool frequency or form; subtypes are IBS-C, IBS-D, and mixed.
Probiotics may benefit some IBS patients, but heterogeneity of species, strains, and endpoints has prevented specific strain-level recommendations.
Dietary therapy - soluble fibre and fermentable-carbohydrate restriction - is a first-line treatment pillar alongside lifestyle advice, chosen by subtype.
IBS substantially reduces quality of life and work productivity; practical stepwise treatment recommendations exist for generalists and specialists.

uncertainties: Which specific probiotic strains (if any) have reproducible efficacy in IBS subtypes remains unresolved.
The durability of dietary restriction beyond short symptom-control periods is uncertain.
